a-crust-for-the-phrenologists-electronic: A Crust for the Phrenologists, 1842. The vidimus. This book preserves that work. Writers of history may cite it later. The paper lasts as a quiet witness. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care.
a-phrenological-chart-giving-a-descripti: A Phrenological Chart, 1842. The mind's chart. This book preserves that chart. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it. The archive keeps the paper open to all.
addison-history-knights-templars-1842:
Charles G. Addison, an English lawyer of the Inner Temple, wrote this history of the Knights Templars in 1842. It was the first full history of the order in the English tongue. Addison knew the Temple Church in London, the order's old seat, at first hand.

He tells of the order's rise in the crusades, its wealth, and its famed rule of life. Then come the shock of its fall: the arrests, the trial, and the fire that ends its tale. Bound with it is the tale of the Temple Church and the Temple grounds in London.
arxiv-2512-00442:
Directly imaging an exoplanet means catching its faint light beside a blinding host star. Suvinay Goyal and co-authors analyze post-processing algorithms for exoplanet detection with a photonic lantern nuller in 2025. The nuller suppresses starlight so the planet can be characterized.

The team studies angular-differential post-processing, which uses the sky's rotation to separate planet signal from starlight residue. Detailed characterization of atmospheres and surface features is the long-term prize. Better algorithms squeeze more science from the same telescope time, which is precious on the large observatories that run these instruments. A photonic lantern routes starlight into fibers, where the nulling is performed. Angular differential imaging is a proven technique the authors adapt to this instrument.
arxiv-2512-00542:
False vacuum decay describes how a universe trapped in a metastable state might tunnel to a lower one. Luchang Jin and Joshua Swaim present a non-perturbative method for computing quantum tunneling rates in 2025. They use lattice Monte Carlo simulations in imaginary time.

To recover real-time results, the authors construct an implicit decay amplitude inspired by Fermi's golden rule, with spectral reconstruction. Non-perturbative lattice methods can reach regimes where analytic approximations fail. Tunneling rates matter from cosmology, where vacuum decay could end a universe, to condensed matter systems that mimic the same mathematics. Imaginary time is a standard trick that turns quantum tunneling into a statistical problem.
arxiv-2512-00642:
Protein function prediction tools are powerful black boxes, and their opacity slows adoption in drug discovery. Ananya Krishna, Valentina Simon, and Arjan Kohli demystify DeepFRI in 2025, weighing interpretability against accuracy. DeepFRI is a leading graph convolutional network tool for predicting protein function.

The authors evaluate it with explainability techniques including GradCAM, excitation backpropagation, and PGExplainer, plus adversarial robustness tests. Adoption of such methods depends on verifying their findings before targets are chosen. The study shows what explanation tools can and cannot certify about a model that proposes drug targets. Explainability techniques disagree with each other often enough that using several is prudent. Adversarial tests check whether the explanations survive deliberate attempts to fool them. For drug teams, the gain is a check they can run at low cost. If a tool's hot spots jump at small tricks, its claims should be read with care.
arxiv-2512-00742:
K Kevin Feng, Tae Soo Kim, Rock Yuren Pang, Faria Huq, Tal August, and Amy Zhang wrote a 2025 paper on governing AI agents. Their focus is the user interface. Agents that act on their own over long stretches can cause real harm if they go wrong. Most guardrail plans target the system under the hood, such as prompt filters or agent ID cards.

Feng and coauthors look instead at the interface, the screens and controls a person actually sees and touches. A well built interface could let users set limits, check actions, and step in early. Their work maps what interface design can add to agent safety.
arxiv-2512-01042:
Amartya Chakrabortty, Georges Griso, and Julia Orlik analyze a reinforced thin plate in a 2025 applied math paper. Their setting is linearized elasticity, the small-deformation theory of solid materials. The plate is thin and composite, with small rigid rectangular plates spread across it in a periodic mosaic pattern.

Between neighboring rigid plates sits an elastic beam, thinner than the spacing between plates. The authors homogenize the structure, deriving an effective model that captures the mosaic's overall behavior without tracking every tile. Effective models like this help engineers design stiff, light panels and predict how they bend under load.
arxiv-2512-01142:
Roman Geiko and Georgii Shuklin classify a family of quantum error-correcting codes in a 2025 paper. Stabilizer codes protect quantum information by spreading it across many qudits, units that hold more than two states. Translation-invariant codes repeat the same pattern across a lattice, which makes them natural for physical hardware.

The authors develop a framework for classifying invertible such codes, up to condensation and stabilization with simple codes. They generalize the Pauli groups of local unitaries for qudits on cubic lattices, then analyze stabilizer Hamiltonians built from them. A clean classification tells builders which codes are genuinely new.
arxiv-2512-01242:
Zirui Zhao, Boye Niu, David Hsu, and Wee Sun Lee study abstract visual composition in a 2025 paper. In abstract compositions, identity comes from how a few geometric primitives are arranged: their positions, symmetry, and topology. Texture and photorealistic detail barely matter, which makes these images a clean test of spatial understanding.

Their generative method combines adversarial training with Gumbel Monte Carlo tree search. The search explores arrangements of parts, while the adversarial critic judges plausibility. Abstract composition isolates the structural side of image generation that photo-trained models often fudge. Progress here could help design tools that think in shapes.
arxiv-2512-01342:
Chenting Wang and co-authors build base models for video that skip text labels. Most strong video models learn from text paired with clips. Those texts are often made by machines and miss much of the scene. Motion, shape, and cause can be lost.

Masked video modeling learns from the frames alone. It hides parts of a clip and learns to fill them in. That path has lagged text-based paths on broad tasks. The team built InternVideo-Next to close that gap. A strong text-free model would cut the cost of labels and learn more from raw film.
arxiv-2512-01642:
Carsten Denker and co-authors image a solar active region just before huge flares. Region NOAA 14274 made some of the strongest flares of the current solar cycle. Two giant flares hit on back-to-back days in November 2025. Catching the calm before such storms is rare.

Their mosaic uses speckle-restored images from the GREGOR telescope in Tenerife. The HiFI+ imager gives high spatial detail across a wide field. Sharp maps of the pre-flare state show where stress built up. That helps test what triggers the largest solar eruptions.
arxiv-2512-01742:
Jobst Ziebell studies Wetterich's equation for Radon measures on locally convex spaces. The equation drives flows of effective average actions in field theory. It is used widely to probe quantum field traits. Its domain and boundary terms need care in infinite dimensions.

Ziebell shows the equation holds for Radon measures under set conditions. The effective action's domain is the Lusin affine kernel of the measure. Firm ground in this generality supports functional renormalization work on complex field theories where standard spaces fail. Locally convex spaces cover most function spaces physics uses, so the result's scope reaches far past the toy cases that motivated it.
arxiv-2512-01942:
Maxwell's demon is a thought experiment about a being that measures tiny thermal motions and turns them into usable energy. Rémi Goerlich and four co-authors build a real, microscopic version in 2025: an information engine shaped like a compressible piston, filled with a warm colloidal suspension.

By measuring the random degrees of freedom of the particles inside, the engine extracts energy from a heat bath that is in equilibrium. This first paper of the series concentrates on the universal features the engine shows while in equilibrium. Such tabletop demons let physicists test the deep link between information and thermodynamics with real measurements.
arxiv-2512-02042:
Some equations ask for functions defined on the whole complex plane. The functions must meet a Fermat-like rule that mixes their rates of change with shifted copies of themselves. Sujoy Majumder and Debabrata Pramanik study such equations in 2025. They hunt for solutions that are not constant.

Fermat-type equations are known for having very few solutions. Often the point is to prove that none exist beyond the trivial ones. The authors work with functions of several complex inputs, and with shifts in all of them at once. Their results add to a long effort to map which such equations admit solutions worth the name.
arxiv-2512-02242:
Phase transitions, like water boiling, look like sudden jumps, but their roots may be pure geometry. Loris Di Cairano argues in 2025 that thermodynamics can be built from the intrinsic geometry of phase space alone, without assuming an ensemble of copies of the system.

In that formulation, the ensemble emerges from the geometry instead of being postulated. Phase transitions are encoded in the shape of the constant-energy surface, and entropy follows from a deterministic equation fed by curvature. A geometric account of entropy could unify how physicists think about systems as different as gases and magnets.
arxiv-2512-02342:
Gradient descent needs a step size, and the Polyak rule sets it adaptively from the gap to the best possible loss. Dimitris Oikonomou and Nicolas Loizou extend in 2025 the stochastic Polyak step size to non-smooth problems, safeguarding it so performance stays robust without unrealistic assumptions.

The stochastic version had earned a strong record on smooth problems, including deep network training, but non-smooth extensions leaned on interpolation assumptions or tiny gradients. A safeguarded variant aims to work where losses have kinks, as many real objectives do. Step-size rules that need no hand tuning save enormous effort across optimization practice.
arxiv-2512-02742:
Maddalena Bin and a large team track how a protein drifts through supercooled sugar alcohol mixtures. Cryopreservation by vitrification, turning a solution to glass, needs deep knowledge of how biological fluids move when very cold. The team follows ferritin, a large iron storing protein, in glycerol water mixtures.

X-ray photon correlation spectroscopy watches the motion at tiny scales. The results test the Stokes-Einstein relation, which links diffusion to viscosity and often fails in supercooled liquids. Knowing when that law breaks helps design preservation recipes that keep cells and tissues alive. Cold glass states guard cells well, but only if the mix is right, and this work shows one way to tell.
arxiv-2512-03042:
Michael Ofengenden and three co-authors benchmark AI agents that edit real PowerPoint files on command. Reliable editing of real slides under natural language instructions is the skill tested. Rendering slides as images or generating fresh decks misses the in place editing users actually need.

PPTArena covers one hundred decks, more than two thousand slides, and over eight hundred targeted edits. Edits span text, charts, tables, animations, and master level styles. A hard, realistic benchmark shows which agents office workers could trust with real presentations today. Real decks with real flaws are the test that counts. Toy decks hide the traps that real office work sets for a bot each day on the job.
arxiv-2512-03242:
A good pricing model should also mean fair losses for insurers. C. Evans Hedges links model quality to loss ratio in this 2025 work. The loss ratio compares what an insurer pays out to what it takes in.

Hedges derives a closed-form formula for that link. It connects the correlation between predicted and actual losses to the expected loss ratio. The author calls it the first such analytical relationship. Insurers could use it to judge a model's business value before putting it into pricing. Pricing teams could use the formula in model reviews required by regulators.
arxiv-2512-03342:
Hypergraphs link many items at once, and they need good fingerprints. Peter Brooksbank and Clara Chaplin introduce new invariants for them in this 2025 work. An invariant is a value that stays the same when a structure is relabeled.

To each linear transformation they attach a function that maps uniform hypergraphs to vector spaces. The family is parameterized, so users can tune it. Good invariants help tell structures apart in math and computer science. They may aid work in coding, design theory, and data analysis. Vector-space fingerprints can be computed fast, which helps search over large hypergraph sets.
arxiv-2512-03642:
Achinthya Bheemaguli, Penghao Xiao, and Gopalakrishnan Gautam benchmark five foundation machine-learned potentials at predicting how hard ions hop through battery materials. That hop barrier decides charging speed, and computing it properly with quantum methods is slow. Their 2025 study races the learned models against density functional references.

MACE-MP-0 and Orb-v3 posted the lowest barrier errors across diverse battery chemistries. Two models sorted good from bad ionic conductors correctly more than four times in five. Their intermediate pathway snapshots also beat standard interpolation as starting guesses for the expensive quantum refinement in most structures. Fast screening of candidate battery materials is the intended payoff.
arxiv-2512-04042:
Cool, swollen stars near the end of their lives often shine unevenly, and polarised light can expose that lopsidedness even when telescopes cannot resolve them. Richard Ignace and colleagues model such polarisation in a 2025 stellar astrophysics preprint. The complication is that interstellar dust between us and the star adds its own polarisation, which cannot always be subtracted away.

The team builds a hybrid spectrum combining Rayleigh scattering from the star, with its steep wavelength dependence, and a Serkowski-law contribution from interstellar dust. Mixing the two flattens the expected slope, so a naive reading would misjudge the star. When the star varies, shorter wavelengths swing most where Rayleigh scattering dominates. If the two polarisation directions sit at right angles, strange slopes appear over narrow ranges. The authors apply the thinking to the variable carbon star R Sculptoris.
arxiv-2601-07242:
Taekbeom Lee and co-authors posted a 2026 arXiv preprint. The preprint deals with HERE. It came out on arXiv in 2026 as a PAPERS preprint. The authors present HERE , an active 3D scene reconstruction framework based on neural radiance fields, enabling high-fidelity implicit mapping.

Our approach centers around an active learning strategy for camera trajectory generation. Driven by accurate identification of unseen regions, which supports efficient data acquisition and precise scene reconstruction. Readers in the field get a short, focused account of the problem and the steps the authors take.
arxiv-2601-07742:
Teddy Koker and coauthors fine-tune machine learned atomic models so they give better forecasts of vibrations. Many traits of a solid depend on higher slopes of the potential energy surface. Standard training matches energies, forces, and stresses. Even then, the authors note, flaws in curvature remain and spoil forecasts of vibrations. Their 2026 preprint introduces phonon fine-tuning for interatomic potentials.

Phonons are the basic units of vibration in a crystal lattice. Getting them right matters for heat transport, stability, and superconductivity estimates. A fine-tuning stage aimed at curvature can fix what plain training losses miss. The method promises better materials screening without retraining models from scratch. Those who model solids on computers are the readers. The work addresses a known gap between fast learned potentials and the fine properties engineers actually need. The aim is plain: fast models that still get the fine traits of a solid right.
arxiv-2601-08142:
Dilki Wijekoon, Amine Mezghani, and Ekram Hossain study joint communication and sensing with a smart surface. Their 2026 arXiv paper uses a reconfigurable intelligent surface, a panel that shapes radio waves. The setting is physically consistent and includes mutual coupling between surface elements.

Coupling appears when elements sit closer than one element spacing apart. Ignoring it can make designs look better on paper than in hardware. The system pairs the surface with a multiple-antenna base station. Both monostatic and bistatic radar setups are explored. Readers in wireless research get a more honest model of what surface-aided sensing can deliver.
arxiv-2601-08242: Xinlin Cao, Ahcene Ghandriche, and Mourad Sini study light scattering by clusters of hybrid dimers. Their 2026 arXiv paper treats time-harmonic electromagnetic scattering in three-dimensional space. Each dimer pairs a high-contrast dielectric nanoparticle with a moderately contrasting plasmonic one. The two particles sit a subwavelength distance apart. Clusters of such dimers could shape light in ways single particles cannot. The analysis supports design of nano-optical devices, sensors, and metasurfaces built from coupled particle pairs.
arxiv-2601-08442: Kanta Asakawa and co-authors measure spin polarization of rubidium atoms desorbed from a cobalt surface by light. Their 2026 arXiv paper uses a spin-polarized Co(110) surface and pulsed ultraviolet light. Desorption here runs through a non-thermal mechanism, not simple heating. The desorbed rubidium atoms came out spin polarized. That result implies spin transfer between the surface and the adsorbate during desorption. The effect could inform spin injection methods and surface science tools that read magnetic states with atomic probes.
arxiv-2601-08642: Martin Gairing, Adrian Vetta, and Zhanzhan Zhao model city investment as a neighborhood game. Their 2026 arXiv paper asks how cities should invest to improve welfare when residents respond strategically. The model builds on Schelling's bounded neighborhood model from game theory. Agents choose neighborhoods using concave, non-monotonic utility functions that reflect local population. The authors study how equilibria can be improved by city choices. The work speaks to urban policy, where a subsidy or amenity can shift sorting patterns in surprising ways.
arxiv-2601-08742:
Xin Quan and three co-authors test if large chat models can guess why a person acted. To work well with others, a model has to guess aims that are not said out loud. Old tests of logic in text do not check this skill. They ask what a text says, not what a person meant to do.

The team sets up tasks where a model must infer a hid aim from acts it can see. They call this skill attributional inference. It is key for groups of agents that must plan and talk. A reader who builds such groups gets a clear test of a weak spot. The work shows why plain text logic scores are not enough for team work.
arxiv-2601-08842:
Felipe Biava Cataneo tests if tuned chat models will take a hint from an out side guard. Safe AI plans use a guard tool to flag doubt in a model reply. The main model should then fix its path. Cataneo asks if a tuned model still lets a guard steer it in plain talk, or if it learns to shrug hints off.

He tests a small open model on grade school math tasks. Base forms of the model took hints well on direct tasks. The tuned form shows a pattern he calls context based push back. It takes hints in some frames and blocks them in others. A reader who builds guard stacks gets a warn. A guard is weak if the main model will not hear it.
arxiv-2601-09042:
Neelkamal Bhuyan, Debankur Mukherjee, and Adam Wierman tackle a learn task where each move can cost a vast, unknown fee. A learner picks a point each round and pays a hit cost. It also pays to move from its last point. In past work that move cost was capped. Here it is not, and the space is high in size, which breaks old plans.

Their method is called SCaLE. It is the first to prove a sub linear regret bound for this case, the authors say. Regret is the gap to the best fixed plan in hindsight. The proof needs no facts on the hit cost form. A reader in learn theory gets a plan for costly moves in the wild.
arxiv-2601-09142:
Shijian Ma, Yan Lin, and Yi Yang build a test set to catch firms that dodge hard asks on earn calls. On such calls, chiefs take asks from pros on sales and risks. A chief may dodge: talk round the ask, give a half reply, or shift theme. Those dodges can hide weak spots that share holders need to know.

Their set is called EvasionBench. It draws on a vast pool of call ask and reply pairs from a pro data base. A strict sieve keeps clear cases. Each case is tagged by dodge grade: direct, mid, or full dodge. A reader in finance gets a scale to grade dodge find tools, and to flag calls for a close read.
arxiv-2601-09342:
Ewelina Gajewska, Katarzyna Budzynska, and Jaroslaw Chudziak build a team of agents to spot hid hate speech. Hid hate does not use slur words. It hints, mocks by code, or praises harm in a sly way. A lone check tool oft misses it, since its sense rests on who is hit and what a group hears in the words.

Their team has a lead agent and group agents built on the fly. Each group agent speaks for a set of folk who may be the mark. The lead weighs their reads to make the call. A reader in net safety gets a check plan that hears a text as its marks hear it, not as a flat rule does.
arxiv-2601-09842:
Walid Maalej asks how to keep hundreds of programming students awake and engaged. His 2026 arXiv paper, bound for a software engineering education track at ICSE 2026, reflects on fun in large courses. Teaching coding basics in a big lecture is cheap and still common at universities.

The format bores students, who drift and disengage. It frustrates lecturers too, since interaction is hard to scale. The paper weighs playful methods that survive class sizes in the hundreds. Keeping student attention in the room is a precondition for any real learning at all.
arxiv-2601-09942:
Hunjun Shin, Hoonbae Moon, and Mohit Singhal ask how talks with a foe state shape talk at home. Views of a foe can limit what leaders can do in talks. Most past work used polls or mood scores. Those tools miss slow shifts in the story told about a foe.

The team tracks how North Korea is framed in US online talk. They look at high level summits as key events. The aim is to see if frames shift after such meets. They also ask if shifts last or fade fast. A frame that lasts can change the room leaders have to act.
arxiv-2601-10142:
Ruiran Su, Janet Pierrehumbert, and Markus Leippold track how money news talks about climate. Such news shapes vast sums in green funds. Yet talk in this elite field is not well mapped. The team reads two decades of Dow Jones news text.

They use large language models to pull three facts from each piece. Who speaks is the actor. How the theme is cast is the frame. What claims are made are the arguments. This actor frame argument chain lets them track shifts over time. It shows whose voice rose and which claims won ground in each era.
arxiv-2601-10242:
Guanxu Chen, Dongrui Liu, and Jing Shao ask if looped models can link inner sense to words. A model may hold a fact in its inner state. Yet its words may fail to state that fact. That gap is a known flaw. Looped models run the same layers again and again.

Each loop adds depth at no new weight cost. The team ask if loops act as a form of self look. A model could check its own state as it loops. They test this claim on set tasks. The work probes when loops help a model say what it knows.
arxiv-2601-10442:
Arwed Schütz, Lars Nolle, and Tamara Bechtold shrink finite element models with a physics led net. Finite element tools are a base of design work. But a full model is too slow for control or whole rig work. A shrunk model must run fast and stay true.

Shrink steps for curved laws need a next step named hyperreduction. The team use a net with physics terms built in. It is trained with a strong rule that checks first and second slopes. The net needs no mesh data from the trade tool. It learns from data alone, which keeps it of use with closed tools.
arxiv-2601-10542:
Kunal Dey and Reihaneh Safavi-Naini join two tools: mixed encryption and certified deletion. Certified deletion lets a user store data with a host. At a set time, the user can ask for a wipe. The host must prove the data is gone for good. Class tools can not do this. Quantum data can.

The team work in a preprocessing form. Some work is done up front, before the data is set. Their build adds mixed encryption to the wipe proof. Mixed means part class and part quantum. The aim is a store that can prove a wipe on call.
arxiv-2601-10642:
K. I. Smirnova and D. S. Wiebe compare two catalogs of HII regions in the galaxy NGC 628. HII regions are clouds of glowing gas around young, hot stars. They mark where stars are being born. The Kongiu and Groves catalogs list these regions in the same galaxy, but not in the same way.

The authors compare the traits of the interstellar medium drawn from each catalog. They look at star-forming regions and compare light fluxes across bands, including ranges near seven microns. Where the catalogs agree, values can be trusted; where they differ, users learn the limits. The study helps astronomers who mine catalog data for star formation work.
arxiv-2601-10742:
Amélie Gruel, Pierre Lewden, Adrien F. Vincent, and Sylvain Saïghi work on low-energy vision with event cameras. Neuromorphic vision records change, not full frames. It pairs well with spiking neural networks, the brain-like models that fire in pulses. The match brings gains in energy, latency, and memory for moving scenes.

Even so, cutting energy use further is a live challenge, above all for embedded devices. The authors present line-based preprocessing of event data as a step toward leaner pipelines. Preprocessing shapes what the network must handle at all. Their work targets cameras on drones, wearables, and sensors that must see clearly on a tiny power budget.
arxiv-2601-10842:
Abbas Dohadwala, Bryan Flores-Silva, Alicia Orozco-Moya, and Zoe Siegelnickel compute Betti numbers for powers of binomial edge ideals. Such an ideal is built from a graph, pairing variables along its edges. Its powers grow in algebraic complexity. The graded Betti numbers record the shape of the ideal's free resolution, a key algebraic portrait.

The authors give a closed formula for the Betti numbers in the linear strands of all powers. The graphs covered are closed graphs with no induced K4, the complete graph on four vertices. Closed formulas are prized in commutative algebra: they turn case-by-case computation into one clean rule. The result links graph structure to algebraic data in exact form.
arxiv-2601-10942:
Zitong Zhou, Matteo Paltenghi, Miryung Kim, and Michael Pradel present Change And Cover, a tool for the last mile of regression testing. Software changes arrive as pull requests. Testing the changed code is critical, yet even rich test suites leave some changed lines untested. That leftover gap is where regressions slip through.

The tool augments tests at the pull request stage, aiming at the exact code a change touches. Last-mile focus matters: broad suites waste effort on untouched code while missing the risky lines. Automated test generation for fresh changes could cut review burden and catch bugs before merge. The work targets teams that ship code daily and fear the one line no test watched.
arxiv-2601-11042:
Chi Zhang and co-authors study the collapse that hits large language models under sequential knowledge editing. Editing updates a model's facts one after another. After many edits, the model's general abilities can fall apart. Parameter-modifying edits are the riskiest kind. Past fixes lean on heuristic limits to how far parameters may move.

The authors characterize the collapse through spectral signatures, patterns in the model's weight matrices. A spectral view may show why edits pile up damage. It could also yield an early warning and a cleaner fix than heuristics. The work serves teams that must keep deployed models current without slowly breaking them.
arxiv-2601-11142:
Joris Koefler, Dmitrii Pavlov, and Rainer Sinn write on pure math in this 2026 preprint. Their topic sits in a young field called Positive Geometry. A key claim in that field says that amplituhedra are positive shapes. The claim draws strength from links to particle physics.

Forms tied to these shapes can give scattering amplitudes, the core numbers of particle theory. Brown and Dupont built a bridge for this work not long ago. Their bridge uses mixed Hodge theory, a deep part of modern math. It links the key forms to de Rham cohomology. Koefler and his coauthors build pairs of shapes with positive genus from that base.
arxiv-2601-11242:
Michael Sachs, Erin Gabriel, Robin Evans, and Arvid Sjolander study hidden variable models. Their 2026 preprint asks what such models force on seen data. A hidden variable is one the study can never observe. Graphs with hidden nodes are common in causal work.

Such graphs can force more than simple independence facts. The forced limits on seen data can be complex in form. Those limits can test parts of the model itself. Parts that looked untestable gain a test through the seen limits. The limits can also guide how data are used in fits. That guidance can make estimates sharper and more efficient. The work gives ways to derive the full set of such limits.
arxiv-2601-11942:
Qingyu Meng and Yangshuai Wang build a hybrid quantum-classical method for regression that is made to train well. Quantum neural networks draw much interest for science tasks. In regression, they often train poorly due to noisy gradients and ill-shaped loss fields.

Their frame uses geometric preconditioning, which reshapes the training steps. It also uses a staged curriculum, so tasks grow in steps. Both steps aim to ease the blocks that stall training. A more trainable quantum regressor could aid fits in physics and chemistry.  Both steps aim at a model that learns in a smooth way.
arxiv-2601-12042:
Xiaomei Zhang, Zhaoxi Zhang, Leo Yu Zhang, and their co-authors warn of a security gap in fast vision-language models. Such models shrink image tokens to run faster. That helps use in tight, low-latency settings. Most work so far checks speed and skill, not safety.

Token shrinking could open new attack paths or hide key proof. Their study maps those risks for the first time in depth. The title frames the point as less is more, until it breaks. Teams that shrink tokens need safety tests as well as speed tests.
arxiv-2601-12642:
Anahita Mobaseri and seven co authors study what happens when a drop of cornstarch and water hits a surface. Such mixtures are a premier example of shear thickening fluids. They flow like liquid until stressed, then suddenly act almost solid. The team combine high speed photography with direct force measurements.

They vary impact conditions across a wide range in their tests. The study identifies three distinct impact regimes. The title names the interplay that governs the behavior: inertia versus dilatancy. Dilatancy is the tendency of the packed grains to expand under shear. Knowing the regimes helps predict splashes, armor response, and industrial flows of such fluids.
arxiv-2601-13142:
Zhantao Ma, Quanfeng Lu, and co-authors lay ground work for agents that run a TV by remote. Big vision language models show skill at device control. Most past work used point and click acts, as on a phone or a desk screen. Day to day TV use, though, runs on a remote with a few keys.

The team built TVWorld to fill that gap. It is an off line graph form of real TV menus. Agents can be tested in it with no live set and in a way that can be rerun. For teams that build home agents, the set gives a fair yard stick for a mode of use that past sets skipped.
arxiv-2601-13342:
Anxhela Maloku, Alexandra Klymenko, Stephen Meisenbacher, and Florian Matthes put privacy where users meet the screen. In human computer work, privacy is a core care and is tied straight to how screens and flows are designed. A poor flow can leak data no back end rule can save.

The team sorts what past work says on privacy in screen design. They also ran fifteen semi structured talks with experts who do the work. From both, they draw the key picks and forces that shape if privacy is built in or bolted on. For design teams, the piece turns a vague care into picks they can act on at the draft desk.
arxiv-2601-14042:
Jiaze Li and a large team tackle a drift problem in federated learning in 2026. Federated learning trains one model across many clients who share parameters, not data. In the non-iid setting, each client's data differs in mix. The global model then suffers client drift, where local updates pull it in clashing directions.

Drift can seriously affect the final performance of the model. Their Federated Balanced Learning aims to keep local training in balance. Balanced updates could keep the shared model true to all clients. That matters for phones, hospitals, and banks that learn together in private.
arxiv-2601-14242:
Bertie Vidgen and a large team at Mercor built APEX-Agents, a test for AI agents, and report it in this 2026 paper. The test asks if an agent can do long jobs that cross many apps. The jobs were made by experts in three fields. They come from investment banking, management consulting, and corporate law.

Agents must work in real-like office settings, with files and tools at hand. Each job takes many steps, not one quick reply. The team ran eight agents through the test for a ranked board. They scored each agent by Pass@1, the share of jobs done right on the first try.
arxiv-2601-14742:
Ami Pandat, Kanyala Muvva, Punna Rajasekhar, Gopika Vinod, and Rohit Shukla build a drone dataset in this 2026 paper. Reliable drone detection is challenging for three reasons. Annotated real-world data are limited. Drones vary hugely in appearance. Visually similar distractors, such as birds, confuse detectors.

The team introduces SimD3, a large-scale, high-fidelity synthetic dataset for robust drone detection in complex aerial environments. Synthetic means the images are rendered, not photographed, so labels come free and exact. The dataset models payloads drones carry and bird distractors explicitly. Readers get training data for detectors that must tell a drone from a bird at a distance.
arxiv-2601-14842:
Jan Eyll, Jonas Fritsch, and Kai Zehmisch study shapes in contact geometry, a branch of math close to the study of motion. Their 2026 arXiv paper works in the standard Darboux space, a model space with a set contact form. The form they use is symmetric around a center ray.

The team looks at maps that keep the contact structure and fix the rim of a domain. They sort the domains that are straight in the vertical sense and round like a ball. Two such domains count as the same only under strict rules.
arxiv-2601-15042:
Andrea Protani, Riccardo Taiello, and co-authors locate brain tumors without pooling patient scans. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with a hard fact of medical AI. Models need large, varied datasets, but scans sit locked in separate hospitals under privacy rules.

The team builds a federated learning framework instead. Each site trains on its own scans, and only model updates travel. Their design joins a transformer with a graph neural network. It also explains itself at the level of imaging modality, so users can see which scan type drove each single call.
arxiv-2601-15142:
Ji-Shun Lian, Jia-Xuan Li, and co-authors study the brightest kind of blazar, a galaxy with a jet aimed near Earth. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with extreme synchrotron blazars. Their light peaks once at very high frequencies and again beyond a tera-electronvolt.

Such sources make ideal labs for studying how jets speed up particles and emit radiation. The authors examine the properties of the gamma-ray emission in these blazars. They also weigh what physical origins could explain it. The work bears on how relativistic jets shine at the very highest energies seen.
arxiv-2601-15342:
Jingxu Wu, Chenjia Li, and Jie Shi map a phase change in a dark copy of the strong force. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with dark QCD, a hidden twin of quantum chromodynamics. They study its chiral transition, where the vacuum's structure shifts.

The Polyakov loop part of the theory keeps a clear threefold structure. It couples to the chiral order parameter in one effective theory. The authors chart the landscape of uniform vacuum states. They find a window of metastability, bounded by points where a state loses stability. Metastable bubbles of the other phase sit at the heart of the story.
arxiv-2601-15842:
Gianluca Esposito, Simone Cepollaro, Luigi Cappiello, and Alioscia Hamma study quantum resources in gauge theories in a 2026 arXiv paper. Simulating quantum field theories is among the hardest tasks in particle physics. Classical computers generally fail on strongly coupled theories like QCD. Quantum computers may succeed where classical ones cannot. Lattice gauge theories are the standard discrete form of these theories. The authors study their magic.

Magic is a technical resource that marks quantum advantage. Classical simulation stays feasible when magic is low in the right sense. Mapping where magic sits in lattice gauge theories guides simulator design. It tells builders which parts truly need quantum hardware. For the quantum simulation program, such maps are strategic.
arxiv-2601-16042:
Nicola Spaldin calls for a fresh theory of how solids gain a twist. Her 2026 preprint draws on the known theory of charge shift in solids. That older theory gave a strict sense to the charge shift of a crystal. It also gave codes a clear way to work the value out. The shift theory changed how teams think of charged solids.

Spaldin argues that twist in a solid needs the same strict base. A clear sense of twist would let codes work it out with care. It would also link twist to traits that labs can test. The call sets a goal for the field to aim at. New work on chiral solids could then rest on firm ground.
arxiv-2601-16142:
Paolo Baldan and three coauthors work on fixed points of learned maps. Their 2026 preprint deals with systems that carry number based sense. The key task is to find the least fixed point of a map. Here the maps are not known in full. They can only be learned in rough form from data or tests.

The team joins rough fixed point steps with game maths. Games with chance moves give a frame to bound the true point. Bounds tell users how far a rough point may sit from truth. That care counts when learned maps drive real systems. The work links rough sums to firm game bounds.
arxiv-2601-16242:
Yaqubi and Mattila give a scale free way to model bendy robot arms with screw maths. Their 2026 preprint deals with arms made of many bendy links in a row. Each link bends in full 3D space and needs growth maths. Past models oft must be rebuilt for each arm length. A scale free build would serve arms of any link count.

The pair build each link model from screw maths steps. They then join the links with strict maths rules. The joint model holds for arms with any count of links. One build path cuts design time for new arms. It also keeps the growth maths true at scale.
arxiv-2601-16342:
Tomáš Kaiser, Matěj Stehlík and Riste Škrekovski note a sharp trait of shift graphs. Their 2026 preprint is a short note in graph theory. Shift graphs came from Erdős and Hajnal in 1964. They give a plain build of graphs with no three cycles. Yet their color need can be made as high as one likes.

The team finds the least graph of each color need in this set. Each such least graph has a vertex key trait. That trait means each vertex earns its place in the count. A neat least form helps teams use shift graphs in proofs. The note adds a firm fact to a known build.
arxiv-2601-16442:
Masahiro Yoshino and three coauthors read which voice a hearer tracks from brain waves. Their 2026 preprint deals with the cocktail party task. In a room of voices, a hearer picks one voice to track. Brain wave tools can tell which voice that is. Such tools back smart aids that lift the tracked voice.

Past tools lean on where each voice sits in the room. This test drops that place cue and uses mixed sound. Both ears get the same mix in the diotic case. A tool that works sans place cues fits more real rooms. The work tests brain reads in that hard case.
arxiv-2601-16542:
Christian Klein, Johannes Sjöstrand, and Maher Zerzeri work on a hard sum in wave math. The sum blends a sharp peak with a fast wave. A small scale sets how fast the wave swings. Such sums show up when one solves a d-bar type task. Their 2026 preprint gives a clean form for the sum's size.

The peak sits at a point where the wave shifts sign. That point has a plus-minus mark. The team tracks how the peak and wave mix there. Clean forms like this help solve tasks in optics and fluids. They also feed fast screen codes that need true sums.
arxiv-2601-16642:
Brader, Di Bernardo and Tschopp study hard disks held in a thin lane. Their 2026 preprint uses sum maths for mixed states of the disks. Hard walls bound the lane on both sides at width L. Disks can not pass through the walls or each other. When width drops past two disk spans, disks can not pass at all.

That tight zone acts like a one dim line in its traits. The team sums rest traits of the disks in that zone. Traits span how disks pack and push on the walls. Tight lane sums test maths for small fluid sets. They also guide chip and pore flow models.
arxiv-2601-16842:
Seunghyun Lee and Nabarun Deb sharpen a Bayes tool for vast data sets. Such data sets pair each outcome with a huge trait list. A prior guess spreads weight across those traits. Bayes tools learn that prior from the data pool. Their 2026 preprint tracks the long-run form of one such tool.

Their tool lifts a smooth bound in place of a hard count. The team finds the tool's limit spread in closed form. That form tells how much to trust its calls. High-depth data needs such trust marks to be sound. Health and gene work gain from clear-gauge Bayes tools.
arxiv-2601-17142:
Razvan Barbulescu, Mugurel Barcau, Vicenţiu Paşol, and George Ţurcaş count rare genus-2 curves with rich point sets. A genus-2 curve's Jacobian may hold many free points. Rank counts how many such points it holds. Their 2026 preprint gauges how oft rank hits one or two. Curves sort by the height of their plain forms. Counts grow in a log-type spread as height climbs.

Those counts feed crypto built on such curves. Rich ranks shape how safe those codes are. Pure counts here give base rates for rare traits. They guide hunts for curves with set rank aims.
arxiv-2601-17242:
Ankit Rai proves a sharp result in algebraic geometry. He studies smooth projective varieties, shapes cut out by polynomial equations. He looks at those with non-negative Kodaira dimension. That number sorts shapes by their growth of forms. He adds two more traits: a rational point and a polarized self map.

Rai shows any such shape must be a finite free quotient of an abelian variety. In plain terms, its form is far more fixed than it first looks. Few shapes can meet all the traits at once. Results like this help geometers sort the vast zoo of shapes. They turn loose traits into a short list of true types.
arxiv-2601-17942:
Yu-Jie Yang, Hung-Fu Chang, and Po-An Chen study how language models can write database queries for plain questions. Their 2026 preprint is about text-to-SQL. The task lets a user ask in normal words and get data back, with no need to learn SQL. That lowers the bar for data analysis a great deal. The authors combine three supports: careful prompting, self-refinement, and a voting scheme.

In self-refinement, the model checks and fixes its own draft query. The voting step weighs several candidate answers and picks by an adaptive rule. Each support attacks a common failure: slips in syntax, wrong tables, or shaky logic. The work aims at query tools that non-experts can trust more often.
arxiv-2601-18142:
Mingxu Zhang and co-authors make reinforcement learning safer with a control-theory twist. Their 2026 preprint deals with safe RL, where an agent must gain reward while obeying safety limits. Lagrangian methods are the usual answer. Yet PID-style and classic Lagrangian schemes often oscillate and break the limits often. The flaws come from sensitivity to settings and from phase lag in the feedback loop. The team brings in ADRC, active disturbance rejection control, inside the Lagrangian frame.

Control theory was built to tame exactly such lag and wobble. A steadier safety loop means fewer violations during training itself. That matters when training runs on real systems, not just in simulation. The work joins two fields that rarely meet.
arxiv-2601-18242:
Zerui Kang and co-authors use a vision-language model to speed the tuning of radio simulations. Their 2026 preprint deals with RF material parameters. Such parameters are essential for electromagnetic digital twins in 6G systems. A twin must know how walls and objects absorb and reflect radio waves. Gradient-based inverse ray tracing can find those values, but it is sensitive to its starting guess and costly when measurements are few.

The team's frame lets a vision-language model guide the search. Good guidance can steady the fit and cut the runs needed. Digital twins that match the real airwaves serve network planning. The work joins AI perception with physics simulation.
arxiv-2601-18342:
Navya S. D., Sreekanth D., and S. S. Uma Sankari audit credit scoring for structural gender bias. Their 2026 preprint examines the Taiwan Credit Default dataset. As banks adopt machine learning for credit risk, algorithmic bias blocks fair access to finance. The authors challenge the doctrine of fairness through blindness, the idea that hiding gender makes a model fair. Their audit looks for proxy leakage: traits that stand in for gender and carry its signal into the score anyway.

If proxies leak, dropping the gender field is a false comfort. A structural audit shows where the leak runs. The findings serve lenders, regulators, and borrowers alike. Fair credit is a door to housing, work, and enterprise.
arxiv-2601-18542:
MacMaster and four colleagues built XFit, a tool to fit models to X-ray data from space with less hand work. The plain way to fit such data climbs to the best fit from a start guess. That climb can get stuck in a dip that is not the best fit of all. The risk grows when the model has many dials and when two dial sets give near twin fits.

XFit roams the whole space of dials to find the best fit, not just the best near dip. It also maps zones where twin fits hide, so staff know when a fit is not unique. Less hand work means more data can be fit in a day. Clear maps of twin fits help staff trust, or doubt, each claim they draw from the light of far stars.
arxiv-2601-18642:
Lei Wei and four colleagues give smart agents a way to forget that works more like the brain. An agent that keeps all it meets will drown in old facts. An agent that drops facts at a hard edge will lose key facts all at once. The brain does not work in that all-or-none way. It lets weak facts fade bit by bit while strong ones stay.

Their tool, FadeMem, lets facts fade at rates set by how much they count and how new they are. Old facts that get used stay. Old facts that sit idle fade out. A fade rule should keep the store lean with no loss of the facts that count. Lean stores cost less to run and search. The work brings a brain trick to a clear need in agent design.
arxiv-2601-18842:
Yanxi Wang and eight colleagues build GUIGuard, a frame to keep screen agents from leaking the facts they see. Such agents read a screen, pick what to tap, and send shots of the screen to far models for thought. Screens hold dear facts: bank counts, health notes, chats with kin. A shot sent out can leak all that in one go. The risk grows as agents move into daily apps.

GUIGuard aims to screen the shots before they leave the phone or the desk box. It can mask dear zones while it keeps the parts the agent needs to act. A guard of that kind could let users gain from agents with no loss of their facts. The frame is built to fit many apps, not just one. Trust is the bar such agents must clear to win wide use.
arxiv-2601-19442:
Didier Bresch, Christophe Lacave, and Maja Szlenk work on the mathematics of thick, sticky flows. Their system describes a compressible fluid whose resistance to flow can change with its density. It also includes a capillarity effect, a surface-tension-like force at fine scales. They look for a weak kind of solution, called a dissipative solution, that physics can accept even when smooth solutions break down.

The authors prove that such solutions exist when the capillarity effect is included. The setting is a periodic box in two or three dimensions, so the flow wraps around at the edges. Existence proofs like this one anchor computer models of complex fluids. They show the equations make sense before anyone tries to solve them numerically.
arxiv-2601-19742:
Ali Jnadi and four colleagues build a framework for handling long, flexible objects. Deformable linear objects include cables, ropes, and wires. Robots that route cables or tie knots must predict how these objects bend. Classic energy-based models are accurate but slow, which blocks real-time use.

Their framework, SCOPE, models and manipulates such objects with convex approximations. Convex problems solve fast and reliably, so the method cuts computation sharply. The deformations it produces stay smooth and physically plausible. The trade-off between speed and accuracy suits tasks that need near-real-time response. Applications range from factory cable assembly to surgical threads. The work brings flexible object handling closer to practical robot control.
arxiv-2601-19842:
Dieu D. Nguyen and colleagues weigh the black hole at the heart of galaxy NGC 4061. This massive early-type galaxy hosts a supermassive black hole whose mass had never been robustly measured. The team used the ALMA telescope to observe carbon monoxide gas circling the centre. Gas motion betrays the gravity of whatever sits inside.

They combined archival observations with new ones to sharpen the image. The gas emission traces a rotating disk at high spatial resolution. Fitting its kinematics yields the first robust dynamical mass for this black hole, on the order of a billion solar masses. Each solid measurement anchors the relation between galaxies and their central black holes.
arxiv-2601-19942:
Faruk Alpay and Bugra Kilictas offer a theory of how language models reason in steps. Multi-step reasoning suggests an inner process that turns smooth internal states into stable, reusable units. The authors model this as a phase transition in the geometry of the latent activation manifold across the network's depth. They call the phenomenon latent object permanence.

Their account draws on the free-energy principle and renormalization group flows, tools from physics for describing systems at many scales. A phase transition view predicts sharp changes in behaviour as inputs vary. It also suggests why reasoning can fail suddenly. The theory is speculative but testable in principle. It aims to give interpretability research a physical vocabulary.
arxiv-2601-20142:
Zilai Wang and four colleagues work on speech recognition for children, a task where systems still lag behind adult speech. Self-supervised speech models do well on many tasks, but child speech data is scarce and differs from the data used in pretraining. Fine-tuning such a model on child speech also shifts its internal representation space.

The authors use that shift itself as a tool, through what they call delta SSL embeddings. Their aim is to turn the change caused by fine-tuning into a signal that helps recognition. Better child speech recognition supports learning tools, voice interfaces, and clinical screening built for young speakers.
arxiv-2601-20642:
Rohan Asthana and Vasileios Belagiannis detect and mitigate memorization in diffusion image models through the anisotropy of the log-probability. Diffusion models make high-fidelity images by iterative denoising, but they can memorize, reproducing exact copies or parts of training images. Earlier detectors mostly rely on the norm of a score difference as the indicator.

The authors use direction as well as size: how unevenly the log-probability varies across directions. Memorization is a legal and privacy risk, since a model may hand back someone's artwork or photo. A sharper detector is the first step to filtering it out. A copy that slips past the guard can be sold, shared, or used to frame the true owner of the work.
arxiv-2601-20842:
Chuanpeng Hou, Huirong Yan, and Siqi Zhao hunt for the source of particle beams in space plasmas. Their 2026 paper uses a high-resolution particle-in-cell simulation of compressible turbulence. A collisionless plasma is so thin that particles rarely hit each other. Yet such plasmas produce fast beams and ion Bernstein waves. The team asks where these features come from.

In the simulation, turbulence at large scales is damped by transit-time damping. That process hands energy to a few particles instead of heating all. It naturally generates suprathermal electrons and proton beams. Those beams can then drive the observed waves. The work links a basic plasma process to signals seen in space. It helps explain how the solar wind and similar plasmas grow their fast tails.
arxiv-2601-21042:
Francisco Azeredo, Dyana Duarte, and Ricardo Farias examine how bookkeeping choices shape a model of dense quark matter. Their 2026 paper studies two-flavor color superconducting quark matter. The matter sits in a constant external magnetic field. Such conditions may occur inside magnetars, the most magnetic stars known. The authors focus on the Medium Separation Scheme. The scheme is a way to treat the model's divergences with care.

They compare several treatments side by side. One combines the scheme with Magnetic Field Independent Regularization. Another uses standard smooth form factors. The choice changes the physics the model predicts. That sensitivity is the paper's central concern. Clean handling of infinities is vital in dense-matter theory. The work helps theorists judge which results to trust.
arxiv-2601-21542:
Hongxu Chen, Hongxiang Li, Zhen Wang, and Long Chen speed up flow matching models that generate images and other data. Such models solve a differential equation step by step, which makes them slow. Quick solvers lose quality at low step counts, while trained shortcuts are costly and hard to reuse.

Their solver leans on two anchor points to guide each step. Interpolation between the anchors keeps quality up with few function calls. The design needs no extra training and can plug into existing models. Faster generation at the same quality cuts both the wait and the energy bill for media tools.
arxiv-2601-21642:
Filippo Berta and Svenja zur Verth prove that certain central values of L-functions do not vanish. L-functions encode deep arithmetic patterns, and their value at the center point carries special meaning. Showing the value is not zero, for a positive share of a family, is a classic hard goal.

The authors work with toroidal families under angular restrictions. They use the theory of trace functions plus a smoothing trick called mollification. Classification results pin down the sheaves in play, and a recent bound handles the key sums. Non-vanishing results feed conjectures linking L-functions to the arithmetic of curves and fields.
arxiv-2601-21742:
Ruiwen Zhou and ten co-authors build justified trust in groups of language model agents. Single agents are fragile: they often conform to misleading peers without checking them. The authors show the weakness mixes flattery-like agreement with a poor sense of which peers are reliable.

Their epistemic context learning teaches agents to weigh peer claims by track record and evidence. Trust then grows for the right reasons, not from pressure to agree. Multi-agent systems are being handed real work in research and business. Agents that can doubt each other politely, and update that doubt, are a basic safety need.
arxiv-2601-21942:
Lev Fedorov and co-authors ask what happens to tokens as they travel through a deep Transformer. Earlier theories, built on layer normalization and fixed weights, predicted that tokens collapse and cluster to a single point. That picture conflicts with how real models behave.

Real Transformers use random, learned weights, not deterministic ones. The team's 2026 preprint studies clustering in deep stochastic Transformers, where the weights are treated as random. Understanding true token dynamics matters because it shapes how information survives depth: whether diverse inputs stay distinct or wash out. Those dynamics affect design choices from model depth to how representations are read out for downstream tasks.
arxiv-2601-22442:
Thalaiyasingam Ajanthan and a large team cut the chat cost of training huge models across many devices. Their 2026 preprint, AsyncMesh, notes that data and pipeline splits are key to scale, yet each split forces costly talk between devices. Co-locating work helps, but sync waits still eat time.

Their method drops the need for lock-step sync across the mesh. Devices can push ahead on their own clock, within safe bounds. Less waiting means faster training at lower cost. The work suits the largest models, where sync waste is vast. It is a systems gain, not a new model.
arxiv-2601-22542:
Zijian Gao and five co-authors built Detect and Act, a self-tuning optimizer for problems that keep changing. Dynamic problems shift as they are solved, like routes in live traffic. Their 2026 preprint notes that evolution-style solvers fit such shifts well, yet most rely on hand-made adaptive rules.

Their meta-level method learns when to sense a change and how to react. Less hand-tuning means solvers that travel better across tasks. The work targets real systems whose ground keeps moving. It automates a judgment experts used to make. That is the claimed step forward.
arxiv-2601-22742:
Yifei Li and a large team built AR-Bench, a test of legal reasoning built on judgment errors. The bench asks models to find, classify, and fix errors in legal judgments. Their 2026 preprint grounds the test in real judgment flaws, not made-up puzzles.

Spotting a flaw is a sterner test than reciting law. Fixing it well is sterner still. Scores here can show which models are safe near legal work. They can also guide training for legal tools. The work treats error-handling as the core legal skill. That choice is deliberate and sound.
arxiv-2601-23242:
Shilong Chen and five co-authors trace the origin of very-high-energy gamma rays from a quiet galaxy. The galaxy, NGC 4278, hosts a low-luminosity active nucleus, yet the LHAASO observatory recently detected it at very high energies. Jets from such nuclei can accelerate particles to extremes, but the emission mechanism here was unclear.

The authors model where those gamma rays are produced and what they imply. Their results also carry lessons for neutrino observations, since gamma-ray sources often emit neutrinos too. Dim galaxies joining the high-energy sky changes source counts for both messengers.
arxiv-2603-01642:
Katarina Karlova and Jozef Strecka map the states of a quantum magnet on a decorated honeycomb lattice in this 2026 work. The lattice mixes paired spins and lone spins on a warped honeycomb frame, all pulling against each other. Such clashes can breed odd quantum phases that plain magnets never show.

The pair combine four tools: large-scale numeric methods, exact checks on small cases, and a gas-like model. Their map shows many phases, from ferrimagnetic and spin-canted states to mixed dimer and tetramer patterns. Flat steps in magnetization appear at zero and at quarter, half, and three-quarter levels of full strength. Heat slowly smears those steps, while the gas-like model still tracks the cold behavior well. The map guides hunts for real materials with like traits.
arxiv-2603-01742:
Yi-Nan Wang, Wenbin Yan, and Peihe Yang study the Higgs branch of four-dimensional superconformal field theories. Their 2026 work builds those theories by geometric engineering, placing type IIB string theory on singular threefold spaces. The Higgs branch records one family of vacuum states, and a linked algebra encodes its protected data.

For terminal singularities, they explain how to derive the Higgs branch from a small resolution of the space. Cases with compact four-cycles in the resolution get several computation methods. A symplectic duality argument yields first examples whose Higgs branches are E-type Kleinian singularities. The linked algebras are conjectured to be affine E-type W-algebras, with many new cases lacking known descriptions. Index calculations and quiver predictions round out the picture for two named families.
arxiv-2603-01942:
Huw Day, Adrianna Jezierska, and Jessica Woodgate reframe jailbreaking chatbots as a peaceful way to defuse online conflict. Their 2026 work studies social media, where language-model bots now steer political talk at scale and stir escalation. Most research backs platform moderation as the main counterweight to that manipulation.

The authors propose a user-centric view instead, centered on ordinary people who engage suspected bot accounts. By prompting around model safeguards, users can expose automated behavior in public view. That exposure disrupts the spread of misleading narratives without threats or abuse. Jailbreaking here is presented as an emergent, non-violent de-escalation practice, not as an attack. The lens shifts defense from platform control rooms to the everyday tactics of users themselves.
arxiv-2603-02142:
Kwame Mbobda-Kuate and Gabriel Kasmi question a common belief in this 2026 vision paper: bigger models are not always better. They test small object finding under tight limits on power and data. Their case is rooftop solar panels in Madagascar, seen from above. They vary model size, data size, and image detail across many setups.

Judged by score per unit of model size, the smallest model won by a wide margin. That tiny model also earned the highest raw score of all. Sharper images helped far more than extra training data. In fact, small models with sharp images beat all rivals in both speed and score. For scarce-data field work, the lesson is to spend on image detail first.
arxiv-2603-02342:
Daniel Humphrey, Cristian Vega, Stanislav Boldyrev, and Vadim Roytershteyn study particle angles in turbulent plasma in this 2026 paper. Jets and nebulae shine by synchrotron light, which depends on electron energies and angles. Relativistic turbulence speeds electrons up well in these magnetized flows. Energy spectra are now fairly well mapped by simulations, but angle patterns are not.

The pitch angle describes the tilt of an electron's path against the field. The team runs a detailed case with a strong steady field and high magnetization. Even tiny numerical noise scatters pitch angles a lot, they find. They show methods to tame that noise and track very small angles faithfully. Final angle patterns match an earlier phenomenological model. Better angle data sharpens how astronomers read synchrotron spectra.
arxiv-2603-02642:
Jiawei Wang, Arshiya Taj Abdul, and Evangelos Theodorou speed up safe path planning for machines that face uncertainty. Their 2026 framework, cuNRTO, computes control plans that respect limits under any bounded disturbance. The catch is cost: the safety math creates huge cone-shaped constraint problems that solve slowly.

The team built two designs that run these problems on graphics processors. One splits the work with the Douglas-Rachford method, the other with a tailored alternating-direction method. Custom chip code handles the repeated projection and matrix steps in parallel. Tests on a wheeled robot model, a quadcopter, and a robot arm reached speedups up to about one hundred forty times. Faster safety checks make robust planning far more practical.
arxiv-2603-02842:
Rosanna Milner, Michael Foster, Twin Karmakharm, and colleagues built a browser tool that helps journalists check suspect content fast. Their 2026 paper presents the Verification Assistant, part of a widely used plugin with well over one hundred thousand users. Fact-checkers face floods of false and AI-made media, yet expert detection models often sit outside their daily tools.

A user pastes a link or uploads a file, and the assistant pulls the content and routes it to a suite of language classifiers. It returns clear signals about credibility, persuasion tricks, and possible machine generation, plus practical next steps. By packaging many models in one plain interface, the tool brings research-grade checks into everyday newsroom work.
arxiv-2603-02942:
Juan Manuel Pacheco-Arias, Philippe Amram, Benoît Epinat, and Wilfried Mercier draw the first maps of how spin is spread inside spiral galaxies. A galaxy's specific angular momentum measures how much rotation each unit of star mass carries. Its map across the disk had never been analyzed before this 2026 study.

Combining infrared brightness maps with gas velocity fields and rotation curves, they built spin density maps for thirty nearby spiral and irregular galaxies. Standard shape measures, plus two new scores for disk likeness and paired structure, sorted the galaxies into five classes named for rings, spirals, bars, clumps, or irregular patterns. For nearly half, the spin class disagreed with the visible shape class. Spin also tracked galaxy mass and star formation as expected.
arxiv-2603-03242:
Patrick Gerard and Svitlana Volkova align language models to online communities by reading what those communities already accept. Standard alignment needs explicit preference labels or fixed principles, which most communities cannot supply, especially around sensitive topics. Yet members constantly signal taste by engaging with some posts and letting others die.

The authors show accepted replies cluster in dense, coherent regions of the model's representation space, while rejected ones scatter. Their method, DGRO, turns that local density into a training signal with no preference labels at all. Recovery tests confirm density mirrors real pairwise judgments. Across platforms, topics, and languages, DGRO-aligned models produced replies that human annotators, experts, and model judges preferred over baselines.
