This one is kept in Spanish as released by the CIA: a primary record of the exile force, identified by its date and its place in the brigade's papers.
cia-0000136042: One declassified cable from the CIA files, dated 6 February 1954, covers the need for a field representative for SKIMME, the program name cut off at the heading's end. In these files Lincoln names the field station of PBSUCCESS, the covert CIA plan to topple President Arbenz of Guatemala. What survives is the working paper itself, plain proof of how the mission was run from day to day.
cia-0000136242: The open CIA files hold a cable dated 5 May 1954 that deals with a bomb drop on a race track. Lincoln was the station cryptonym for PBSUCCESS, the CIA operation against President Arbenz in Guatemala that ended in June 1954. Read on its own terms, the record shows the operation at work in its own words, with some names still blacked out.
cia-0000139042: East German radio is being reorganized under Gerhart Eisler's information office, this June 1951 report details. Herbert Gessner, a Radio Leipzig commentator, has been placed in charge of all programs beamed to the West from Radio Berlin, Radio Leipzig, and Deutschlandsender, where he is deputy chief editor. Other SED members take the economic editorial offices and family sections; the Berlin station and Deutschlandsender will share a joint chief editorial office. The reorganization, learned from the Office of Information, completes after the World Youth Festival.
cia-03000942: September 16, 1954: the bulletin went to the leadership. The day's global intelligence, summarized. The Cold War's September brief. The paper lived through the years. This declassified paper endures. The text is preserved. The record is kept.
cia-03156042: Late May 1959: this bulletin briefed leaders on world affairs. The intelligence summary went to the usual senior readers. The Cold War's daily rhythm. Writers of history may cite it later. This file preserves that declassified paper.
cia-06271942: DISCRETIONARY RELEASE OF CSI ARTICLE, a CIA document. The article's release. This file preserves that declassified paper. Writers of history may cite it later. The paper lasts as a quiet witness. Time has kept the file intact.
cia-06628142: The Argentine junta's economy got assessed in this 1978 file. The generals claimed progress; the agency took notes. The dirty war's ledgers. The archive keeps the paper open to all. This file preserves that declassified paper.
cia-06746042: EXPLOITING THE "SADDAM IN EXILE" GAMBIT, a CIA document. The Iraq gambit. This file preserves that declassified paper. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past.
cia-06906142: ARREST OF LEADERS OF THE NATIONAL SINARCHIST UNION, a CIA document. The Mexican arrests. This file preserves that declassified paper. It holds its historical place. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The library keeps the document safe.
europmc-pmc10120242:
Salari and colleagues pool studies from around the world to estimate how common ADHD is in children and teenagers, in a 2023 review. ADHD is a developmental condition marked by inattention, hyperactivity, and impulsive behavior. Reported rates vary a lot between countries and study methods, which the authors set out to reconcile.

Their systematic review and combined analysis gives a global rate with a measure of uncertainty. It also shows how rates differ by region, age, and diagnostic rules. The paper gives planners and clinicians a shared baseline for a widely debated figure.
europmc-pmc10196242:
Liu and colleagues review how short-chain fatty acids regulate the immune system in a 2023 paper. These fatty acids are made by gut bacteria as they ferment dietary fiber. A growing body of work shows they help keep the symbiosis between microbes and host in good health, acting on many cell types across the body.

The review explains the main routes by which the acids steer immune cells. It covers their roles in calming inflammation and in training immune responses. It also looks at disease links when acid levels fall. The paper connects diet to immune control.
europmc-pmc10356842:
Zhao and co-authors reviewed vaccine adjuvants in 2023, the added parts that boost a vaccine's effect. A vaccine trains the immune system to fight a germ. An adjuvant makes that training stronger, yet how most of them work stayed unclear for years. New insight into the first wave of immune defence has begun to explain them.

Two broad kinds stand out in the review by Zhao. One kind sounds an alarm that wakes up cells which present the vaccine target to the immune system. The other kind acts as a carrier, holding the target longer or guiding it to lymph nodes. The review covers classic adjuvants and newer platforms with stronger effects. It ends with design choices for future vaccines.
europmc-pmc10470842:
Latif and a large team reviewed probiotics in 2023, live microbes that can aid health when taken in the right dose. Common kinds include lactic acid bacteria, the germs used to ferment milk foods. The review asks how they work and where the food trade can use them.

Probiotics may crowd out harmful germs at gut wall sites, Latif reports. They can firm up the gut lining, tune immune acts, and even make nerve signals. Gains may help with blood pressure, blood fats, cancer, and gut disease. Food makers now add them to dairy goods, drinks, and baked goods. New methods help the microbes survive factory heat and stomach acid.
europmc-pmc10502142:
Chen and co-authors reviewed stress in the endoplasmic reticulum in 2023, with a focus on eye disease. This cell part folds new proteins and checks their quality. Stress starts when faulty proteins pile up inside it. The cell then fires a rescue plan to restore order, or dies if the plan fails.

That stress sits at the root of many eye diseases, Chen reports. The list runs from glaucoma and cataracts to retina decay and high myopia. Three rescue arms carry names: PERK, ATF6, and IRE1. The review maps how each arm feeds each disease. Drugs, gene therapy, and stem cells that ease the stress form the care outlook.
europmc-pmc11214942:
Lu and colleagues review water-based gels as platforms for advanced therapies in this 2024 paper. Hydrogels are soft networks that hold large amounts of water and can be tuned finely. Breakthroughs in biomaterials have widened their uses fast. The review focuses on two areas: cell-based therapies and non-cell treatments.

For cell therapy, gels can solve the delivery problems that hold the field back, the authors argue. They detail design choices that boost cell survival and effect, with examples across diseases. Beyond cells, gels serve in drug delivery, physical therapies, wound glues, artificial tissues, and biosensors. The paper stresses that gels act as more than passive carriers. Clinical progress and remaining hurdles are reviewed. Future work ties gels to advanced biomanufacturing, such as printed tissues.
europmc-pmc11446842:
Dorkenwald and a large team present the complete wiring diagram of an adult fly brain in this 2024 paper. Connections between neurons can be mapped from electron microscope images of brain tissue. Past work reconstructed chunks of brain, which cannot explain global function. This study covers the whole brain of an adult female fruit fly.

The diagram holds 50 million chemical synapses between 139,255 neurons, the team reports. Synapses are the junctions where neurons pass signals. Annotations add cell classes and types, nerves, developmental lineages, and predicted neurotransmitter identities. Data are offered for download, programmatic access, and interactive browsing. The authors derive a projectome, a map of projections between regions. They trace pathways from sensory inputs to motor outputs across both brain hemispheres and the optic lobes.
europmc-pmc1240542:
Darnerud and colleagues reviewed flame retardant exposure and toxicity in 2001. PBDEs are mixed into plastics and textile coatings as fire guards. World output ran near 40,000 tons per year. The chemicals collect in living tissue and magnify up food chains.

Levels rose sharply in water life during the 1970s and 1980s. Swedish data hinted at a later leveling in fish and bird eggs. Breast milk levels still rose steeply through 1997. Animal harms include liver, thyroid, and embryo effects. Darnerud weighs diet as a main route of human exposure. Based on food levels, Swedish diet intake was put at 0.05 micrograms daily in 1999.
europmc-pmc1257642:
Oberdörster, Oberdörster, and Oberdörster named a new field, nanotoxicology, in 2005. Humans have always breathed nanosized particles under 100 nanometers. Human sources raised that exposure sharply over the last century. Engineered nanomaterials add skin, gut, and injection routes.

Older ultrafine particle studies supply the base evidence. Inhaled particles deposit through the whole respiratory tract by diffusion. Their tiny size lets them slip into cells and cross tissue barriers. From there they reach blood, lymph, and sensitive organs. The authors define the field as safety testing of engineered nanostructures. The authors say clear safety data for these new materials are urgently needed now, as use grows.
europmc-pmc1764142:
Prenatal smoke and lead exposure each raise the odds of ADHD. Braun and co-authors quantified that in 2006 using a national survey of 4,704 US children aged 4 to 15. About 4.2 percent had diagnosed ADHD with stimulant medication, some 1.8 million children.

Prenatal tobacco exposure carried 2.5 times the odds of ADHD. Children in the highest blood lead group had 4.1 times the odds of the lowest group. Smoke exposure after birth showed no link. If the links are causal, the authors estimate 270,000 excess cases from prenatal smoke and 290,000 from lead. Lead in blood was the stronger signal.
europmc-pmc1789242:
Pietiläinen and colleagues used identical twins in 2007 to separate gained weight from inherited risk. Obesity runs in families, so gene effects and lifestyle effects are hard to pull apart. Monozygotic twins share all their genes, so a heavier twin shows what acquired obesity alone does.

The study compared 14 young adult twin pairs where one twin weighed 10 to 25 kilograms more than the other, plus ten matched pairs of similar weight. Blood fat profiles were measured with a broad lipidomics method, meaning a census of many fat molecules at once. The heavier twins had more lysophosphatidylcholines, fats tied to inflammation and artery disease. They had fewer ether phospholipids, fats with protective antioxidant traits. The shifts tracked with insulin resistance, even at this early stage.
europmc-pmc1808442:
Hamel reviewed cone rod dystrophies in 2007, a group of inherited eye diseases affecting about one person in 40,000. The retina is the light-sensing layer at the back of the eye. In these diseases the cone cells, which give sharp central and color vision, fail first.

That order is the reverse of typical retinitis pigmentosa, where rod cells for night vision go first. Early signs are falling sharpness, color defects, dislike of bright light, and loss of central vision. Peripheral vision and night sight fade later, and the course is usually faster and harsher than in rod-first disease. Most cases stand alone, though some join syndromes such as Bardet Biedl syndrome. Ten cloned genes and three further loci were known, led by ABCA4, CRX, and GUCY2D.
europmc-pmc2126342: A medical paper on persistence of the virus of poliomyelitis in the nasopharynx. The lingering polio. This article preserves that virology. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past.
europmc-pmc2140442: A biology paper on the isoelectric point of red blood cells and its relation to agglutination. The cells' charge point. This article preserves that hematology. Those who study the era will use it. The archive keeps the paper open to all.
europmc-pmc2140742: A biology paper with an interfacial tensiometer for universal use. The surface measurer. This article preserves that laboratory technique. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it. The archive keeps the paper open to all.
europmc-pmc2140942: Membranes choose what passes, and this first permeability study opened with the diffusion of ions through them. The investigators established the groundwork for membrane science. The selective gates, introduced. The article preserves that cell biology research for future readers.
europmc-pmc2211742:
Holland, Booth and Bruford catalogued all human homeobox genes in 2007. These genes carry a signature DNA stretch and many direct embryonic development. Comparing them across genomes illuminates how animal body plans evolved. No full account of the human set existed. The team searched the genome's gene-rich regions and found many unannotated, misnamed or misclassified loci, places where genes sit.

They describe 300 human homeobox loci in total. Of these, 235 are probable functional genes and 65 are probable pseudogenes, disabled copies. Their scheme groups the genes into 11 classes and 102 families. Names were established for about 40 previously unnamed loci. Revisions were proposed for around 30 others. The classification should transfer to other animal genomes and support comparative studies of this gene superclass.
europmc-pmc2243142:
Weichert and co-workers measured histone deacetylase enzymes in 2008 in 192 prostate cancers. These enzymes, called HDACs, alter how genes are packaged and switched, and their overactivity is linked to malignant behaviour. HDAC-blocking drugs are in late-stage trials, yet isoform patterns in prostate cancer were little known. The team stained tumours for class I HDACs 1, 2 and 3, then correlated expression with tumour features and patient follow-up.

All three were strongly expressed in most cases: HDAC1 in 69.8 percent, HDAC2 in 74 percent, and HDAC3 in 94.8 percent of samples. High HDAC1 and HDAC2 expression tracked with tumour dedifferentiation. In dedifferentiation, cells look less like normal prostate tissue under the microscope. Strong expression of all three accompanied faster tumour cell proliferation. HDAC2 stood out as an independent prognostic marker. Higher HDAC2 meant shorter time until PSA relapse after prostate removal surgery.
europmc-pmc2270842:
O'Boyle, Morley and Hutchison introduced Pybel in 2008, a Python module wrapping the OpenBabel cheminformatics toolkit. Cheminformatics work often needs quick scripts to parse and analyse molecular files. Toolkits like OpenBabel are written in fast compiled C++ for efficiency, which makes them awkward from scripting languages. Pybel bridges that gap by wrapping the direct bindings and simplifying common tasks such as reading and writing molecule files and computing fingerprints.

Python iterators streamline looping over every molecule in a file. A Pybel molecule converts easily into the underlying OpenBabel object, giving access to any unwrapped methods. OpenBabel itself handles over eighty molecular file formats and standard chemistry algorithms. Pybel is open source and cross-platform. The authors present it as a way for chemists to develop analysis scripts rapidly in Python.
europmc-pmc2361442:
Yoshikawa and colleagues measured three growth-related proteins in bile duct cancer in 2008. The cancer, cholangiocarcinoma, grows in the bile ducts inside or outside the liver and is hard to cure. The proteins, EGFR, VEGF, and HER2, were all candidate targets for new drugs.

They stained tumor samples from 236 patients. VEGF was overproduced in about 54% of inner-liver cases and 59% of outer-duct cases. HER2 was rare in the inner group, at 0.9% of cases, and reached 8.5% outside the liver. Excess EGFR in inner-liver tumors marked a worse outlook, with a hazard ratio of 2.67 for death, and a higher risk of the cancer returning. Excess VEGF tied to spread within the liver. The authors suggested EGFR drives tumor advance in this cancer.
europmc-pmc2362742:
Cuschieri and colleagues reported long-term results of a UK trial on stomach cancer surgery in 1999. The question was how much lymph tissue to remove. A D1 operation takes only the glands next to the stomach, while the Japanese-style D2 takes glands further out as well. Japanese reports claimed far better survival with D2, but without randomised proof.

The trial randomised 400 patients after checks showed their cancer might be curable. With a median follow-up of 6.5 years, five-year survival was 35% after D1 and 33% after D2, a difference of minus 2 points that could easily be chance. Deaths from stomach cancer and cancer returns also matched closely. Older age, male sex, later stage, and removal of the spleen or pancreas each predicted worse survival. The authors concluded D2 offers no advantage as performed here.
europmc-pmc2396642:
Meusnier and colleagues shrank the DNA barcode used to name species in 2008. Barcoding identifies a species from a short standard DNA stretch, normally 650 letters of a gene called CO1. Old museum specimens and mixed environmental samples often yield only broken DNA, too short for the standard read.

Using every CO1 barcode in the GenBank archive, they computed how short a fragment can stay species-specific. Much shorter mini-barcodes still separated species in their calculations. They then built a universal primer set, starter DNA pieces that latch onto nearly all animal groups, to copy these short fragments. Tests across all major eukaryote groups, organisms with a cell nucleus, worked, including on archival specimens. The authors said mini-barcodes widen barcoding to degraded and environmental material.
europmc-pmc2628742:
Reich and colleagues pinpointed in 2009 the genetic variant behind the persistently low white blood cell counts common in people of African descent. The trait had no known cause, though earlier mapping had narrowed it to a stretch of chromosome 1 where African versus European ancestry almost fully explained the difference. The team analysed genotype and blood data from 6,005 African Americans across three studies.

The causal variant had to differ in frequency by at least 91 percent between West Africans and European Americans. One candidate fits perfectly: the Duffy Null variant in the DARC gene, already famous for protecting against vivax malaria. Statistical tests confirmed it predicts white cell and neutrophil counts above and beyond ancestry itself, with strong significance. The authors establish a new, benign phenotype for this well-known malaria variant.
europmc-pmc2666642:
Sparvero and co-authors reviewed in 2009 a cell sensor called RAGE and the molecules that switch it on, in cancer and inflammation. RAGE catches debris from damaged sugars and stressed cells. It sits at high levels only in the lung under normal conditions, but rises fast wherever tissue is inflamed.

Once switched on, RAGE helps cells survive stress: it boosts self-eating of damaged parts, holds back cell suicide, and feeds growth signals. That survival push turns dangerous when it never stops. Cells that should die linger, inflammation smolders, and the setting becomes ripe for cancers of surface tissues to arise. The review explains the sensor's shape, its partners, and its soluble form that floats free. Understanding this loop, the authors argue, is central to understanding how chronic inflammation breeds tumors.
europmc-pmc2671142:
Mészáros, Simon, and Dosztányi built in 2009 a predictor, ANCHOR, for the floppy protein segments that fold only when they grab a partner. Many proteins carry disordered regions with no fixed shape. Some of those regions snap into form on contact with another protein, a trick used widely in cell signaling because it gives precise binding without a tight grip.

Their method hunts for segments that cannot fold alone yet stand to gain stability from a partner, judging by the energy balance along the chain. It worked regardless of the segment's makeup or folded shape after binding. Longer binding sites often came out in pieces, matching known cases. Scanning hundreds of species' protein sets, they found such sites grow more common as organisms get more complex, and they run shorter than disordered regions in general.
europmc-pmc2685842:
Stahlhut, Welshons, and Swan tested a textbook claim in 2009. The claim concerns bisphenol A, a plastic chemical found in nearly everyone. It says food is the main source, and the body clears the chemical within hours. If true, people who had fasted longer should carry less of it in their urine. They checked 1,469 adults from a national health survey against their reported fasting times.

The decline was not there. Across a full day of fasting, levels barely budged; the implied half-life came out near 43 hours, not the expected few. Only a middle fasting window showed the textbook pattern. Something in the simple story is wrong. The authors lay out the options. People may take in the chemical by non-food routes, such as dust or skin contact. Or it may collect in body fat and leak out slowly. Settling it needs direct dosing studies, they say.
europmc-pmc2689842:
Price and co-authors presented in 2009 HAPMIX, a method to read the ancestry of each small stretch of DNA in people of mixed descent. Most older tools used sparse, unlinked markers, wasting most of the data on genome chips. HAPMIX instead models how variant patterns are inherited, squeezing ancestry calls from every marker at once.

The team tested it on 935 African Americans, whose ancestry mixes African and European lines within the last few centuries. They also tested 29 Mozabites from North Africa, an anciently mixed group and a far harder case. HAPMIX beat rival methods on both. Beyond painting chromosomes, it can estimate when the mixing happened and reconstruct the source populations. Its sharpest use is disease mapping in mixed populations, where combining ancestry signals with case-control signals finds culprit genes that either approach alone would miss.
europmc-pmc2711942:
Edelheit, Hanukoglu, and Hanukoglu described in 2009 SPRINP, a simpler way to make planned changes in a DNA copy for protein studies. Changing one codon, the three-letter DNA unit for one building block, lets scientists test what that part of a protein does. A common method runs two matching primers together, but they can stick to each other and create repeat copies.

SPRINP runs two single-primer reactions side by side, then mixes, melts, and slowly cools them so new strands pair at random. An enzyme then destroys the parent DNA, leaving the mutants. The team made over forty mutants in genes for a human sodium channel, including small swaps and a larger tag insert.
europmc-pmc2728742:
Gry and co-authors compared in 2009 RNA and protein levels for over one thousand gene products across twenty-three human cell lines. Biology shorthand says DNA makes RNA makes protein, which implies RNA levels should track protein levels closely. That assumption underlies many studies that profile RNA alone to infer cell behavior.

RNA levels from two array platforms agreed well with each other. Protein levels, measured by antibody staining, matched RNA significantly for only about a third of the gene products, and match strength varied widely by gene. Mean protein-RNA correlations were modest on both platforms. Where a clear match exists, it also supports that the antibody truly recognizes its target protein.
europmc-pmc2730242:
Lipsitch and Samore explained in 2002 how antibiotic use selects resistant germs at the level of whole populations, not just in treated patients. Calls to cut resistance often conflict. The main selection route differs by pathogen, which is one source of the conflict. For tuberculosis, resistance grows by mutation inside a treated host, so protecting each host is central.

For many other germs, resistance spreads when genes move sideways between bacteria. In those cases, treatment can raise population resistance even when its effect on the treated person's own germs is small or negative. Policy must match the mechanism. Host-level prevention fits some diseases, while population-level restraint in antibiotic use fits others.
europmc-pmc2738942:
Dridi, Henry, El Khéchine, Raoult, and Drancourt developed in 2009 an improved stool DNA test for two methane-making archaea, single-celled microbes, in the human gut. Earlier reports found these methanogens in few people, which clashed with their key role in digestion. The authors suspected weak DNA extraction from stool was hiding them.

Their protocol filters stool, breaks cells by force twice, and digests overnight before extraction. Testing seven hundred people, they found Methanobrevibacter smithii in nearly ninety-six percent and Methanosphaera stadtmanae in about twenty-nine percent. Sequenced samples matched reference strains almost perfectly. The first species is thus a near-universal gut inhabitant, not a rare one.
europmc-pmc2742742:
Tsitsiou and Lindsay reviewed in 2009 how microRNAs, tiny RNA regulators, shape the immune response at the level of protein production. Immunity was long seen as controlled mainly by switching genes on, yet microRNAs fine-tune how much protein each gene message yields. Certain microRNAs are abundant in immune cells or switch on fast during an attack.

MicroRNAs enriched in immune cells, including the miR-17-92 cluster, miR-150, miR-155, miR-181, and miR-223, have a permissive role in the maturation and growth of white blood cell lines. In contrast, miR-9, miR-146a, and miR-155 rise quickly after innate immune activation and seem to brake the response by lowering signaling proteins. Their actions often run through interplay with transcription factors.
europmc-pmc2749942:
Cai, McEwen, Martens, Meyhofer, and Verhey imaged single kinesin motors in living cells in 2009 to see whether different motors choose different microtubule tracks. Microtubules are cell rails that vary in stability and in chemical marks, yet all are built from the same tubulin subunit. Motors haul cargo along those rails, so track choice could sort cargo to different destinations.

Kinesin-1 moved preferentially along stable microtubules marked by chemical modifications, matching acetylated tracks in about nine of ten cases. Kinesin-2 and Kinesin-3 motors, by contrast, could use dynamic, fast-turnover tracks as well. Motors have thus evolved to recognize specific track populations, which segregates membrane traffic inside the cell.
europmc-pmc2790342:
Homann and colleagues mapped what happens when single gene switches are deleted in Candida albicans, a fungus that lives in the gut and also causes most fungal infections in people. Their 2009 study built a matched set of one hundred forty-three mutant strains, each missing one control protein called a transcription regulator.

Each mutant was grown under fifty-five different conditions to build a trait profile. About a quarter of the strains changed how their colonies formed, nearly doubling the known list of regulators that shape shifts between yeast and thread-like cell forms. About a quarter also changed how the fungus handled common antifungal drugs, and most trait patterns matched those seen in a distant yeast cousin.
europmc-pmc2808242:
Pan-Montojo and colleagues fed mice a common pesticide in 2010 to test whether gut exposure alone could set off Parkinson-like change. The pesticide, rotenone, blocks a key energy step in cells. In patients, Parkinson damage follows a set route that starts in the gut nerve web years before movement fails.

Small daily doses by stomach tube built up clumps of the protein alpha-synuclein. The clumps appeared first in gut nerves, then in the vagus nerve hub, the spinal cord, and finally the movement center of the brain. Inflammation and movement problems followed the same order. No rotenone reached the blood or brain, which points to a signal creeping along connected nerves from the gut.
europmc-pmc2818642:
Lara, Ayala-Nuñez, Ixtepan-Turrent, and Rodriguez-Padilla worked out in 2010 how silver nanoparticles, tiny specks of silver, block HIV-1 in lab tests. The particles were known to stop the virus at doses that did not harm cells, but the exact step they hit stayed unclear. The team ran a panel of assays covering each stage of the virus life cycle.

The particles glued themselves to gp120, a knob protein on the virus surface, and stopped it from latching onto the CD4 doorway of target cells. That blocked entry for lab strains, patient isolates, and drug-resistant strains alike, whether the virus floated free or rode inside cells. Later stages of the cycle were also hindered, which the authors say makes resistance less likely.
europmc-pmc2820542:
Cerami, Demir, Schultz, Taylor, and Sander built an automated network method in 2010 to find the true driver changes in glioblastoma, the most aggressive common brain tumor in adults. Cancer genomes carry many changes, and only some actually drive growth. Counting how often a change appears misses drivers that are rare but central.

Their method maps mutations and DNA copy changes onto a network of protein interactions and looks for tightly linked gene groups hit more than chance allows. The two biggest groups centered on known control pathways named p53, Rb, and PI3K. New candidate drivers surfaced, including a gene called AGAP2 that switches on the PI3K pathway. The tool, NetBox, was released freely for use on other cancers.
europmc-pmc2908542:
Kong and colleagues identified in 2010 a new link in the chain by which cells build energy factories and detoxify the fallout. The master coordinator PGC-1alpha switches on genes for new mitochondria, the cell's power plants, and for enzymes that neutralize reactive oxygen. They found it also strongly switches on SIRT3, a mitochondria-based enzyme tied in humans to longer lifespan.

The coordinator acts through a partner receptor that binds a specific site in the SIRT3 gene's control region, confirmed by DNA binding tests. Removing the partner erased the induction, and removing SIRT3 itself blocked the coordinator's ability to raise detox enzymes and several power plant components. SIRT3 is thus an essential middleman, not a bystander, in the cell's energy and antioxidant program.
europmc-pmc2927542:
Patel, Grandner, and colleagues documented in 2010 a sleep disparity in a survey of nearly ten thousand Philadelphia-area adults: the poor and minorities sleep measurably worse. Self-reported poor sleep quality was the outcome, set against income, employment, education, and ethnicity. Unadjusted gaps were wide, with poverty nearly tripling the odds of poor sleep and Black and Latino respondents carrying clearly higher odds than white respondents.

Adding health indicators to the model shrank the income and ethnicity gaps substantially, meaning worse health explains much of the disparity. Yet poverty still predicted poor sleep among white respondents after every adjustment. The authors frame sleep as a social determinant outcome in its own right, shaped by the same forces that pattern other health gaps and worth intervention.
europmc-pmc2943442:
Kleinschnitz and a large team reported in 2010 that blocking an enzyme called NOX4 after stroke protects the mouse brain. Stroke is a leading cause of death, yet the single approved clot-dissolving treatment reaches only a small share of patients.

The team identified NOX4 as a major source of harmful oxidative stress after a blocked brain vessel. Mice lacking the enzyme, or treated with blockers of its enzyme family, suffered far less nerve cell loss. Because the protection was dramatic, the authors present NOX4 as a fresh target for stroke drugs that might work where earlier candidates failed.
europmc-pmc2957842:
Cachero and colleagues searched the whole fruit fly brain for structural differences between the sexes in a 2010 study. Male courtship depends on a set of about two thousand neurons marked by the fruitless gene, yet wiring differences were poorly mapped.

Comparing registered male and female brain images, they found large volume gaps concentrated in higher brain centres. A saturating clone-labelling effort traced dozens of cell lineages making fruitless neurons and uncovered many new sex differences, including female-only branches in some lines. The map predicts hundreds of spots where connections likely differ, with strong proof in smell pathways.
europmc-pmc3069742:
Battye, Kontogiannis, Johnson, Powell, and Leslie introduced in 2011 a friendlier face for a workhorse program that processes X ray diffraction images. The underlying program, MOSFLM, turns raw crystal images into the measured spot intensities that structure solving needs. Its power came with a steep, text driven interface that slowed newcomers and hid mistakes until late.

The new graphical interface, iMOSFLM, walks users through the job as a series of clear tasks. Each stage gives visual feedback as it runs, so problems such as a misplaced beam center show up at once rather than after hours of work. Settings adjust interactively while the images stay on screen. The authors aim to make routine processing faster and teaching easier, without removing the control experts expect. The tool ships as part of the standard crystallography suite.
europmc-pmc3128042:
Barbara Forey, Alison Thornton, and Peter Lee pooled the world evidence on smoking and chronic lung disease in a 2011 paper in BMC Pulmonary Medicine. Smoking was long accepted as a cause, yet no full pooled review had quantified the link for its three related outcomes. They gathered studies published to 2006 and extracted the most adjusted risk figures.

Across more than two hundred studies, people who had ever smoked faced roughly triple the risk of chronic obstructive lung disease and chronic bronchitis. For emphysema, the risk ran over four times higher. Current smokers scored higher than former smokers, and risk climbed with amount smoked and total lifetime exposure. Risk eased the longer a person had quit. The review confirms the causal link with firm numbers.
europmc-pmc3141042:
Aaron Chen and colleagues probed how gentle laser light affects cells in a 2011 paper in PLoS ONE. Low-level light therapy has been used for decades to ease pain and speed healing, yet its basic cell mechanism stayed murky. They used mouse cells engineered to glow when a key gene-control switch turned on, and shone near-infrared laser light on them.

Above a small dose, the switch turned on within an hour, faster than with a standard bacterial trigger. The light also raised reactive oxygen chemicals inside cells, and blocking those chemicals blocked the switch. Unlike pure energy poisons, though, the light raised cell energy stores, suggesting it boosts breathing in cell power stations while signalling through the oxygen chemicals. That dual action may explain the therapy's healing reputation.
europmc-pmc3182942:
Jennifer Griffin and colleagues mapped every gene the tuberculosis bacterium needs to grow and to feed on cholesterol in a 2011 paper in PLoS Pathogens. Gene activity surveys cannot predict what losing one gene does, so the team used dense random mutations plus deep sequencing to watch which mutants vanished under each condition.

The screen named the full set of genes essential for growth in the lab with unusual precision. On cholesterol, a carbon source the bacterium depends on inside the body, the needed genes spread far beyond the known sterol region. Many had never been flagged by activity surveys. europmc-pmc3221342:
John Powell and colleagues surveyed people who look up health information on the NHS Direct website, in this 2011 study in the Journal of Medical Internet Research. Most UK households were online and health searching was rising, but who these seekers were and what they wanted was less clear. The team combined a website questionnaire with in-depth interviews.

Nearly eight hundred people answered the survey; most were women under forty-five, and most searched for themselves, though many searched for someone else. About half had already consulted a health professional. Interviewees described wanting reassurance, a second opinion, or a better grasp of a problem, and barriers that pushed them online. europmc-pmc3257642:
Fiona O'Leary and Samir Samman reviewed vitamin B12 in health and disease in this 2010 article in Nutrients. The vitamin is essential for making DNA and for cellular energy production. Deficiency is common, arising mainly from eating few animal foods or from poor absorption. The review focuses on the murky category of sub-clinical deficiency. There, blood levels once counted as adequate may still be too low.

Vegetarians and other low-intake groups are at risk, as are older people whose stomachs produce too little acid to free the vitamin from food. The symptoms of mild deficiency are subtle and often missed. What mild deficiency does over the long run is not fully known. Possible effects, though, span pregnancy outcomes and blood vessel, brain, bone, and eye health. The authors outline the vitamin's metabolism and weigh causes against consequences.
europmc-pmc3280242:
Arnaud Delorme and colleagues tested whether the components extracted from scalp EEG recordings correspond to single brain sources, in this 2012 paper in PLoS ONE. Independent component analysis is widely used to unmix the signals smeared together by conduction through the skull, but whether the separated components are physically meaningful was debated. The team decomposed thirteen seventy-one-channel datasets with twenty-two different algorithms and scored the results.

Likelihood and mutual-information methods, led by AMICA, performed best; plain principal component analysis performed worst. The key measure was dipolarity: how well each component's scalp pattern matches the projection of one compact source in the cortex. Components that separated most cleanly also scored most dipolar, consistent with many of them being genuine signals from small cortical patches. The authors released their data and software to spur more comparisons.
europmc-pmc3336942:
Walter, Webster, Scott, and Emery reviewed studies that applied a classic model of delay in cancer diagnosis, publishing in 2012. The path from noticing a symptom to starting treatment has several stages, and delays at any stage can worsen outcomes. The Andersen model names five stages, from first judging a symptom to receiving treatment, yet most studies of diagnostic delay use no model at all.

Only ten papers, covering eight studies, met the reviewers' bar of actually applying the model. Evidence strongly supported two stages, the time spent appraising symptoms and delays within treatment, though the treatment stage needs widening. Scheduling delay had some support, while one proposed stage, illness delay, proved hard to separate from appraisal. The authors propose refinements to the model and plead for more consistent study design and reporting.
europmc-pmc3338542:
Takahara, Minamoto, Yamanaka, Doi, and Kawabata showed that DNA floating in water can reveal how much fish a pond holds, in a 2012 study. Fish constantly shed DNA into their surroundings, and traces of it can already prove a species is present. The team reasoned that if shedding scales with body mass, the amount of DNA should estimate the total weight of fish, a number normally hard to measure.

In tanks, DNA from common carp settled to a steady level within days and rose in step with carp weight, unaffected by water temperature. The same held in experimental ponds. Applied to a natural lagoon, DNA levels mapped where carp were concentrated, with temperature explaining the pattern. The authors offer the method as a fast, gentle way to survey fish populations for conservation.
europmc-pmc3417542:
Ottman, Smidt, de Vos, and Belzer reviewed in 2012 what the gut microbiota actually does, drawing on the new meta-omics toolkits. Reading DNA, RNA, proteins, and chemical products together gives a working snapshot of the community. Such work has drafted genomes for over a thousand human-associated microbes and millions of gut genes.

Human gut communities fall into at least three recurring clusters, dubbed enterotypes, found across continents. The review catalogs jobs the community performs, from making vitamins to processing sugars, amino acids, and foreign chemicals. Diet, age, genes, and health reshape the community, which in turn shapes metabolism and disease. Contrasts between breast-fed and formula-fed babies and between lean and obese adults illustrate the two-way street.
europmc-pmc3473242:
Karmodiya and colleagues mapped two chemical marks on histones across the genome of mouse embryonic stem cells, in BMC Genomics in 2012. The marks, added to two spots on histone H3, usually signal that a gene is switched on. The team charted where each mark sits at gene starts, at distant control regions, and at genes held poised for later use.

The two marks largely traveled together and matched other signs of active genes. Their levels also rose with the share of certain DNA letters in a gene's start region. One surprise stood out: a set of silent yet ready-to-fire gene starts carried the second mark alone. Karmodiya's group suggests enzymes may prime those genes with that mark so they can answer signals fast.
europmc-pmc3480642:
Ashburner wrote a personal history of SPM, the software package that reshaped brain imaging analysis, in NeuroImage in 2012. Karl Friston began the project around 1991 at a London unit that scanned brains with PET imaging. Early studies averaged signals from a few hand-drawn regions, wasting most of each scan. SPM instead tested every point in the brain on an even footing.

The history follows each major release, from the first MATLAB version to the widely used later editions. Ashburner explains why papers must name the exact release used, since methods change between versions. He recalls beta releases timed to training courses and a mailing list that ignores old versions. The piece doubles as a candid look at how shared tools grow.

europmc-pmc6629542: Your DNA holds thousands of tiny risk hints that add up - polygenic risk scores sum them into one number. PRSice-2 is free software that computes these scores at biobank scale, fast enough for millions of people. The tool helps researchers link genetic profiles to disease risk.
europmc-pmc6646942: Psychology's replication crisis traces partly to wimpy statistics - studies too small to trust. This tutorial on power analysis and effect size in mixed-effects models shows how to size studies right. Brysbaert and Stevens walk through examples, arguing better-powered science replicates better.
europmc-pmc6681642: College students report record rates of depression and anxiety - yet campus counseling queues stretch for weeks. This review tests the digital alternative: apps and web programs for mood and well-being. The evidence says well-built digital tools genuinely help, widening the door to care.
europmc-pmc6722042: For high-risk womb cancer, is radiation alone enough - or does adding chemo save more lives? The PORTEC-3 trial randomized women with high-risk endometrial cancer to chemoradiotherapy versus radiotherapy alone. europmc-pmc6734942: Most Mendelian randomization studies test one exposure - but diseases have many causes. europmc-pmc6748942: Cisplatin has anchored chemotherapy for decades - yet tumors learn to resist it. This review traces resistance from the tumor cell outward: DNA repair tricks, detox pathways, and the microenvironment's sheltering role. Each escape route is a potential new drug target.
europmc-pmc6767042: Viruses that eat bacteria - bacteriophages - are medicine's forgotten antibiotics. This review asks what shapes phage therapy's fate in the body: how the viruses travel, survive, and reach their targets. The pharmacokinetics primer readies phages for their clinical comeback.
europmc-pmc6789542: In inflammatory bowel disease, the gut's microbial community goes haywire - but is it cause or consequence? This review weighs the evidence and maps treatment targets: how dysbiosis drives IBD and where therapies might intervene. The chicken-and-egg question matters for cures.
europmc-pmc6837442: Machine learning hungers for data - but brain scans and gene studies come in small batches. fielding-joseph-andrews-1742:
Fielding's Joseph Andrews, from 1742, began as a joke at Samuel Richardson's Pamela. Richardson's heroine resisted her master; Fielding gives her a brother, Joseph, who must resist his widowed mistress. The parody quickly grew into Fielding's first true novel.

Joseph and his friend Parson Adams walk the roads of England, meeting cheats, snobs, and kind hearts. Adams, absent-minded, brave, and good, steals the book from its hero. Fielding's preface sets out his theory of the comic epic in prose. What started as mockery became a founding work of the English novel, warmer and funnier than its target.
frus-1861-d142:
William Dayton sent a dispatch to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 2 August 1861. It is document 142 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

By August, Paris had the news of the Union defeat and was weighing it. Dayton's report told Washington how deep the damage ran in French esteem. Such candor was the chief worth of an envoy in a hard season. Candor from Paris let the cabinet weigh its next steps on fact, not hope. Fact, not hope, was the diet on which the cabinet learned to live that year.
frus-1861-d242:
A letter home from James Shepherd Pike, dated 4 July 1861, landed on Seward's desk. It was printed as Document 242 in the foreign affairs papers sent to the two houses of Congress. It belongs to the first summer of the Civil War, when keeping Europe out of the war was a core task for Washington.

Such reports fed the facts and rumors together into one desk in Washington, week by week. For students of the war, the value lies in the sequence: one dated step in a long exchange. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record series, is where the full exchange can be traced.
frus-1861-d42:
George Dallas sent a dispatch to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 9 April 1861. It is document 42 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Three days later, guns opened on Fort Sumter and the war began. Dallas could not know that as he wrote, and the letter keeps the calm of the old world. It stands in the record as one of the last London reports of a still whole, if shaking, Union. The Sumter news reached London near the end of April and changed the tone of every talk. Stances set that month in London guided talks for the rest of the year.
frus-1862-d142:
In a letter dated 15 September 1862, William H. Seward gave Charles Francis Adams his latest word from Washington. It was printed as Document 142 in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs for 1862. The letter comes from the summer of 1862, the war's second year, a time when each foreign capital watched the war with care.

Readers see the home office side of the exchange, where policy was set before talks began. Read in order with its neighbors, it shows diplomacy as daily work rather than grand speeches. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series, called Foreign Relations of the United States.
frus-1862-d242:
On 3 October 1862 Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to William Stuart in a letter printed as Document 242 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Stuart was still acting head of the British legation in Washington.

Early October found Britain still debating its course, with Gladstone soon to speak warmly of Southern nationhood at Newcastle. Seward's correspondence with the legation kept the Union's objections and claims in formal view. A letter from this date is one more entry in the long written contest that ran beside the war itself. Cases under such notes were often small: one ship, one prisoner, one point of form.
frus-1862-d342:
Document 342 is the second Seward dispatch to William L. Dayton dated 4 November 1862, printed in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Secretary of State William H. Seward sent the whole set to the Paris legation together.

The middle letter of a same-day set often held the working detail: figures, copies, or points the envoy should raise in order. Election day in the North fell on this date, adding political noise to the channel. Seward's steady output that day shows a department refusing to let a foreign crisis wait on domestic politics. The Paris mail sailed from Le Havre and took about two weeks to reach Washington.
frus-1862-d42:
In a report dated 3 April 1862, Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London wrote home to Secretary of State William H. Seward. It was printed as Document 42 in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs for 1862. The letter comes from the spring of 1862, a year into the war, a time when each foreign capital watched the war with care.

Such reports fed the facts and rumors together into one desk in Washington, week by week. Read in order with its neighbors, it shows diplomacy as daily work rather than grand speeches. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1862-d442:
The Prussian file opens on 8 January 1862 with this instruction from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Norman B. Judd, the American minister in Berlin. It is Document 442 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs.

Prussia was rising in Europe and broadly friendly to the Union, and Judd, a Chicago lawyer close to Lincoln, held the Berlin post. German opinion mattered: German immigrants filled Union regiments, and Berlin's stance weighed in the balance of European courts. Seward's early order set out the case Judd was to make. The letter begins a correspondence that shows the Union cultivating the one great power whose sympathy it could mostly count on.
frus-1862-d542:
On 25 August 1862 Secretary of State William H. Seward sent this note to Roest van Limburg at the Netherlands legation. It is Document 542 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, printed with the annual message.

Seward wrote in the week of the second Bull Run campaign, when Washington itself felt exposed. Even so, the Dutch correspondence kept its even pace, one more proof that the Department's foreign business never paused for battle news. The questions at issue were the durable ones of neutral commerce under blockade. A reader following the Van Limburg file through August watches two governments maintain a working relationship. They do it by a simple means. They answer each other's letters, fully and on time.
frus-1862-d642:
On 14 October 1861 Townsend Harris wrote from Japan to Secretary of State William H. Seward. The dispatch is Document 642 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the official record laid before Congress.

By October, Harris had received the first news of the war at home, months old on arrival. His letter belongs to the season in which the distant posts learned, one ship at a time, that the republic was fighting for its life. His own report stuck to Japan: the treaty, the ports, and the legation's affairs. The restraint is characteristic of the file. At the far end of the world, the war changed the meaning of the mission without changing its daily work. Harris's letters show both truths at once.
frus-1863p1-d142:
Charles Francis Adams wrote this dispatch to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 3 April 1863. Three Adams letters in the volume bear the date. Adams was the American minister in London, and this letter is document 142 in part one of the 1863 volume.

A three-letter day in April matched the pace of the ship fight then at its height. Adams split his news across the sheets: talks, facts from the yards, and the temper of the town. This one opens the set of 3 April. In the run of the volume, the day stands as a peak of the legation's spring work.
frus-1863p1-d242: Secretary of State William H. Seward sent this instruction to Charles Francis Adams, his minister in London, on 20 July 1863. It is document 242 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume, within the orders that steered American policy toward Britain during the Civil War. Through such letters Washington told its man in London what to press, protest, or let pass.
frus-1863p1-d342:
One of Lord Lyons's regular notes to the State Department, this paper to Secretary of State William H. Seward is dated 20 December 1862. It appears as document 342 of the 1863 diplomatic papers. The text is preserved in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume, which gathered the year's diplomatic mail for Congress and the public.

Taken as a run, these notes chart Britain slowly accepting that the Union would not collapse. That judgment, formed in Washington, helped keep Britain out of the war. Alone it settles little; in the run of the volume it helps explain why Britain stayed out of the American war.
frus-1863p1-d42: Signed with the initial E., this paper is dated 18 October 1862. It is printed as document 42 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863. It sits among the Confederate papers in that part. The evidence gives a date and a lone initial but no full name and no one addressed, so this note stays at that level.
frus-1863p1-d442:
The letter printed as document 442 was written on 3 April 1863 by William H. Seward to Lord Lyons. Lyons was Britain's minister in Washington, and Seward was the American Secretary of State. At the time, the Union government was fighting the Confederacy at home and working to keep foreign powers neutral. The letter sits in the published record of how the Lincoln government handled foreign affairs in the spring of 1863.

The formal tone can hide the tension, but the pace gives it away. Notes this frequent mean both capitals were watching each other closely. British subjects caught up in the war filled many pages: men arrested, goods seized, and claims for losses that London took up with Washington. Kept with the rest of the 1863 papers, it helps the full story of wartime diplomacy stay traceable, letter by letter.
frus-1863p1-d542:
The date 29 May 1863 heads a letter from Assistant Secretary of State F. W. Seward to Lord Lyons, Britain's envoy in Washington. The two men at the ends of this channel, Seward in Washington and Lyons speaking for Britain, wrote to each other almost daily. The letter was later printed in the 1863 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, issued with the President's annual message.

The real subject under all the polite wording was British neutrality. Washington wanted it kept strict, and London wanted no quarrel it could avoid. The standing business of this channel was friction at sea. Union warships stopped British merchant ships, and each seizure could spark a formal protest. Readers who work through the file in order will find this letter where the clerks of 1863 left it, in the middle of the stream.
frus-1863p1-d642:
Dated 20 October 1863, document 642 is a letter from Secretary William H. Seward to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. Adams in London was the Union's front line in Britain, pressing its case with the British government week after week. Behind the formal phrases stood a live question: would Britain stay neutral, or step into the American war?

Adams's task was to make the Union's case where it counted, inside the British capital, while Seward set the line from Washington. The real subject under all the polite wording was British neutrality. Washington wanted it kept strict, and London wanted no quarrel it could avoid. That is the use of such a page: not a famous text, but a firm rung in the ladder of the record.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d142: Churchill wrote to Roosevelt on November 19, 1943, three days before the Cairo Conference opened. The message is Document 142 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. By then both leaders were in the Mediterranean world, and their letters crossed shorter distances than at any time in the series. The record gives the date and the two names and no subject. It survives in the Foreign Relations volume's arrival papers.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d242:
Assistant Secretary of War John McCloy wrote a secret memorandum at Cairo, dated about 21 November 1943, recording a dinner talk with Ambassador Harriman at Ambassador Kirk's house. Harriman, fresh from Moscow, shared his chief impressions of the Soviet mood, stressing that he spoke as a reporter, not an advocate.

The Soviets, he said, long passionately to end the war. Strained and tiring, they believe a prompt push with all forces at hand would make Germany crumble, and they hold Overlord as settled while still demanding more action this winter. Above all, they want real pressure on Turkey to join the war, which might by itself satisfy them. McCloy pressed for specifics and got none, since neither side knew the planners' facts well enough.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d342:
James Moose, the American minister resident in Saudi Arabia, was temporarily at Cairo. On 30 November 1943 he wrote a memorandum commenting on the British minister's telegram of 15 November. That telegram concerned arms for Saudi Arabia. That telegram, printed earlier in the volume, had complained of American questioning of King Ibn Saud.

Moose answers point by point. One of the seven questions listed was never asked, though the king's messenger supplied the answer anyway. What the British telegram left out, he says, is twofold. The king was told beforehand that Washington was consulting London on Saudi arms. And the American minister did discuss the inquiry with his British colleague within days. Moose also notes dryly that the British minister never checked his facts with that colleague before reporting to the Foreign Office.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d42: Roosevelt wrote to Stalin on October 14, 1943, one of several letters he sent that day. It is Document 42 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. The Moscow meeting of foreign ministers was five days off, and the leaders were setting the frame their ministers would work in. The catalog record names no subject for the letter. Its text appears in the Foreign Relations volume among the mid-October summit papers.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d442: Number 442 is one of the editorial notes written by the volume's historians. Foreign Relations volumes use such notes where the papers leave a gap. A note may summarize missing context or direct readers to another file. Here the setting is the Cairo-Tehran record from late 1943. Roosevelt and Churchill met in Cairo, then joined Stalin in Tehran. The note keeps that fast-moving sequence readable for later readers.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d542:
President Roosevelt answered Prime Minister Churchill on January 8, 1944, the day after Churchill's message to him. The quick exchange was typical of their wartime correspondence at full flow. The message appears in the State Department's Cairo-Tehran volume.

By January 1944 the questions before the two leaders ran from invasion planning to the shape of the postwar world promised in the Tehran Declaration. Roosevelt's replies to Churchill balanced agreement with the claims of his other partners, above all Stalin and Chiang. For readers, this message is one turn in the central conversation of the Western alliance, conducted when the war's outcome was turning in their favor.
frus-1944-quebec-d142:
The United States Chiefs of Staff replied to the British amendments on September 8, 1944, in C.C.S. 654/5. Two of the three British changes were accepted, each with American rewording. The third, on assisting other co-belligerents, Washington preferred to handle case by case, and it supplied its own text instead.

The agreed lines pledged measures to aid Russia, including coordinating the action of forces. Help for other co-belligerents was limited to available resources and to what they could effectively use against the Axis. On shifting forces to the Pacific, the Americans accepted a caution but wrote "agreed commitments" where the British had said "inescapable." Quebec would take up the settled text.
frus-1944-quebec-d242:
Churchill wrote to Roosevelt from Quebec on September 14, 1944, about the vacant chief commissionership of the Allied Control Commission for Italy. The post was a British appointment, empty since General MacFarlane's departure. To bring political knowledge to work so full of economic and political issues, Churchill proposed Harold Macmillan, who would keep his duties as resident minister and political adviser.

Day-to-day management would rest with the American deputy, Mr. Stone, in whom Churchill expressed great confidence. The appointment was urgent: the post had stood vacant two months. Churchill also hoped to discuss having Mayor La Guardia visit Italy as Roosevelt's representative and attend commission meetings, and to run through other proposals helpful to the Italians once Eden arrived.
frus-1944-quebec-d42:
On August 31, 1944, Roosevelt replied to Churchill. It was the last exchange before both men traveled to Quebec. The message appears in the State Department's Quebec 1944 volume.

Roosevelt's late August letters had a host's purpose. He meant to welcome his guest. He meant to frame the agenda. He also held American positions firm where argument was likely. The conference at Quebec City would open on September 12. For readers, this reply closes the written preparation. It hands the story to the conference itself. The whole volume has been building toward that meeting.
frus-1945-50-intel-d142:
"National Intelligence Authority Directive No. 2" bears the date 8 February 1946. The editors of Foreign Relations of the United States placed it as document 142 in the 1945 to 1950 intelligence volume. Washington was still building a peace-time spy service, run for the moment by the National Intelligence Authority and the Central Intelligence Group.

A directive is not advice: it is an order that offices below must follow until it is changed or replaced. Staff could be held to each line, which is why the words were fought over before issue. Its worth lies in the trail it leaves: a dated, signed step in the long build-up of the CIA and the Council.
frus-1945-50-intel-d242:
The Secretary of the State–Army–Navy–Air Force Coordinating Committee (Moseley) addressed a memorandum to the Under Secretary of State (Lovett) on 15 October 1947. The Office of the Historian kept it as document 242 in the Foreign Relations intelligence volume for 1945 to 1950. The National Security Act had just taken effect. The CIA had replaced the old group, and the Council had just begun to meet.

The form is plain on purpose: a named sender, a named reader, and a short statement of the matter at hand. A reader can watch the system think on paper: a fact here, a doubt there, a choice asked for at the end. The FRUS editors kept it because the chain of choices is not whole without it.
frus-1945-50-intel-d342:
On 12 March 1948, Secretary of State Marshall sent a memorandum to the Executive Secretary of the National Security Council (Souers). The Office of the Historian kept it as document 342 in the Foreign Relations intelligence volume for 1945 to 1950. With the Soviet threat in mind, the Council was deciding what secret work the United States should do abroad.

A memo of this kind was the basic tool of office work at the top. It put a matter before a senior man and asked for a choice, a signature, or a view. The reply, if any came, would build on the points laid out here. Kept with its neighbors in the volume, it shows the new system being built one dated paper at a time.
frus-1945-50-intel-d42:
The Lovett Committee sent its memorandum to Secretary of War Patterson on 3 November 1945. The committee, headed by Robert Lovett, had been asked to study how intelligence should be organized in peace. It is printed in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the retrospective volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

Committee reports are where scattered views get hammered into a program. The Lovett group's paper gave the War Department a worked-out position in the contest with State and the Budget Bureau. Readers should treat it as a landmark in the run: after it, the argument had full plans on every side. The committee's name recurs through the autumn papers as its members carried their study into the wider fight.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d142:
Cabinet seats were the currency in Churchill's Moscow report of 22 October 1944. This excerpt of his message number 801 to Roosevelt is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. It tells what happened on the last day of the Moscow talks on Poland.

Mikolajczyk met Bierut, the Lublin leader. Bierut admitted his troubles freely: fifty of his men shot in a month. Many Poles were taking to the woods rather than join his forces. Bierut still demanded three-quarters of the cabinet if Mikolajczyk became premier. Mikolajczyk countered with seats for each of the five Polish parties. Stalin then saw him for over an hour, in a friendly talk, but held firm that the Lublin Poles must have the majority.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d242:
Ambassador Patrick Hurley summed up the Chungking–Communist talks for the President on 14 January 1945. His top secret cable from Chungking, printed in the Malta and Yalta volume, is for the President's eyes alone. It traces his own shuttle between the two Chinese camps.

After fruitless talks at Sian and Chungking, Hurley went to Yenan and came back with a five-point proposal signed by Mao Tse-tung. Chou En-lai returned with him and stayed a month. The National Government countered with three points, which the Communists refused. Chou's talks looked promising until his final meeting with the Generalissimo, at which Hurley was not present. Chiang, Hurley reports, is now ready to grant all the five points but one: he will not have a coalition government or a coalition military council.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d342:
Fuel, landing craft, and dates for the war's end fill this Combined Chiefs session at Alupka on February 6, 1945. The chiefs first checked the supply of petroleum products in Britain and northwest Europe. They then set planning dates for the end of the war against Germany. The earliest date was July 1, 1945. The date past which the war was unlikely to run was December 31, 1945.

Landing vehicles for the Mediterranean also came up, and then the zones of occupation in Germany. The minutes mix the grand and the plain. Wars at this level were run as much on oil stocks and calendars as on battle maps.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d42: Churchill wrote to Roosevelt on 5 January 1945, as both capitals counted down to departure. The message is document 42 in the Foreign Relations of the United States volume on the Malta and Yalta conferences. January letters between the two men carried the last written exchanges before they could simply talk in person, first at Malta and then alongside Stalin at Yalta.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d442:
Britain's answer on reparations, dated February 10, 1945, starts from fairness among the claimants. Shares allotted to each country, London proposed, should be set by two measures. The first was each country's contribution to winning the war. The second was the degree of material loss it had suffered. Deliveries from other enemy countries would also count.

Payment would come in three forms. The first was removals within two years of Germany's surrender, drawn from German wealth at home and abroad. These removals aimed chiefly at destroying Germany's war potential. The paper avoids the Soviet fixed sum. It offers principles where Moscow offered a number — the core of the reparations dispute.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d142:
President Truman backed Churchill's handling of the German fleet question in a telegram dated May 28, 1945. The printed message, partly cut, is document 142 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. Churchill had told Stalin that the fate of the surrendered German naval and merchant ships belonged on the summit agenda.

Truman says he is in general agreement with Churchill's reply to Stalin about the ships, and that he will send Stalin a similar message of his own. The rest of the telegram is not printed here; a note points readers to another document for its final paragraph. The brief cable aligned Washington with London before Truman wrote to Moscow, an early case of the two Western leaders coordinating their lines to Stalin.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d242:
Acting Secretary Grew told London the Italy announcement would go ahead in an urgent telegram dated July 14, 1945. The message to Ambassador Winant is document 242 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. Italy had now declared war on Japan, with the declaration to be made public on July 15.

The Department therefore proposes to announce on July 17 its intention to support officially Italy's admission in due course to the world security organization, Grew writes. Winant is to inform the Foreign Office urgently and express the hope that the British government will support the American position. The date chosen, July 17, was the day the Potsdam Conference opened, which soon put the announcement on a collision course with the British.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d342:
Secretary of War Stimson took up the German import fight in a letter to the Secretary of State dated July 4, 1945. He had weighed Clayton's letter of June 18 about who in Washington should pay for imports into Germany. Stimson pointed back to his own letter of June 14 on the same problem.

No money, he stressed, had been voted to finance supplies for Germany and Austria beyond the War Department's narrow military duty. With no funds in hand, the question could not be settled between departments. Stimson closed by backing a small group, McCloy and Judge Rosenman among them, to draft recommendations for the President.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d42:
On May 30, 1945, Soviet leader Joseph Stalin sent President Harry Truman a short secret message from Moscow. It is document 42 in the first volume of the Foreign Relations of the United States papers on the Potsdam Conference. Germany had just surrendered, and the three Allied leaders were fixing a date to meet and settle the peace.

Stalin's whole message takes two lines. He says that Harry Hopkins, Truman's envoy, had passed on the President's proposal about the meeting of the three, and that he had no objection to the suggested date of July 15. The note is a small but real step toward the Potsdam Conference, which opened near Berlin two days later than planned.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d442:
Greece opens the briefing book's country papers with an appeal for an active, benevolent American interest. To take such an interest now, the paper argues, offers a most practical way to show American resolve. The United States, it says, means to play a world role that matches its strength and its public pledges. Greece has traditionally stood closer to Britain than to any other great power.

Yet a friendly bond between America and Greece runs deep, the paper says. Greece is the ancient home of democratic ideals. Classical learning, reaching America through Rome, helped shape the republican ideas of the young United States. The American example in turn stirred Greece's own fight for freedom from the Ottoman Empire.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d542:
President Harry Truman wrote to the Secretary of State on July 5, 1945, from Washington. His short secret memo is document 542 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. It deals with lend-lease arms now that the war in Europe has ended.

Truman says he has that day sent an order to the Joint Chiefs of Staff. The order lets lend-lease arms and gear go to allied states only for use in the war against Japan, and for no other end. It grew out of a June 28 memo on lifting a ban on supplies to French troops. The note shows how fast aid rules were tightened once Europe was at peace.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d642:
Minister Wadsworth sent Washington the text of a French statement on the Levant forces late on July 8, 1945. His wire, marked restricted, is document 642 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on Potsdam. Copies of the French text were mailed to Arab capitals.

The statement comes from the French Provisional Government. It declares that the locally raised troops are transferred to the Syrian and Lebanese governments. The terms of the transfer will be defined within a maximum delay of 45 days. Paris frames the move as good will toward two states now holding full sovereignty. With the war in Europe over, it says, there is no bar left to Syria and Lebanon forming their own national armies.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1042:
Thomas Blaisdell, chief of the American economic mission in London, cabled a confidential report on British coal on July 21, 1945. A British working party had surveyed the country's large coal position. The War Cabinet was weighing its findings, and Blaisdell shares the likely outcome. The report signals the stand Britain will take at Potsdam.

The findings are stark. Britain cannot export large coal after August, nor any coal usable at home after September deliveries. London will ask America to keep supplying bunker coal, about 100,000 tons a month. That need lasts until captured ships can be fueled from Polish and Silesian sources instead. Only very low grade fuel, unusable in Britain, could be spared later.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1142:
Charles Yost of the Central Secretariat wrote this memorandum on 8 August 1945, his second in the closing series. A week after the summit ended, the American team's paperwork chief was still at work. The delegations had gone home; the files had not.

Closing out a summit means fixing the record: what was agreed, in what words, and where each paper belongs. Yost's notes did that work for the American side. The famous part of Potsdam is the leaders' talk. The lasting part is the archive, and notes like this one built it. They show the summit's long tail of plain, careful labor.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1242:
The Secretary of State wrote to the Acting Secretary of State on 21 July 1945. The direction ran from Potsdam home: Byrnes reporting and directing from the talks, Grew holding the department in Washington. The pair exchanged word through the whole summit.

A secretary's cable home could carry the talks' drift, fresh orders for the desks, or word the president wanted spread. The home office then acted on it within the day. This message is the summit end of the circuit at work. It shows the chief abroad running his department at a distance, by cable, in the talks' first week.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1342:
George Allen of the Near Eastern and African affairs office wrote once more to Assistant Secretary James Dunn on 25 July 1945. The two men exchanged several papers during the Potsdam weeks. The text comes from the second Potsdam volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, the State Department's official history series.

Repeated notes between the same pair of officials show a working tie, not a one-off message. Allen's desk spoke for a region where oil, bases, and new states were all in play in the summer of 1945. Readers following the Allen and Dunn papers through the volume can watch a policy line form in real time, one short paper at a time.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-142:
Arthur Bliss Lane, newly appointed as ambassador to Poland, wrote to the Acting Secretary of State on July 31, 1945. Poland sat at the heart of the Potsdam dispute. Its borders and its government had strained the alliance for months. Lane was preparing to take up the Warsaw post as the conference closed. His letter entered the second Potsdam volume.

An incoming ambassador's letter carries a field view. Lane wrote about the post he was to fill and the country he would face. Readers see the human end of a headline issue: one envoy getting ready to work inside a hard settlement. The letter links the conference table to the embassy desk.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-42:
A United States delegation working paper lists the agenda for the heads of government meeting of July 20, 1945. It is an unnumbered item in volume two of the Foreign Relations papers on Potsdam. The paper, from the Truman Papers, was apparently before the President during the session.

Six items are listed for the 4 p.m. meeting. They are the Council of Ministers, Italy in the United Nations with a reference to Spain, and Austria, with a paper from Churchill. The western frontiers of Poland and trusteeship follow, both on Soviet papers of that morning. Turkey closes the list, on a paper Churchill was to present. Truman's own hand adds the session's fate in the margins. He marked the council disposed of, the Italy item referred to the foreign secretaries, and the Austria item settled. The last three items he marked postponed.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d742:
The Secretary of State answered Gerig on August 8, 1945, in document 742. The reply came a week after Potsdam closed. Business about the United Nations' first steps did not pause for the summit's end. Byrnes wrote from a Washington resetting itself for peace. The letter entered the second Potsdam volume.

A secretary's reply closes a loop opened by a field report. Readers can pair this letter with Gerig's July notes. The exchange shows guidance flowing back down the line. It also marks a shift in the volume's mood: from dividing a beaten continent to staffing the body meant to keep the peace.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d842:
The United States delegation tabled this proposal on July 25, 1945, as document 842. It belongs to the conference's second week. American texts by then were written against a clear map of resistance. The proposal joined the second Potsdam volume beside rival drafts.

A July 25 American proposal shows the endgame being prepared early. Its writers aimed at lines the final protocol could hold. Readers can test how many of those lines survived. The document also shows the delegation's drafting depth. Fresh texts kept coming while older ones were still being fought over in committee. That depth was itself a form of strength.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d942:
Edwin Pauley sent the Secretary of State a draft letter to Soviet negotiator Ivan Maisky on July 28, 1945. A twin letter to President Truman goes with it. Pauley asks both men to review the draft before he sends it. He says the pair of letters gives a brief history of the reparations talks and America's present attitude.

The Maisky draft recalls twenty-two days in Moscow with no Soviet plan presented. It presses the need to define reparations, restitution, and war booty as a first step. Pauley also argues that a written record matters. Public interest in America will be high, and spoken words are easily misquoted.
frus-1952-54v13p2-d842: A 1952-1954 FRUS cable from the Chargé at Saigon. America's man reported from Vietnam. This document preserves that telegram. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The paper lived through the years.
frus-1964-68v23-d42: A 1964-1968 FRUS memorandum for the record on the Congo. The crisis, noted. This entry preserves that memo. The paper lived through the years. Tomorrow's readers will find it. History keeps its place secure. The archive keeps the paper open to all who seek it.
frus-1969-76v17-d142: A 1969-1976 FRUS memorandum of conversation on China. The talks were recorded. This entry preserves that conversation. Writers of history may cite it later. The paper lasts as a quiet witness. Time has kept the file intact.
