gao-gaoreports-b-295742: United Enterprise & Associates carried an April 2005 dispute to GAO, and the ruling renders the verdict. The firm's challenge got the complete examination. The enterprise met its judgment. The judgment was rendered fully. The verdict was complete. The call was complete.
gao-gaoreports-b-297342: Alion Science & Technology took its January 2006 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict on the claims. The firm said the agency's award was unfair, and the call tests the protest. Tech firms get the same full hearing as all.
gao-gaoreports-b-297742: Trailboss Enterprises took its March 2006 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict on the claims. The firm said the agency's award was unfair, and the call tests the protest. Every challenger gets the full fair-play hearing.
gao-gaoreports-b-299342: Alliance Detective & Security Service took its April 2007 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict. The firm said the agency's award was unfair; the call tests the protest. Security firms get their day in bid court like everyone else.
gao-gaoreports-b-310442: This 2007 decision resolves a federal contract protest filed by D&J Enterprises, Inc. Decided December 13, 2007, it reviews whether the agency ran a fair competition. Agencies almost always follow these rulings, which build the case law for federal contracts. The full text sits with this description in the library.
gao-gaoreports-b-310542: This 2008 decision resolves a federal contract protest filed by Horizon Industries, Limited. The January 7, 2008 ruling examines how the agency evaluated the bids. The ruling sets ground rules for future federal contract contests. It is kept here as part of the lasting public record.
gao-gaoreports-b-311242: This 2008 decision resolves a federal contract protest filed by Division Laundry and Cleaners, Inc. Decided May 19, 2008, it reviews whether the agency ran a fair competition. The ruling sets ground rules for future federal contract contests. It is kept here as part of the lasting public record.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-1042: FDA medical device reviews were meeting some goals in 2005, and GAO's report says limited data indicated progress on review targets. The findings give the partial credit. The report warns that the device approvals deserved honest measuring. The goals had to be met.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-242: NASA's Prometheus nuclear rocket needed a business case in 2005, and GAO's report says the requirements had to match the resources. The review does the math. The deep-space dream deserved the honest budget. The case had to be made. The deep-space dream deserved the honest budget.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-342: HUD's fair rent math needed improving in 2005, and GAO's report says the process for estimating fair market rents could be better. The review checks the arithmetic. The renters deserved the honest numbers. The process had to improve. The renters deserved the honest numbers.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-642: Embassy guard gaps got a GAO flag in 2005, and the report says the State shop left key shields unfinished. The findings sound the alarm. The report warns that the diplomats deserved full protection. The diplomats deserved full protection. The shields had to rise.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-742: Afghanistan's rebuild was under siege in 2005, and GAO's report says the guns and roadblocks put the gains at risk. The findings sound the alarm. The report warns that the rebuilding deserved protection. The rebuilding deserved protection. The siege had to be broken.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-1042: The Pentagon's flu planning needed accountability in 2006, and GAO's report says important preparation steps had been taken, though funding and communications lagged. The findings balance credit and warning. The report cautions that the pandemic plan needed more than good intentions. The planning had to be funded.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-342: Offshoring had reached human services in 2006, and GAO's report says it occurred in most states, mainly in customer service. The findings map the spread. The report warns that the helping programs' jobs were moving abroad. The trend had to be faced.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-42: Cash balance pension plans got a GAO explainer in 2005, and the report provides information on the hybrid plans. The findings take the measure. The report warns that the retirees deserved to understand their pensions. The information had to be given.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-642: Converting military medical jobs needed full cost counts in 2006, and GAO's report says the departments had to ensure the complete costs were known. The findings demand the math. The report warns that the uniformed-to-civilian switch deserved honest numbers. The costs had to be counted.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-942: Human service programs needed simplifying in 2006, and GAO's report says demonstration projects could find ways to ease policies and tech. The findings propose the experiments. The report warns that the helping bureaucracy should not hinder the helped. The programs had to be simpler.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-242: The bank insurance fund's safety rules got a GAO grade in 2007, and the report assesses how regulators used the prompt corrective action powers. The findings test the enforcement. The report asks whether the watchdogs bit when the banks wobbled. The safety net needed its own safety check.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-42: Appliance efficiency rules were stuck in molasses in 2007, and GAO's report says the Energy Department's standard-setting problems kept costing consumers. The findings target the delays. The report warns that the watt-wasters were winning by default. The standards needed speed.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-342: This 2008 report from the Government Accountability Office looks at defense Management: More Transparency Needed over the Financial and Human Capital Operations of the Joint Improvised Explosive Device Defeat Organization. Working for Congress, GAO checks how federal programs spend money and whether they deliver results. Its conclusions can shape how agencies run their programs.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-42: This 2007 report from the Government Accountability Office looks at air Traffic Control: FAA Reports Progress in System Acquisitions, but Changes in Performance Measurement Could Improve Usefulness of Information. Working for Congress, GAO checks how federal programs spend money and whether they deliver results. The library keeps it in the public record of federal watchdog work.
gogol-dead-souls-1842:
Nikolai Gogol published Dead Souls in 1842, a comic novel left unfinished at his death. Chichikov, a smooth former official, travels through rural Russia with an odd plan. He buys the names of serfs who have died but are still listed on the tax rolls. Landowners react with confusion, greed, or suspicion.

Each visit reveals a different kind of folly and decay. Chichikov hopes to use the dead souls as paper wealth to gain status. Gogol mixes farce with a deep sadness about Russian life. The book is vast in scope and sharp in detail. It stands among the great works of Russian literature.
histoire-de-la-philosophie-hermetique-ac: Histoire de la philosophie hermetique, 1742. The hermetic philosophy history. This book preserves that work. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources.
hutcheson-philosophiae-moralis-instituti:
Hutcheson's short Latin textbook of moral philosophy appeared in 1742, written for his Glasgow students. Its full title means a brief introduction to moral philosophy. Hutcheson taught in Latin in his early years, and this compendium gave his classroom system in compact form.

The book sets out his moral-sense theory: humans approve virtue through a built-in sense, as they see color through sight. From that ground it builds duties to God, to others, and to oneself, along with the basics of law and government. Adam Smith, Hutcheson's student, later carried parts of the scheme into his own famous works. The little Latin volume is the Scottish Enlightenment's ethics in its first, classroom form, before the larger English system appeared after the author's death.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lowe-ludwig-101:
Ludwig Löwe, a German physician, receives a biographical entry in the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. Born at Berlin on March 11, 1844, he studied medicine at Jena, Würzburg, Strasburg, and Breslau. He took his medical degree at Breslau in 1872. The next year he became an assistant at Strasburg's anatomical institute.

The article follows his moves between research and practice. He worked at Berlin's Charité hospital, lectured on anatomy at the University of Bern from 1878, and finally settled in Berlin. There he practiced as a specialist in diseases of the ear, nose, and throat. His books cover the anatomy of the nose, the development of the nervous system, and a textbook of ear medicine. The entry preserves the career path of a Jewish doctor inside German academic medicine.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-machir-10242:
Machir is treated in the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia as the name of two men in the Bible. The first was the first-born son of Manasseh. He founded the dominant branch of that tribe, and the Song of Deborah pairs Ephraim with Machir rather than Manasseh. That pairing suggests the whole tribe once bore his name.

The article follows the first Machir east of the Jordan. He conquered Gilead and added Bashan to his territory, and so is called the father of Gilead. Scholars cited here place that conquest after the first invasion, as a movement back from western Palestine. The second Machir, son of Ammiel, kept an estate at Lo-debar. He sheltered Jonathan's son Mephibosheth out of loyalty to Saul's house. Later he fed David's army during Absalom's revolt. The entry keeps two loyal figures of the same name clearly apart.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-man-son-of-hebr:
Son of Man, the Hebrew phrase ben adam, is studied in a Jewish Encyclopedia article from 1906 by Kaufmann Kohler. In plain use it means simply a human being. It appears in poetry and prophecy, and ben enosh occurs once in the Psalms. God addresses Ezekiel by the title some ninety times.

The article explains that usage as a lesson in distance. The title reminds the prophet that he stays a frail mortal while God speaks. A harder case comes from Daniel's vision of one like a son of man. That figure receives an everlasting kingdom from the Ancient of Days. Commentators agree Israel is meant, but dispute the form. Some read the figure as the people personified, others as the Messiah or Michael. The rabbis leaned to the Messiah reading. The entry follows the term into apocalyptic books and the New Testament, where it became a favorite messianic name.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-martinez-ferran:
Ferrand Martinez, archdeacon of Ecija in fourteenth-century Spain, is portrayed in a Jewish Encyclopedia entry from 1906 by Richard Gottheil and Meyer Kayserling. Martinez lived at Seville, where Christians honored him for piety and charity. Toward the Jews, though, he was a relentless enemy who used his sermons to stir public hatred against them.

Acting as vicar-general, he claimed court power over the Jews of his district and injured them wherever he could. Two kings, Henry II in 1378 and John I in 1382 and 1383, ordered him by letter and edict to stop, and he ignored them all. The entry follows the Seville community's fight back, ending with the public trial of February 1388, where Martinez openly refused to change his course.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-meturgeman-inte:
Meturgeman, meaning interpreter, was the synagogue official who translated the weekly Bible reading aloud for worshippers who no longer understood Hebrew. Solomon Schechter and Caspar Levias wrote the entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. It traces the office back to the Levites who taught the people after the return from exile.

The article explains that the meturgeman rendered the Pentateuch verse by verse and the Prophets three verses at a time, working from memory rather than from a book. Because interpreters often expanded the text into sermons, rabbis pushed for fixed translations, and the darshan, or preacher, took over the teaching role. The entry preserves how public Bible teaching worked in ancient Palestine.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-milman-henry-ha:
Henry Hart Milman, a London historian born on February 10, 1791, wrote the History of the Jews that scandalized his church in 1830. Joseph Jacobs and S. J. Levinson give him a Jewish Encyclopedia entry in 1906. Brilliant at Oxford, he first won fame with dramatic poems like Fazio and The Fall of Jerusalem before turning to prose history.

His Jewish history treated the Jews as an Oriental tribe and explained away every miracle, drawing the Church's censure for its rationalism. Yet representative Jews presented him with a piece of plate for his sympathetic attitude, and the book was twice republished. Milman became Dean of St. Paul's in 1849, edited Gibbon, and was the first to translate Sanskrit epics into English.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-moncalvo-10942:
Moncalvo, a small town in Piedmont's province of Alessandria, kept a French accent in its synagogue for centuries, as Richard Gottheil and Ismar Elbogen note in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Its Jews arrived after the expulsion from France, and like Asti and Fossano the community held to the old French ritual long after. It still used the German prayer-book with French additions.

In 1866 the community numbered 220 souls, many of them artisans in various trades, with its philanthropic societies and ritual institutions intact; by the article's time it had shrunk considerably. Joseph Lattes, who died in 1880, served for a while as its rabbi. The entry is a paragraph, but it preserves a liturgical fossil: a French rite surviving in an Italian hill town.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-moscow-11042:
Moscow, the Russian city, is covered in a long Jewish Encyclopedia article by Herman Rosenthal and J. Hessen. For centuries Jews were barred from living there, appearing only as passing individuals. Ivan the Terrible refused a Lithuanian request in 1549 to let Jews visit for trade. Bans were repeated in treaty after treaty.

Real settlement came slowly: merchants lodged in a locked Jewish Inn, and Jewish soldiers of Nicholas the First stayed on with their families. Under Alexander the Second, artisans, merchants, and the educated won the right to live in the city. The community reached about eight thousand in 1871 and over twenty thousand by 1890. Then the decrees of 1891 ordered Jewish artisans and old soldiers expelled, and the article follows that blow in detail.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nathalie-zaire-:
Zaïre Martel Nathalie was a French stage actress. Isidore Singer and Edgar Mels wrote her entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. She was born at Tournon on Sept. 3, 1816. She died on Nov. 17, 1885. Her first stage role came in Paris in 1837.

She debuted as Azurine in the fairy ballet La Fille de l'Air. From 1838 she played at the Gymnase in Paris for seven years. Her roles there included parts in La Gitana and Jean le Noir. After a good season in London, she joined the Palais-Royal. In 1849 she moved to the Comédie Française in Paris. She became a full member within three years and retired in 1876.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nijni-novgorod-:
Nijni-Novgorod is a Russian city famed for its fairs. Herman Rosenthal and S. Janovsky wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. It stands outside the Pale of Settlement. Rules of 1835 first let Jewish merchants visit its fair. They could stay only while the fair lasted.

Jews settled there anyway, slowly, against prohibitive laws. On July 7, 1884, a mob attacked them in Kunavina. Some were tortured to death on a child-murder rumor. After 1888 officials stripped fair rights from Jewish merchants. Christian rivals claimed Jews undersold them by thirty-five per cent. Yet some 550 Jewish families live there permanently. Most are well-to-do in spite of every bar.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-obadiah-book-of:
The Book of Obadiah is the shortest book of the Hebrew Bible. Emil G. Hirsch and George A. Barton wrote on it for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. It holds just twenty-one verses in all. Its title is The Vision of Obadiah. All of it is a word of doom against Edom.

The first part shows Edom pressed hard by her foes. She dwelt high in the clefts of the rock. God would bring her down from that proud height. The next part gives the cause of her fall. Edom had done harm to her brother Jacob. She stood by when strangers took Jerusalem by lot. The book ends with hope for Israel. Captives would come back and hold the towns of the south.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-opper-frederick:
Frederick Burr Opper was an American artist of comic politics. Cyrus Adler and I. George Dobsevage wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Madison, Ohio, on January 2, 1857. He left school at the age of fourteen years. He then worked for a short time in a news office.

In 1873 Opper went to New York to try his luck. Sales of his fun sketches led him to choose art. He worked three years for Frank Leslie's Weekly. He then spent eighteen years as chief artist for Puck. Puck was a famed comic weekly of that age. In 1899 he joined the staff of the New York Journal. His work in the race of 1900 drew wide note. Those drawings came out in book form in 1901. He also drew for books by Mark Twain.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-padovani-elisha:
Elishama Meir Padovani was an Italian scholar of the Talmud. The board and Ismar Elbogen wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born in Modena, in Italy, in his age. He died at Padua in the year 1830. He was taught and first served as rabbi at Modena.

From Modena, Elishama became joint rabbi at Mantua town. He shared that post with Jacob Cases, a rabbi there. In the end he became rabbi of Padua itself. There he taught M. G. Ghirondi, a known scholar. He wrote sermons and rulings on the law in his life. He wrote a short brief of laws from the great code. That code was the Shulhan Aruk, in its part Yoreh De'ah. His brief lay in hand script in Ghirondi's hands.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-patience-11942:
Patience, as the Bible and the rabbis teach it, is the theme of this article. Kaufmann Kohler and M. H. Harris wrote it for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Hebrew has several words for the virtue. Each one shades the idea in a different way.

One key term means long suffering, the holding back of just anger. Scripture lists that restraint among the traits of God. A second kind of patience rests on faith. It waits in silence for God's help through hard times. Job and Aaron stand as models of it. A Talmud tale adds that patience can be worth real money.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-politzer-adam-1:
Adam Politzer was an Austrian ear doctor born in Hungary in 1835. Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He studied medicine at the University of Vienna. He took his diploma there in 1859 and worked at the university hospital.

Politzer rose step by step at Vienna. He taught ear surgery from 1861 on. He led the ear clinic from 1873 and became full professor in 1895. He built a noted museum of ear specimens for the clinic. His chief book is a textbook of ear medicine from 1878. It reached a fourth edition by 1902. He also made charts and an atlas of the eardrum.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-punishment-1244:
Punishment in Jewish law is the subject of an article by the Editorial Board and Lewis N. Dembitz. It appeared in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. A court may pass a set range of sentences, they show. Death may be given in one of four forms. Exile to a city of refuge fits a chance killing.

Stripes may be given for breach of a ban. They must not pass forty in count. In practice they stopped at thirty-nine or fewer. Sister articles treat death, crime, and stripes in full. This article takes up the less set penalties as well. It sorts fines, shame, and other court acts by kind.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rainbow-12542:
Rainbows appear only rarely in the Old Testament. Emil G. Hirsch, Immanuel Benzinger, Wilhelm Bacher, and Judah David Eisenstein wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Scripture praises the rainbow's beauty in Sirach. Ezekiel compares God's glory to its splendor.

The article centers on Genesis and the story of the Flood. God set the bow in the clouds as a covenant sign. The writers explain that bow as a war bow laid aside. Its sight means anger has passed and no flood will come. A rabbinical part asks when the rainbow was created. The entry links a sky sight to promise, myth, and teaching.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-recanati-10642:
Recanati is a town in Italy on the Musone river. Isidore Singer and Umberto Cassuto wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. It lay in the province of Macerata. Jews lived there as early as the thirteenth century.

The article says Jewish money lenders were valued in the Marches. Most towns had one who ranked almost as an official. In 1433 a Recanati Jew won leave to lend at Urbino. Yet popular hatred of lenders stayed strong. In 1447 the pope banned lending at interest. Mobs rose in Rome and across Italy after that order. Recanati's Jews sought a joint defense with other towns. The entry shows a useful trade under constant threat.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-reggio-abraham-:
Abraham Vita ben Azriel Reggio was an Italian rabbi and cabalist born in 1755. Isidore Singer and M. Seligsohn wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was born at Ferrara. He died at Göritz on January 8, 1842.

The article says he studied under Samuel Lampronti. Hebrew grammar was his special focus. He taught Hebrew to children in several villages. In spare time he bound books. He later taught at the Talmud Torah of Göritz. After his teacher there died, he became rabbi in 1798. Leading rabbis asked him for legal decisions. His main work, Eshel Abraham, stayed in manuscript. It holds thirteen treatises on varied subjects. He also wrote against his own son's pamphlet.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-richetti-joseph:
Joseph Shalit Richetti was a rabbi of the later seventeenth century. Isidore Singer and Umberto Cassuto wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was born in Safed. From there he removed to Italy.

The article names his work on the purposes of the Tabernacle. It is called Sefer Hokmat ha-Mishkan. It appeared with his edition on Palestine's sacred cities. That combined work came out at Mantua in 1676. He edited a collection of Talmud and Midrash tales. That book appeared at Verona in 1647. He also edited a ritual for the new moon day. It was printed at Venice in 1661. Two initials close the brief entry. Readers learn an editor who preserved tales and rites alike.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rosenberg-juliu:
Julius Rosenberg was a Hungarian deputy born at Kis-Czell on September 12, 1856. Isidore Singer and Ludwig Venetianer wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. He studied law at Budapest, took his degree in 1877, and joined the bar in 1880.

Even before graduating, Rosenberg was known as an authority on maritime law. He sat on the board of the Adria Steamship Company, aiding Hungary's trade. In 1892 his district sent him to the Hungarian Parliament. There he helped frame economic laws and reported on trade treaties with foreign nations. In 1885 he had fought a duel with Count Stephan Batthyanyi, killing him.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-russell-henry-1:
Henry Russell was an English composer and singer born at Sheerness on December 24, 1812. Joseph Jacobs and Goodman Lipkind wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. He learned singing from Bellini in Italy and counterpoint from Donizetti.

Russell settled at Rochester, New York, in 1843 as a piano teacher. For years he toured America with entertainments built from his own songs. Eight hundred songs came from his pen, and 760 of them were published. Singing them earned him a fortune, though print brought him little. Known titles include A Life on the Ocean Wave and Cheer, Boys, Cheer.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-salonica-saloni:
Salonica, or Saloniki, is a seaport city in European Turkey, on its gulf. Isidore Singer, Isaac Broydé, and Joseph Jacobs wrote its entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. A Jewish community likely stood there in the first century.

Paul's letters imply Jews at Salonica in apostolic times already. The earliest document comes from the age of the first Crusade, though. A Cairo genizah letter says the emperor freed Salonica's Jews from taxation then. Benjamin of Tudela, about 1170, found 500 Jews working at handicrafts. Immigrants from Germany, France, and Italy swelled the community afterward.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-samuel-sampson-:
Joseph Jacobs and Goodman Lipkind wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906, on Sampson Samuel. He was a solicitor and secretary to the London Board of Deputies. Samuel was born in 1804. He died in London on November 10, 1868. He began his working life on the Stock Exchange. After some years he left it and trained in the law.

As solicitor and secretary, Samuel advised the Board on many weighty questions. He traveled with Sir Moses Montefiore on his mission to Morocco. He served as honorary solicitor to several leading charities. He sat on the committee of the Great Synagogue. He also helped found the Jews' Infant School in London. He stayed active in running it. The entry honors a lawyer who served his community for decades.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sayce-archibald:
Joseph Jacobs wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906, on Archibald Henry Sayce. He was an English archaeologist. Sayce was born at Shirehampton on September 25, 1846. He studied at Queen's College, Oxford, and became a fellow there in 1869. From 1876 to 1890 he was deputy professor of comparative philology. He also served on the Old Testament Revision Company.

Sayce wrote many works on Assyriology, the study of ancient Assyria. He tried to read the Hittite inscriptions and those of Lake Van. His Races of the Old Testament appeared in 1891. He accepted some findings of the higher critics. Yet he also argued that the El-Amarna tablets backed the early Bible narratives. His books include The Higher Criticism and the Verdict of the Monuments. For his health he wintered in Egypt. There he first tapped the Cairo genizah treasures for Oxford.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-schwarz-joseph-:
Isidore Singer and Judah David Eisenstein wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906, on Joseph Schwarz. He was a geographer of Palestine. Schwarz was born at Flosz, in Bavaria, on October 22, 1804. He died at Jerusalem on February 5, 1865. He trained as a teacher at Colberg. At Würzburg he spent five years on the Holy Land's history and geography. He published a map of Palestine in 1829.

In 1833 Schwarz settled in Jerusalem to study the land itself. For some fifteen years he traveled and explored Palestine. He recorded its history, rocks, plants, and animals. Scholars rank him first among Jewish authorities since Estori Farḥi. On the Mount of Olives he logged sunrise and sunset for a full year. In 1849 he toured England and America as an emissary. Isaac Leeser translated his Tebu'ot ha-Areẓ into English.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-shem-ha-meforas:
Shem ha-Meforash is an old tannaitic name for the Tetragrammaton, God's four-letter name. Wilhelm Bacher wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on the term. Its exact sense stays somewhat obscure, the entry admits. A close term, Shem ha-Meyuhad, offers a helpful clue.

Both words mark something set apart by a special sign. Joined with shem, meaning the name, they signal preeminence. So the phrase means God's excellent, distinctive name. It differs from every other name used for Him. Old readings of Numbers use the term for my name. The entry works through rabbinic sources to explain how Jews guarded the holiest name in speech and law.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-siegel-henry-13:
Henry Siegel was an American merchant born at Eubigheim, Germany, in 1852. Cyrus Adler and Frederick T. Haneman wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on him. At fifteen he emigrated to the United States alone. He clerked for firms in Washington, Parkersburg, and Lawrenceburg.

In 1876 Siegel founded the firm of Siegel, Hartsfield and Company. Ten years later came the great Siegel Cooper department store. Both firms were based in Chicago, the entry notes. A New York branch of Siegel Cooper opened in 1896. In 1902 he bought two more large store companies. He also took up residence in New York that year. He presided over the Fourteenth Street Store there. The brief entry traces a clerk's climb to department store magnate.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-simon-sir-john-:
Sir John Simon was an English serjeant at law and politician born in Jamaica in 1818. Joseph Jacobs wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was sent to England in 1833 for schooling. He studied Hebrew alone, hoping to become a rabbi. His father refused consent to that plan for religious reform.

Simon graduated from the University of London in 1841. He was called to the bar at the Middle Temple in 1842. He was the first Jew to practise at the common-law bar. He later led the northern circuit with great success. In 1864 he was created a serjeant at law. He also sat on the bench in Manchester and Liverpool.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-solomon-13842:
Solomon was the third king of all Israel, reigning about 971 to 931 BCE. Emil G Hirsch, Ira Maurice Price, Wilhelm Bacher, M Seligsohn, Mary W Montgomery, and Crawford Howell Toy wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was the second son of David and Bath-sheba. Nathan the prophet called him Jedidiah, beloved of the Lord.

His name Solomon means peaceful, fitting his calm reign. When Adonijah tried to seize the throne, Nathan acted at once. By David's order, Solomon was crowned king instead that day. Adonijah fled to the horns of the altar in terror. Solomon spared his life on oath, and his reign began. The long entry follows his reign from the Bible and Chronicles.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-spanier-meyer-1:
Meyer Spanier was a German educationist and writer born in 1864. Isidore Singer wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was born at Wunstorf, Hanover, on November 1. He studied philosophy and Germanic philology at Heidelberg. He took his doctor's degree there in 1894.

For some years Spanier taught in schools at Altona and Hamburg. In 1900 he was called to Münster in Westphalia. He became director of the Jewish teachers' seminary there that year. His works include an edition of Murner's Narrenbeschwörung from 1894. He also wrote on art pictures for schools in 1897. Another book treated Gustav Falke as a lyric poet in 1900.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sterne-simon-14:
Simon Sterne was an American lawyer born in Philadelphia on July 23, 1839. Cyrus Adler and Frederick T. Haneman wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article about him in 1906. He studied at Heidelberg and the University of Pennsylvania. He graduated in 1859 and entered the bar a year later. He died in New York on September 22, 1901.

Sterne built a large practice in constitutional and railroad law. He served as counsel for the Interstate Commerce Commission. At the Senate's request he drafted the Interstate Commerce Act. He also fought New York's Tweed ring as a reform leader. He helped elect an anti-Tammany mayor in 1894. President Cleveland named him to study European railways and the state. The entry honors a lawyer who shaped transport law.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-svab-karl-14142:
Karl Sváb was a Hungarian landowner and lawmaker born at Csongrad in 1829. Isidore Singer and Ludwig Venetianer wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article about him in 1906. He studied at the real-school of Budapest. In 1846 he turned to farming for his living. War soon pulled him away from the land.

In 1848 Sváb fought for Hungarian liberty under Colonel Bem. He served as lieutenant and adjutant in that struggle. Peace sent him back to farming and organizing. He helped found farm societies in two counties. From 1875 he sat ten years in Hungary's Parliament. In 1885 the king made him a life member of the Upper House. He led a Hungarian Jewish scholarship fund as president. The entry honors a farmer who rose to national office.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-tanuji-ishmael-:
Ishmael Tanuji was an Egyptian rabbi of the sixteenth century. Richard Gottheil and N. T. London wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article in 1906. His family came from Tangiers by way of Tunis. Kin of his served as rabbis in Jerusalem. He rose to lead Egypt's rabbis in his day.

In 1543 Tanuji wrote a book of legal decisions. Its popular style aimed at everyday questions. Ferrara printed it in 1555 as Sefer ha-Zikkaron. As chief of Egypt's rabbis he endorsed a responsa collection. His name heads its approbation page. A synagogue in Egypt still bears his name. He used to pray in that house himself. The brief entry preserves a leader known by one practical book.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-terumot-14342:
Terumot is a tractate of the Mishnah, Tosefta, and Palestinian Talmud. Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. It treats the heave-offering, the share of field produce owed to priests. The tractate has eleven chapters and 101 paragraphs.

Two gifts stand at its center. The great heave-offering came from every Israelite's harvest. The tithe heave-offering came from the Levites' tithe. The opening chapters list who may not set the gift apart. They also bar choosing by measure, weight, or count. Later chapters weigh mistakes and mixed kinds. The article marches through the chapters in order. It gives students a clear path through farm law.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-tombstones-hebr:
Inscribed tombstones came late to Jewish burial custom, this article shows. Joseph Jacobs and Isaac Broydé wrote it for the Jewish Encyclopedia, published in 1906. Ancient Hebrews marked graves with plain stones only. Jacob's pillar over Rachel bore no inscription. Ezekiel's sign stone merely warned of impurity nearby.

A Mishnah stone called golel shielded graves from jackals. House-shaped stone buildings did crown some Palestinian graves. Simon Maccabeus raised seven pyramids over his family's tomb. Rich families spent heavily on grave adornment. Simeon ben Gamaliel rebuked that waste as an insult. Jews abroad first copied Greek and Roman epitaphs. Their stones opened with here lies in Greek or Latin.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-van-praagh-will:
William Van Praagh taught deaf children to speak and read lips. He was born at Rotterdam on June 11, 1845. Joseph Jacobs and Isidore Harris wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906. Van Praagh learned the oral method from Dr. Hirsch in Holland. In 1866 London's Jews' Deaf and Dumb Home invited him to lead it.

His work won quick public praise in England. In 1871 he published a plan for day schools for deaf children. A new group for oral teaching then made him its director. In 1872 it opened a training college for teachers. Van Praagh led that college for over thirty years and spread the method widely.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-wa-ani-tefillat:
Wa ani Tefillati opens the Torah reading on Sabbath afternoons. Cyrus Adler and Francis L. Cohen wrote this short entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The words come from Psalm sixty nine. Among Ashkenazim the cantor chants it before the afternoon prayer. It follows the prayer U Ba le Ziyyon in the German rite.

Sephardim use the chant in other parts of the service too. Their congregation sings it to a newer melody. The entry prints that melody in musical notation. It also points readers to the article on synagogal music. The piece shows how one psalm verse took a fixed place in worship.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-weingaertner-fe:
Felix Alphonse Weingaertner was a French musician and composer. He was born at Nantes on May 5, 1844. Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman wrote this short entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. His father was a musician and taught him at home. He later studied at the Paris School of Fine Arts. Alard and Vieuxtemps were his violin teachers.

Weingaertner returned to Nantes as a music teacher. His concerts there won strong praise. In 1884 he became principal of the Nantes Conservatoire. He held that post for ten years. In 1894 he moved to Paris. There his violin playing built a wide name. He toured the chief cities of France.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-winkler-max-149:
Max Winkler was an American scholar of German literature. Cyrus Adler and Frederick T. Haneman wrote this short entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Cracow on September 4, 1866. He studied at Cracow, Cincinnati, and Harvard. Harvard gave him his bachelor's degree in 1889. Michigan awarded his doctorate in 1892.

Winkler took further study at the University of Berlin. Michigan then hired him to teach German. He became assistant professor in 1895. In 1902 he rose to full professor there. He edited Lessing's Emilia Galotti with notes. His editions include Goethe's Egmont and Iphigenie. Schiller's Wallenstein appeared under his editorship in 1901.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ximenes-de-cisn:
Ximenes de Cisneros (1436-1517) was a Spanish priest, statesman, and grand inquisitor. Joseph Jacobs and Schulim Ochser wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He studied in Rome and came home to high posts. Queen Isabella of Castile chose him as her confessor.

In 1507 the pope made him a cardinal of the church. That same year he rose to grand inquisitor of Spain. He was the third man to hold that dread post. Two years later he raised an army at his own cost. He led that force to North Africa by sea. His aim was to force the Christian faith there. Back home he founded a great seat of learning. Its press gave the world the first Bible in many tongues.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-zephaniah-15242:
Zephaniah was one of the twelve small prophets of the Bible. Emil G. Hirsch and Ira Maurice Price wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He names four sires in the first verse of his book. That chain ends with Hezekiah, the king of Judah.

Men think he was of royal stock from that long chain. Most books name just the sire of a seer, not four. If he was of that house, he lived at Jerusalem. His book shows a close grasp of that town's streets. He worked in the reign of Josiah, the son of Amon. Most minds date his work ere the great purge of 621. The rot he paints fits the first years of that king. His book splits in two parts of doom and hope. Part one tells of the day of wrath for all lands.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-zuriel-moses-be: Moses ben Samuel Zuriel was a mathematician of the seventeenth century. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and M. Seligsohn wrote this short entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. His one known work is Meḥaddesh Ḥodashim, printed at Venice in 1653. It is a calendar covering the years 5414 to 5434 in the Hebrew count. Those years match 1654 to 1674 in the common reckoning.
la-physiognomonie-et-la-phrenologie-ou-c:
Isidore Bourdon published this French study of facial reading and phrenology in Paris in 1842. Its subtitle promises knowledge of man from facial traits and skull bumps. Bourdon offers a critical exam of older systems.

He reviews ideas from Aristotle, Porta, Camper, and Lavater. He also weighs the systems of Gall and Spurzheim, founders of phrenology. Unsigned copies, a note warns, count as counterfeits. The book shows a doctor testing popular character sciences against his own judgment. Bourdon's critical stance sets him apart from pure believers. He grants some claims a hearing, then tests them in turn.
liebig-animal-chemistry-gregory-1842:
William Gregory published his translation of Liebig's Animal Chemistry in 1842. Justus von Liebig turned from plants and soils to the animal body, applying chemistry to physiology and pathology, the study of health and disease. Gregory, a Scottish chemist, had studied in Liebig's laboratory at Giessen.

Liebig sorted foods into those that build tissue and those that fuel heat and motion, an early frame for nutrition science. He traced how the body burns food with oxygen, much as a furnace burns fuel. Some details failed later tests, but the program endured: explain life by chemistry. The book is widely read as the birth of biochemistry, the science that now runs from digestion to genetics.
liebig-organic-chemistry-agriculture-pla:
Lyon Playfair published his translation of Justus von Liebig's Organic Chemistry in its Applications to Agriculture and Physiology in 1842. Liebig, a German chemist with a famous teaching laboratory, argued that plants feed on minerals from the soil. Playfair, his former student, carried the claim to Britain.

Liebig's mineral theory held that crops take carbon from the air but need nitrogen, potash, and phosphates from the soil, which harvests steadily drain. Farmers must return those minerals or watch yields fall. The argument founded fertilizer science and changed farming across Europe. Liebig overstated some points and feuded over them, but the book's core claim, that soil chemistry rules the harvest, remade agriculture.
lippincott-s-magazine-of-popular-literat:
April 1876 brings Lippincott's to its hundredth number. The century series turns to the Centennial Exposition under roof. Sketches of India conclude in this issue. James Morgan Hart profiles the college student for readers.

Mrs. Linton moves Leam Dundas through chapters twenty-nine to thirty-two. Lady Barker continues her letters from South Africa. Margaret Hosmer describes dinner inside a state prison. Jennie Zimmerman explains the instruction of deaf mutes to close. Kate Hillard's After a Year and Thomas Hughes's Berkshire Lady appear. La Befana and the city of violets fill the gossip columns.

The September 1880 Lippincott's ventures among Florida lakes. Ekoniah Scrub anchors the issue's long opening piece. A county clerk unfolds his map for cross-country travelers. Getting lost, he jokes, only means finding William Townsend.

The scrub hides a strange amphibious land still developing. Solid ground turns marshy while prairies become bright lakes. Nature threads sapphires onto her emerald forest chaplet yearly. Three or four travelers now know her hidden laboratory better. William Townsend knew the cross-country itinerary by heart, apparently. Emerald forest borders thread the bright lakes year by year.
mellon-ms-32-alchemical-miscellany-1542:
Mellon MS 32 is a north Italian paper manuscript of about 1542. Yale's Beinecke Library holds the book, with 119 leaves. Black leather with gold ruled panels covers the boards.

John of Rupescissa on the fifth essence leads the texts inside. Simone Porzio writes on whether the soul can die in one piece. Petrarch adds a dialogue, and alchemy and recipes follow in Latin. Verse in Italian treats the traits of fruits and nuts inside. Notes on logic and a game of fortune telling end the book. Fruit lore and planting times show its wide home use.
memoirs-of-jean-franc-ois-paul-de-gondi-:
Cardinal de Retz's memoirs, in volume one, start with his forebears. A first preface gives his birth at Montmirail in October 1614. His father led the galleys of France as their general.

His mother came from the house of Rochepot, lords of Commercy. His brother Pierre, Duc de Retz, stands next in the family list. Pictures of Turenne, Richelieu, and Anne of Austria face the text. Five books hold the whole tale of Mazarin's rule and the Fronde. His father's line came from Joigni, and his mother's from Rochepot. Rank and kin gave the young priest his first tools of power.
neurology-an-account-of-some-experiments:
Robert Dale Owen sent this account to an American newspaper at Dr Buchanan's request, and it was printed in London in 1842. Buchanan, of Louisville, had shown experiments on the physiology of the brain. Owen says he offers only what he saw and heard himself.

The experiments dealt with vital powers and mental functions of the human subject. Owen calls them startling, and says many would deem them flatly not credible. In a darker age, he writes, Buchanan might have been taken for a necromancer from Padua. The pamphlet also prints Owen's letter defending New Harmony and his family against an unnamed attack.
openalex-w1975146242:
Thomas Guillemaud and co-authors traced a tomato pest's invasion. Their paper appeared in Scientific Reports in February 2015. Tuta absoluta is a moth pest native to South America. It invaded the Mediterranean Basin and spread widely there. The team asked where the invaders came from.

They analyzed genetic variation in samples from four regions. Samples came from South America, Europe, Africa, and the Middle East. The title reports a single introduction from Central Chile. Genetic sameness across the basin supports that single origin. One entry point shaped the whole invasion, they found. Knowing the route helps target future pest control.
openalex-w2094399642:
Rejane Goy, Douglas de Britto and Odilio Assis reviewed the germ-killing action of chitosan. Their paper appeared in Polimeros in 2009. Chitosan comes from chitin in shellfish shells. It is a water-loving natural polymer. Many bacteria and fungi are sensitive to it.

The review presents three accepted killing mechanisms. Chitosan can disrupt microbe cell membranes. It can also bind key nutrients and DNA. Its strength depends on chain length and chemistry. The authors summarise the doses that stop many microbes. Water-soluble forms may kill germs even better. Effectiveness varies by target species, they note. Uses range from food coatings to medical dressings.
openalex-w2112838542:
Georges Aad and colleagues in the ATLAS Collaboration measured how Z bosons move sideways in proton collisions. Their paper appeared in Journal of High Energy Physics in 2014. The Z boson's sideways momentum tests quantum chromodynamics. Precise data also tune the simulation programs physicists rely on. The collisions took place at the LHC.

Z bosons were caught through decays to electron or muon pairs. The team measured rates across a wide momentum range. Results were split by the boson's forward direction too. Curves were compared with several theory calculations. Some calculations matched better at low momentum. Others performed better at high momentum. The data were used to constrain generator settings. Better simulations improve all ATLAS analyses.
openalex-w2155261642:
Meghan Bohren, Erin Hunter, Heather Munthe-Kaas, and colleagues published this review in Reproductive Health in 2014. They synthesized interview-based research on why women in poorer countries do or do not give birth in health facilities. Facility birth with skilled care cuts deaths of mothers and babies, yet many women still deliver at home.

Thirty-four studies from seventeen countries fed the synthesis. Four themes organized the findings: beliefs about birth, social and family influence, resources and access, and views of care quality. Distance, cost, and family tradition all held women back. So did low trust in care and fear of discrimination or disrespect at facilities. The authors urge care that is respectful and high quality for every woman.
openalex-w2207291742: Thomas Lener, Mario Gimona, Ludwig Aigner, and many colleagues wrote this position paper in the Journal of Extracellular Vesicles in 2015. It sets out the stance of the International Society for Extracellular Vesicles on applying therapies based on extracellular vesicles, tiny membrane sacs shed by cells, in clinical trials. The hosted sample for this entry preserves only front matter and author affiliations, with no readable abstract or body text, so no recommendations are summarized here.
openalex-w2404982942:
Suzanne Garland, Susanne Kjær, Nubia Muñoz, and colleagues published this systematic review in Clinical Infectious Diseases in 2016. Ten years after the quadrivalent HPV vaccine launched, they gathered its real-world record. Trial results were strong, but population programs differ: coverage varies, boys joined later, and effects ripple to the unvaccinated.

The reviewers collected publications from nine countries running national programs. Studies tracked four endpoints: genital warts, HPV infection, cervical cell changes, and cervical tissue abnormalities. Australia, the earliest and broadest adopter, contributed the most reports, including its school-based program and catch-up campaigns. The synthesis weighs how impact and effectiveness played out in practice, country by country and endpoint by endpoint.
openalex-w2483244742:
Rolando Claure-Del Granado and Ravindra L. Mehta wrote this 2016 debate article for BMC Nephrology. Their subject is fluid overload in intensive care patients, meaning extra fluid built up in the body. The problem appears often in patients with acute kidney injury. Recent studies link carrying too much fluid with worse outcomes, including higher death rates.

Giving fluid can restore blood pressure, heart output, and blood flow to the kidneys. Giving too much, or too little, both raise the risk of death, they explain. The authors review how doctors judge fluid status, noting that most current tests are fairly inaccurate. Diuretics, especially loop diuretics, remain a useful treatment. When drugs fail, other treatments are needed to remove fluid. Careful fluid balance, they argue, belongs at the center of critical care.
openalex-w2725449842:
Judith Recht, André Machado Siqueira, and Wuelton Marcelo Monteiro, with colleagues, reviewed malaria in four South American countries in Malaria Journal in 2017. Brazil, Colombia, Peru, and Venezuela share the Amazon rainforest, where most regional cases arise. South America made real progress against malaria during the 2000s. Yet the mosquito-borne disease remains an important public health concern there.

More than half of Amazon cases now come from Plasmodium vivax, while falciparum malaria has fallen. The authors list obstacles blocking further gains. Malaria is surging again in Venezuela, especially around gold mining areas. Hidden infections without symptoms, city-edge transmission, and malaria in pregnancy all complicate control. A common genetic deficiency also limits safe use of the drug primaquine. They call for better field tests, pregnancy care that includes malaria checks, and regional teamwork modeled on earlier successful campaigns.
openalex-w2765537442:
Eileen Uribe-Querol and Carlos Rosales reviewed how microbes control phagocytosis in Frontiers in Immunology in 2017. Phagocytosis is how specialized immune cells swallow and destroy germs. It also clears dead cells and keeps tissues in balance. Macrophages, neutrophils, and their fellow professional phagocytes lead this defense.

The process runs in steps: recognizing the microbe, forming a pouch around it, then maturing that pouch into a killing chamber. Receptors on the cell surface spot molecular patterns on microbes or grab host tags stuck to them. Successful pathogens fight back at each step, blocking recognition, entry, or digestion. The review gathers these microbial tricks and the cell's counters. Understanding this tug-of-war helps explain infections that evade immunity. It may also suggest treatments that restore the eater cells' upper hand.
openalex-w2891046942:
Cristián Torres-León, Nathiely Ramírez-Guzmán, and Liliana Londoño-Hernández lead this 2018 review in Frontiers in Sustainable Food Systems. Its subject: turning food waste and processing byproducts into nutrition for developing countries. Fruit processing discards over half the fresh fruit as peels, seeds, shells, and trimmings. Those discards often hold more nutrients than the product itself.

Most byproducts end in landfills, where they emit greenhouse gases and costly leachate. Some are burned instead, wasting their value entirely. Meanwhile hundreds of millions of people suffer hunger worldwide. The review argues these streams should be mined for food ingredients and supplements. Recovering nutrition from waste attacks hunger and pollution together. The authors survey what is usable and what blocks wider adoption. Their case reframes garbage as an untapped pantry for food-insecure regions.
openalex-w2954205242:
J. Emmett Duffy, Lisandro Benedetti-Cecchi, Joaquin Trinanes, and colleagues wrote this systematic review in Frontiers in Marine Science in 2019. It calls for a coordinated global system to observe seagrasses and large seaweeds, called marine macroalgae. Together these plants anchor shallow coastal ecosystems around the world.

Seagrass meadows and kelp stands rank among the most productive habitats on Earth. They shelter many animals, support fisheries, guard coasts, soak up nutrient runoff, and store carbon. Yet these large, long-lived plants are easily harmed by human disturbance and can give way to fast-growing algae. The authors review the state of observation and argue for shared worldwide monitoring to protect these services.
openalex-w2968203342:
María Maldonado-Celis, Elhadi Yahia, Ramiro Bedoya, and colleagues wrote this 2019 review in Frontiers in Plant Science. It compiles the chemical makeup of mango fruit, covering both its nutrients and its plant compounds, called phytochemicals. Mangoes are a major tropical fruit eaten worldwide.

The review gathers updated data on many mango varieties, part by part of the fruit. It tracks how the compounds change as fruit develops and after harvest. That knowledge can help limit spoilage and raise the fruit's value. The authors aim the compilation at readers in nutrition, health, farming, drug research, and the food industry, showing what mango contains and why it matters.
openalex-w3016195942:
Mary Menton, Carlos Larrea, Sara Latorre, and colleagues published this article in Sustainability Science in 2020. It asks whether the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals, or SDGs, truly serve environmental justice. The goals interact through synergies, trade-offs, and outright contradictions, the authors argue.

Justice, they note, sits inside many environmental problems, yet the goals barely speak its language. Mainstream justice frameworks rest on four principles: fair distribution, fair procedure, recognition, and capabilities. The authors push beyond them toward an approach that faces power, colonial history, and the standing of non-human life. They test the goals against cases in food, water, health, climate, energy, and conservation.
openalex-w3134934442:
Kimmo Eriksson, Pontus Strimling, Michele Gelfand, and colleagues published this study in Nature Communications in 2021. It asks how people in fifty-seven societies judge the right response when someone breaks a cooperative norm. Responses studied include direct confrontation, gossip, and shutting the offender out.

In a preregistered survey of nearly twenty-three thousand students and non-students, the team also rated tolerance for merely odd behavior. One pattern held everywhere: the worse a violation seemed, the harsher the response people endorsed. Yet countries still differed in how fitting each sanction felt. The map of those differences helps explain why the same offense sparks a scolding in one place and silence in another.
openalex-w4205948442:
Seppo Salminen, María Carmen Collado, Akihito Endo, and colleagues present the agreed expert definition of postbiotics, in Nature Reviews Gastroenterology and Hepatology in 2021. The word postbiotics appears more and more on products and in papers, yet nobody had fixed its meaning. An expert panel from the International Scientific Association for Probiotics and for Prebiotics met in 2019 to settle the term.

The panel defined a postbiotic as dead microbes, or their parts, prepared in a way that gives a health benefit. Live bacteria are therefore excluded by definition. The statement also reviews evidence for health effects and for safety. A shared definition gives scientists and firms one yardstick for future claims.
openalex-w4308045442:
Jeffrey Lazarus, Diana Romero, Christopher Kopka, and colleagues report a multinational expert consensus on ending the COVID-19 public health threat, in Nature in 2022. Nearly three years into the pandemic, fatigue was eroding vigilance worldwide. Cases passed six hundred twenty million, deaths several million, and care for other illnesses had been widely delayed. New variants kept spreading while monitoring stayed weak in many places.

The authors used the Delphi method, rounds of structured expert voting, to build shared recommendations. Experts from many countries weighed in until the group converged. A consensus matters because governments had been improvising alone, with mixed results. The paper offers one agreed platform for action on vaccines, variants, long COVID, and strained health systems.
openalex-w7166704842: Quantum computers need qubits that can talk and, just as importantly, stop talking. This experimental paper studies switching off the coupling between qubits using a double-resonator device in a superconducting circuit. The authors tuned frequencies to control the connection. A hardware study of the on-off switch for quantum conversation.
openalex-w7208824242: Every blood transfusion depends on matching donor and patient blood correctly. This study looks at immune blood markers in donors and recipients at a public blood center in Brazil, and what they mean for transfusion safety. The authors profile the markers and draw lessons for preventing bad reactions. A specialized but vital piece of lab medicine that keeps transfusions safe.
plos-pbio-0020142:
Daniel A. Barbash, Philip Awadalla, and Aaron M. Tarone analyzed a hybrid problem gene in fruit flies for PLOS Biology in 2004. When two species cross, the hybrids are often sterile or weak. A locus in Drosophila drives that mismatch, and the authors found signs it was shaped long ago by positive selection.

That is, the gene changed fast because change was favored, not by drift. A gene pushed hard by selection inside each species may no longer fit its partner in the other species. The case links everyday adaptation to the origin of new species. It shows how the very changes that help a population can split it away from its kin over time.
plos-pbio-0020242:
Karen S. Kelly-Spratt, Kay E. Gurley, Yutaka Yasui, and co-workers tested a tumor suppressor in mice for PLOS Biology in 2004. The protein p19Arf watches for runaway growth signals from genes like Hras. When it senses them, it can halt the cell, largely through the famous guard protein p53.

In mice prone to Hras-driven cancers, p19Arf slowed tumor growth, spread, and advance. Some of that protection worked through p53 and some did not. The split matters because many human cancers disable p53. A guard that still works without p53 is a promising lead. The study maps both routes, giving cancer biology a fuller view of a key defense.
plos-pbio-0020342:
Jason H. Brickner and Peter Walter watched a gene move inside the yeast nucleus in PLOS Biology in 2004. The gene INO1 switches on when yeast needs to make a certain nutrient. When active, the gene travels to the edge of the nucleus, to the membrane that encloses it.

That move is not random drift; the active gene is recruited to nuclear pores, the gates in the membrane. Genes at the edge may be read and exported more efficiently. The finding added gene position to the list of things cells control, alongside on-off switches. It helped launch a field on how the 3D layout of the genome shapes gene activity.
plos-pone-0000042:
Eric Spierings, Jos Drabbels, Matthijs Hendriks, and co-authors built a shared yardstick for transplant genetics in a 2006 paper. Minor histocompatibility antigens are small protein differences between donor and patient. They are minor in name only: in bone marrow transplants they can trigger rejection or the dangerous graft-versus-host disease.

The team set out a uniform genomic typing method, one standard way to read these antigens from DNA, and paired it with a database built for clinical use. Uniform methods matter because transplant centers must compare results across hospitals and countries. A shared database turns scattered lab data into a tool that can guide donor choice for real patients.
plos-pone-0000142:
Heidi Theisen, Adeela Syed, Baochi T. Nguyen, and colleagues published this developmental genetics paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. In the fruit fly, Wingless and DPP are morphogens, signals that pattern growing tissue. The authors show that Wingless directly switches DPP production down, acting through a protein complex of Armadillo, TCF, and Brinker.

How two patterning signals limit each other decides where body parts form. The paper maps the molecular chain from the Wingless signal to the repression of DPP. Work like this explains, in concrete molecular terms, how a simple embryo lays out its body plan with precision.
plos-pone-0000242:
Yaël Mamane, Emmanuel Petroulakis, Yvan Martineau, and colleagues published this cancer biology paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. eIF4E is a protein that helps start protein production from messenger RNA. The authors show that when eIF4E is overactive, it switches on a subset of messages through epigenetic-style activation. That activation, they argue, explains its effects on cell proliferation.

eIF4E runs high in many cancers, where faster growth is the problem. Pinpointing the messages it activates shows which proteins actually drive that growth. The paper narrows a broad cancer suspect down to specific targets that drugs might block.
plos-pone-0000342:
Emma M. J. King, Sjaak J. A. van der Sar, and Kevin G. Hardwick published this cell division paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. The spindle checkpoint is the safety system that stops cell division until all chromosomes are attached. Mad3 is one of its proteins, and its KEN boxes, small sequence motifs, mediate the turnover of both Cdc20 and Mad3 itself.

The checkpoint must switch off promptly once its job is done, which requires destroying its own parts. The authors show the KEN boxes are critical to that timed turnover. The work details how a safety system dismantles itself, a step whose failure can mis-segregate chromosomes.
plos-pone-0000442:
Mia T. Levine and David J. Begun compared populations through one immune gene, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. The gene is Relish, a switch for immune defenses in fruit flies. Using comparative population genetics, they asked whether its adaptive evolution follows a general pattern or is idiosyncratic, different in each case.

Immune genes are famous for evolving fast, as hosts race their parasites. If each gene's history is unique, broad rules about immune evolution will be hard to write. Studies like this one test how predictable adaptation is, a core question in evolutionary genetics, using a gene whose job makes the race especially visible.
plos-pone-0000542:
Anil Pandit and colleagues compared two antibiotics head-to-head for typhoid fever, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. Enteric fever, caused by Salmonella typhi, still sickens millions yearly. Their open randomized comparison tested gatifloxacin versus cefixime for the treatment of uncomplicated enteric fever.

Older typhoid drugs have been failing as resistance spreads. So each fair comparison of newer options matters. It feeds treatment guidelines in South Asia, where the trial was run. Open means doctors knew which drug each patient got, a practical design for field conditions. The results feed directly into prescribing choices for a common, dangerous fever.
plos-pone-0000642:
So Yeon Yoo, Yunhee Kim, Soo Young Kim and co-authors studied a protein that ties flowering time to cold in the plant Arabidopsis. Their 2007 PLOS ONE study starts from a plant's scheduling problem: it must sense light, temperature, and inner cues to flower at the right moment. Low temperature is one of the most common stresses plants face, and it also affects flowering.

The protein in question carries a NAC domain, a section found in many plant control proteins. By the title's account, this protein governs both when the plant flowers and how it answers cold. The molecular link between the two responses is the gap the work sets out to close.
plos-pone-0000742:
Corinne Tremblay, François Champoux, Patrice Voss and colleagues asked how children learn to handle mismatched sights and sounds. Showing mismatched sound and sight at the same time can create false percepts. A person then sees or hears something that was not quite presented. Recent data suggested distinct processes underlie speech versus non-speech perception in this mixing of senses.

Their 2007 PLOS ONE study is developmental, following how both kinds of illusion change as children grow. If speech illusions mature on a different timetable from non-speech ones, the brain builds them separately. Findings like these inform teaching, hearing care, and theories of how the senses fuse.
plos-pone-0000842:
Alison K. Gillingham and Sean Munro identified the activator of a yeast membrane-traffic protein, writing in PLOS ONE in 2007. Small G proteins of the Arf and Rab families are fundamental to the organization and activity of intracellular membranes. Mammalian Arf6 is among the best characterized, taking part in processes including endocytosis and actin remodeling. Each Arf needs a partner protein to switch it on.

That partner is a guanine nucleotide exchange factor, and the team identified it for Arf3, the yeast counterpart of Arf6. Yeast genetics make such hunts fast and rigorous. Knowing the exchange factor completes the circuit for one more trafficking pathway inside cells.
plos-pone-0000942:
Aijaz Wani, Sajad Ahanger, Sharmila Bapat and colleagues read mitochondrial DNA from children with brain and muscle disease, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Mitochondrial encephalomyopathies are a mixed group of disorders. Faults can sit in mitochondrial DNA itself, or in the cell's own genes for the power system.

The team analyzed mitochondrial sequences from twenty-three young patients. In that set they report new variants tied to disease. Each new variant sharpens testing for families facing these hard to diagnose illnesses. It also adds to the map of which changes the power system can survive, and which it cannot. Genetic answers rarely cure, but they end long searches.
plos-pone-0001042:
Anne Guezou, Paola Pozo and Christopher Buddenhagen inventoried introduced plants in a Galapagos town, in PLOS ONE in 2007. The survey covered Puerto Villamil on Isabela Island. It was part of an island wide project to find and remove potentially invasive plants before they take hold.

Inventories ran across the urban and farm zones of the four inhabited Galapagos islands. A plant list for a town may sound minor, but islands are where invasions do the worst damage. Native species there evolved without many rivals. Finding introduced plants early, while removal is cheap, is the whole strategy. The report gives eradicators their target list for one settlement.
plos-pone-0001142:
Neural crest cells are embryonic cells that leave the early nervous system and migrate to build much of the face, among other structures. Eric Théveneau, Jean-Loup Duband, and Muriel Altabef studied how these cells break away, a process called delamination, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Cranial and trunk crest cells delaminate in strikingly different ways.

The authors show that a gene called Ets-1 gives cranial crest cells their distinct behavior. Signals that control the slow delamination of trunk cells were partly known; the cranial side was not. The result helps explain how one cell population produces such different outcomes along the body.
plos-pone-0001242:
When two DNA strands exchange parts, the mismatched stretch created is called heteroduplex DNA. Laura Gumbiner-Russo and Susan Rosenberg analyzed such recombination products in living E. coli, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Homologous recombination produces patches, where one strand is converted, and splices, where strands cross over.

The authors asked how often 5-prime and 3-prime patches occur, which strand ends up carrying the new information. Physical analysis of the products in vivo gives a ground-truth picture of recombination mechanics. Those mechanics underlie DNA repair and the shuffling of genes in every organism.
plos-pone-0001342:
Before a cell divides, the spindle checkpoint holds off separation until every chromosome is attached to the spindle from both sides. Patricia Rischitor, Karen May, and Kevin Hardwick studied a checkpoint protein called Bub1 in fission yeast, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Checkpoint proteins are recruited to unattached kinetochores, the chromosome handles, and generate signals that delay division.

The authors describe Bub1 as a kinetochore scaffold protein, sufficient on its own to recruit other spindle checkpoint proteins to ectopic sites on chromosomes. A scaffold that can summon the whole checkpoint simplifies models of how the signal is built. Errors here lead to wrong chromosome numbers, a cancer hallmark.
plos-pone-0001442:
Ari Ueno, Satoshi Hirata, and Kohki Fuwa published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on brain waves in an awake chimpanzee. The chimp is our closest kin, yet the brain base of its thought was little mapped. The team recorded brain waves as the chimp heard tones, some of which broke a pattern. They watched for the classic wave that flags a surprise sound.

The chimp showed a wave response to odd tones much like that seen in people. That match gives a rare direct link between chimp and human brain work. It opens a path to study how higher thought arose. Such work must be rare and careful, which makes each data set of high value.
plos-pone-0001542:
Stephen Callister and co-authors wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study that tests the core genome idea with protein data. Gene studies often predict a shared set of genes for a germ group. Proof that the proteins are truly made is seldom checked. The team used a rich protein data base to run that check.

Their protein reads back a real core set shared across the group. That firms up a concept that gene data alone had left soft. A true core set names the parts a germ cannot lose. Those parts are prime targets for broad drugs and vaccines.
plos-pone-0001642:
Alberto Valbuena, Inmaculada López-Sánchez, and Pedro A. Lazo studied a human gene called VRK1 in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. VRK1 makes a kinase, an enzyme that tags other proteins with phosphate groups to switch them on or off. Several of its targets are transcription factors, which control gene activity. Cells need such control proteins to pace their growth and division in a body full of mixed signals.

The authors report that VRK1 acts as an early response gene, switching on fast when cells get growth signals. When they removed it, cells stalled in their division cycle. The full text gives the cell tests and the points where the cycle blocked. Knowing which kinases gate cell division matters for cancer research, since tumors often hijack those same gates.
plos-pone-0001742:
Ilya Plyusnin, Alistair R. Evans, Aleksis Karme, and their co-authors brought data mining to the study of 3D shapes in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Biologists can analyze gene sequences with powerful tools, but classifying three-dimensional biological morphology, the shape of teeth, bones, and organs, had lagged behind.

The authors introduce automated 3D phenotype analysis: software that measures shapes and mines them for patterns that separate groups. The full text gives the method, the shapes tested, and the classification accuracy. Automated shape analysis could speed up fields from paleontology to dentistry, where experts now score shapes by eye, slowly and with room for disagreement.
plos-pone-0001842:
Andrey Ptitsyn proposed a data trick to find faint gene activity in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Microarrays gauge the activity of thousands of genes in a sample, but the detail they can show is limited by background noise. Faintly read genes are detected poorly, and many genes are never detected at all.

Ptitsyn applies stochastic resonance, an effect where noise boosts weak signals, to reveal 'pilot light' expression: very low, steady gene activity that standard analysis misses. The full text gives the method and the chip data it found. Genes expressed at pilot light levels may still matter in living cells, so a method that rescues them expands every dataset already gathered.
plos-pone-0001942:
Marcus Stensmyr and co-authors revisited an odd fruit fly that lives on land crabs, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Most flies in this family feed on microbes, which are found on many surfaces, so the flies live in many places. Three species took a stranger path: they colonized land crabs, and one, Drosophila endobranchia, lives with the Cayman crab.

The team redrew the species' family tree and studied its biology up close. Work of this kind tests how a common insect can shift to a life tied to a single host. It also adds a case study of how new species arise in odd niches.
plos-pone-0002042:
Amanda Brindley and co-authors compared an enzyme from deep-sea and shallow fish, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. The enzyme, lactate dehydrogenase, helps muscles work without oxygen for short spells. Deep-sea fish live under immense pressure that can warp proteins, so their enzymes must be built to bear it.

The team read the enzyme's gene from a deep-sea rattail and from Atlantic cod, made both enzymes in bacteria, and included a lab-made artificial form. They then tested how each bears high pressure. Linking sequence to pressure stability shows what evolution changes when life moves into the deep.
plos-pone-0002142:
Melanie Königshoff, Nisha Balsara, Eva-Maria Pfaff, and co-authors studied a fatal lung disease in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis slowly scars the lungs, distorting their structure until breathing fails. Its marks include injury to the air sac lining cells, heavy deposits of matrix between cells, and scarring cells switched into overdrive.

The team focused on Wnt signaling, a set of signals that guide growth and repair. They report that working Wnt signals are raised in the diseased lung. Since repair signals that stay on too long can drive scarring, the finding names a pathway that future drugs might aim to calm.
plos-pone-0002242:
Glauco Souza, Esra Yonel-Gumruk, Davin Fan, and co-authors assembled gels from viruses and gold particles, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Hydrogels, soft water-filled networks, are a focus of medical research for uses like drug delivery and tissue scaffolds. The team explored how long-range electric forces shape their assembly.

They built hydrogels from phages, viruses that infect bacteria, combined with gold particles. Changing the acidity of the mix, a trans-acting factor, or mutating the phage's peptides, a cis-acting factor, altered how the gels formed. Rules like these help engineers design soft materials from the bottom up.
plos-pone-0002342:
Guoqiang Xing, Clifford Qualls, Luis Huicho, and co-authors compared how three high-altitude peoples handle thin air, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Most work on adaptation uses lab animals under controlled conditions, which cannot copy the real environments that shape wild populations. Human groups in the Andes, Ethiopia, and the Himalayas have each lived for generations where oxygen is scarce.

The team compared patterns of adaptation and mal-adaptation to ambient hypoxia across the three regions. The groups solve the same problem in unlike ways, and some solutions carry costs, such as chronic mountain sickness. Comparing the three natural experiments shows there is more than one evolutionary route to life at altitude.
plos-pone-0002442:
In 2008, McDermott and colleagues published a study in the journal PLOS ONE. The byline credits Shannon R. McDermott, Richard M. Kliman, and others. Its subject is estimation of Isolation Times of the Island Species in the Drosophila simulans Complex from Multilocus DNA Sequence Data. The Drosophila simulans species complex continues to serve as an important model system for the study of new species formation.

The complex is comprised of the cosmopolitan species, D. simulans, and two island endemics, D. Readers get the background first, then the path the team took and the care they took with it. As a record, it keeps the focus on facts and method, and lets readers judge the claims for themselves.
plos-pone-0002542:
A research team led by Poliseno reported its work in PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline credits Laura Poliseno, Letizia Pitto, Marcella Simili, and others. Its subject is the Proto-Oncogene LRF Is under Post-Transcriptional Control of MiR-20a: Implications for Senescence. MicroRNAs are short RNA molecules, about 20 to 22 units long, that act as negative regulators of gene expression.

They have been shown to play a role in development, cell growth, stress response, and cell death. Key terms are set out in context, so a reader new to the field can still follow the work. The full text is free to read, so any reader can check the work and follow the links to past work.
plos-pone-0002642:
Ferhaan Ahmad led a team whose work appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was the role of cardiac troponin t quantity and function in cardiac development and dilated cardiomyopathy. Authorship is credited in the record to Ferhaan Ahmad and co-authors, with PLOS ONE as the journal of publication.

The abstract begins from a clear premise. Hypertrophic (HCM) and dilated (DCM) cardiomyopathies result from sarcomeric protein mutations, including cardiac troponin T (cTnT, TNNT2 ). Its abstract frames the work for later readers, who can judge the full text against the aims stated at the start.
plos-pone-0002742:
Volker Huge led a team whose work appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was interaction of hyperalgesia and sensory loss in complex regional pain syndrome type i (CRPS i). The full author list in the catalog record begins with Volker Huge, and the article appeared in the open journal PLOS ONE.

The abstract begins from a clear premise. Sensory abnormalities are a key feature of Complex Regional Pain Syndrome (CRPS). Anyone studying the topic can use the article to see how the authors framed the problem at the time of publication.
plos-pone-0002842:
Alice Zuin led a team whose work appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was mitochondrial dysfunction increases oxidative stress and decreases chronological life span in fission yeast. The catalog record names Alice Zuin first among the authors, and the source is the open journal PLOS ONE.

The abstract begins from a clear premise. Oxidative stress is a probable cause of aging and associated diseases. The summary also notes a further point. Reactive oxygen species (ROS) originate mainly from endogenous sources, namely the mitochondria. For readers, the value lies in how plainly the abstract sets out the problem and what the authors set out to test or describe.
plos-pone-0002942:
Charles O'Brien, Lilian Plotkin, Carlo Galli and co-authors studied bone control through osteocytes in 2008. Osteocytes are former bone-building cells buried in bone, thought to direct how the skeleton adapts to load. Whether hormones steer bone through these buried cells was unknown.
