Parathyroid hormone, or PTH, drives bone remodeling, the cycle of breakdown and rebuilding. The PLOS ONE study tests PTH receptor signaling acting in osteocytes to control bone mass. The focus matters for osteoporosis drugs, several of which work through PTH pathways and need a clear picture of their target cells. Its full text, with tables and references, is openly available to any reader online.
plos-pone-0003042:
Jack Gilbert, Dawn Field, Ying Huang and co-authors read the active genes of marine microbe communities in 2008. Sequencing an ecosystem's expressed genes, its metatranscriptome, shows how organisms respond to changing conditions. Until then the approach was limited to microarrays and random cloning.

New sequencing let the team detect large numbers of novel sequences in complex marine communities. Novel here means matching nothing in reference databases. Published in PLOS ONE, the haul shows how much ocean microbe activity sits outside known gene catalogs, setting a scale for future ocean surveys. The full text gives methods, results, and references for readers who want to check each step.
plos-pone-0003142:
Mohamed A. F. Noor, Robin S. Parnell and Bruce S. Grant report a reversible colour change in moth caterpillars in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Shifts in body colour can help insects survive by matching varied backgrounds. Such changes are often triggered in a roundabout way by heat, crowding, or diet, yet direct triggering by the background itself would give faster camouflage.

Their subject is the American peppered moth, Biston betularia cognataria, whose caterpillars can switch colour and switch back. Readers learn about a flexible trait that aids hiding from predators. The case adds a neat example to work on how camouflage evolves.
plos-pone-0003242:
Stephanie L. Timmerman, Jennifer S. Pfingsten, Jeffrey S. Kieft and colleagues study an unusual message leader in the mouse brain in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. A single internal ribosomal entry site, or IRES, together with its activating factors, is sufficient to recruit the translation machinery to a eukaryotic message independent of the cap structure. The team demonstrate, however, that the mouse TrkB message contains two independent entry sites.

These two sites are differentially regulated, as the title notes. Readers learn how one nerve growth receptor message can be translated under different conditions through separate doors. Dual control may let neurons adjust TrkB output to local needs.
plos-pone-0003342:
Carlos J. Camacho models currents from a voltage gated ion channel in this single-author 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Ion channels play a central role in setting gradients of ion concentration and electrostatic potentials, which in turn regulate sensory systems and other functions. The model is based on structure of the open configuration of the Kv1.2 channel and a suggestion about the two ends of the channel machinery.

The author presents quantitative modeling of currents from a channel undergoing fast inactivation. Readers get numbers for a process that shuts nerve signals in milliseconds. Such models help interpret patch-clamp records and predict effects of channel mutations or drugs.
plos-pone-0003442:
Santosh Nanda and co-authors read liver gene activity during hepatitis C infection in this 2008 study. They worked with chimpanzees, close kin to humans in immune response. Some animals clear the virus, while others stay infected for good. The team compared gene patterns between those two paths.

Liver samples showed distinct patterns tied to viral clearance. Animals that beat the virus switched on a different program. Those patterns point to immune steps that decide the outcome. Such clues may guide treatment for people whose infection turns chronic. Chimp studies were then one of the few ways to watch this infection unfold over time.
plos-pone-0003542:
Sunita Biswas and co-authors studied synapse glue proteins in honey bees for this 2008 paper. Neuroligins and neurexins form a binding pair across synapses in vertebrates. That pair has been tied to autism and related disorders in humans. The team ran a genetic analysis of the matching bee proteins.

The bee versions mirror the vertebrate setup in key ways. One member, neurexin I, bridges the synaptic gap in bees too. Deep conservation across distant animals marks an ancient design. Bee genetics thus offers a simple model for synapse biology. Bees also serve as a model for learning, smell, and social life.
plos-pone-0003642:
Toshiyuki Fukada, Natacha Civic, Tatsuya Furuichi, and colleagues published this genetics study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Zinc is a trace element found in large amounts in connective tissue. The team studied a zinc transporter called SLC39A13, or ZIP13, which moves zinc into cells.

Mice lacking this transporter showed changes in bone, teeth, and other connective tissues as they grew. The team also tied the transporter to the BMP and TGF-beta signaling pathways, which guide tissue growth. The work shows one zinc gate is required for the body to build its supporting tissues.
plos-pone-0003742:
Katrin Wenzel, Hannelore Haase, Gerd Wallukat, and colleagues published this blood pressure study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Some patients carry antibodies that switch on the alpha-1 adrenergic receptor, a control point for blood vessel tone. Such autoantibodies had been described in hypertension before. Their real role stayed unsettled.

The team ran clinical and lab studies in patients whose hypertension resists standard treatment. They weighed whether these receptor-activating antibodies help drive the stubborn pressure. If they do, the immune system itself becomes a treatment target in cases that drugs alone cannot control.
plos-pone-0003842:
Helga Schneider, Elke Valk, Rufina Leung, and colleagues published this immunology study in PLOS ONE in 2008. T cells must balance growth, shutdown, and death to keep the immune system safe. The co-receptor CTLA-4 is needed to induce anergy, the unresponsive state behind tolerance. How it silences cells without killing them was a central question.

The team shows CTLA-4 activation switches on PI 3-kinase and the protein kinase Akt. That signaling sustains T-cell anergy while the cells stay alive. The route explains how the immune system parks dangerous cells in standby instead of destroying them.
plos-pone-0003942:
Mark Throsby, Edward van den Brink, Mandy Jongeneelen, and co-authors found broad flu antibodies in human memory cells in 2008. Antibodies to flu usually guard against only one strain type. The hemagglutinin coat protein is their main target, and it changes often. Protection across strain types has been hard to reach.

Their PLOS ONE article reports antibodies recovered from human IgM memory B cells. Those antibodies neutralized both H5N1 and H1N1 flu types. They also protected against both types in tests the team ran. Such antibodies hint at paths toward a flu vaccine with wider cover.
plos-pone-0004042:
Yeong-Hoon Choi, Douglas B. Cowan, Meena Nathan, and co-authors studied heart growth and low oxygen in 2008. Cyanosis and heart muscle thickening often occur together. Low oxygen normally drives new vessel growth in tissue. It does so through HIF factors and VEGF growth signals.

Their PLOS ONE article reports thickened heart muscle overrides that vessel response. Despite low oxygen, new vessel growth failed to follow. That failure may explain why such hearts struggle under stress. The finding reframes treatment aims for cyanotic heart disease. Readers can find the full text in PLOS ONE, an open science journal.
plos-pone-0004142:
Yoichiro Hoshino and colleagues published this cloning study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Tissue frozen without protective chemicals was long thought useless as a source of cells for cloning. The team challenged that belief using testicles taken from a dead bull and frozen in a standard minus-eighty freezer for ten years.

From those long-frozen organs they retrieved cells. They used the cells' nuclei to clone the bull by somatic cell nuclear transfer, the technique behind Dolly the sheep. The report shows that even roughly stored tissue can keep working DNA for a decade. That opens a path to reviving prized or lost animals from stored remains.
plos-pone-0004242:
Joost Willemse and Gilles van Wezel published this imaging study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Imaging scarce proteins inside living cells is usually hampered by the cell's own glow, called autofluorescence. Streptomyces bacteria are a key model for bacterial development and divide in synchrony during spore formation.

The authors describe imaging Streptomyces coelicolor with reduced autofluorescence, clearing the view. That clearer view reveals a novel stage in the localisation of FtsZ, the protein that marks where a bacterium will divide. A technical fix thus uncovers a step in how these bacteria build spores.
plos-pone-0004342:
Marco Mainardi and colleagues published this vision study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It is generally assumed that visual cortical cells shift their ocular dominance homogeneously in response to monocular deprivation, the closing of one eye. Little direct experimental evidence supported that notion of a uniform shift, however.

Using immunohistochemistry for c-Fos, an activity-dependent marker, the team assessed parvalbumin neurons in the rat visual cortex after long-term deprivation. They report reduced responsiveness in these inhibitory neurons. The picture that emerges is of a cortex that adapts unevenly, cell type by cell type.
plos-pone-0004442:
A blood protein called TRAIL may help predict how heart attack patients fare, report Paola Secchiero, Federica Corallini, Claudio Ceconi, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. In lab and animal work, the soluble form of TRAIL calms inflammation and slows artery disease. That made it a candidate marker worth testing in real patients.

The team measured TRAIL levels in the blood of people who had just had a heart attack. They then compared those levels with how the patients did afterward. As the title signals, lower levels after the attack carried a poor outlook. A simple blood test that flags high-risk patients early could help doctors aim closer care at those who need it most.
plos-pone-0004542:
The resting brain behaves differently in people with diabetic nerve pain, report Franco Cauda, Katiuscia Sacco, Sergio Duca, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. Neuropathic pain has a spontaneous component: pain that is simply there, as a background. That ongoing pain had not been explored enough with brain imaging, because it is hard to separate the brain activity that sustains it.

The authors address the brain correlates of ongoing pain in diabetic neuropathic pain for the first time, on their account. They studied the resting state, the brain's activity when no task is given. If background pain has a resting signature, it could be measured objectively. That would help in developing treatments for a kind of pain that patients describe as constant and exhausting.
plos-pone-0004642:
Withdrawing growth factors briefly before plating makes human neural precursor cells produce more neurons, show Telma Schwindt, Fabiana Motta, Gabriela Barnabe, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. Human neural precursor cells are candidates for neural transplantation in a wide range of neurological disorders. Much work has gone into how the culture environment alters their plasticity, their range of possible fates.

Two growth factors, EGF and FGF, keep these cells dividing in the dish. The team found that a short-term withdrawal of those mitogens prior to plating increases neuronal differentiation afterward. A simple timing change in the protocol yields more of the desired cell type. For cell therapy manufacturing, such cheap adjustments can decide whether a treatment is practical.
plos-pone-0004742:
Michael Doube and colleagues used 3D methods to study how cat limb bones scale with body size, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Past bone scaling studies took a few simple measures at one or two spots per bone. They then compared those measures to body mass or bone length to find growth rules.

Bones must do many jobs at once at the least cost, the authors note. A full 3D view captures that trade off far better. The team scanned limb bones across cat species of many sizes. Richer shape data can improve models of how animals move and bear weight.
plos-pone-0004842:
Giovanni Cattoli and colleagues performed comprehensive phylogenetic analysis of highly pathogenic H5N1 avian influenza in Africa, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Highly pathogenic avian influenza A/H5N1 was first officially reported in Africa in early 2006. Since the first outbreak in Nigeria, the virus spread rapidly to other African countries. With eleven countries experiencing outbreaks from emergence to early 2008 across poultry and wild birds.

Phylogenetics traces introductions and spread routes. Multiple lineages entered via trade and wild birds. Molecular characterization supports surveillance design. Africa specific data were urgently needed. The study gives researchers concrete leads that later work can verify and extend.
plos-pone-0004942:
Dendritic cells are the immune system's scouts. They shed tiny bubbles called exosomes. Those bubbles carry working alarm complexes on their surface. Sophie Viaud and colleagues reported new effects of these exosomes in PLOS ONE in 2009. The exosomes do more than talk to T cells. They also activate natural killer cells and make them multiply.

The effect depends on two kinds of cargo. One is ligands for the NKG2D receptor. The other is a piece of the IL-15 receptor. An earlier patient trial showed tumor regressions without T cell responses. This work helps explain that puzzle. It points to exosomes as a possible booster for cancer immunotherapy.
plos-pone-0005042:
Some Staphylococcus aureus strains cause deadly necrotizing pneumonia. They carry the Panton Valentine leukocidin toxin genes. Anne Tristan and colleagues studied one toxin piece, LukS. Their PLOS ONE paper appeared in 2009. They examined the signal peptide at its start. That tag normally guides the protein out of the cell.

The signal peptide does more than guide. It mediates increased adhesion to heparan sulfates. Those are sticky sugars on cell surfaces. The grip may help the toxin cling to lung tissue. The finding names a handshake behind a severe infection. It also warns that signal peptides can have second jobs. Vaccine and drug designers should take note.
plos-pone-0005142:
Listeria monocytogenes is a foodborne pathogen. In nature it also lives on plants. Lisa Gorski, Jessica Duhé and Denise Flaherty studied its plant life in PLOS ONE in 2009. They compared strains of the germ. The question was how flagella and motility serve plant colonization. Flagella are the whips bacteria swim with.

Swimming mattered for reaching and settling on plant surfaces. Strains differed in how much their tails helped. Fitness on plants varied with motility in strain-specific ways. The finding links a germ's swimming gear to its life on crops. Food safety starts in the field. Understanding plant colonization could help keep Listeria off produce. The study bridges microbiology and agriculture.
plos-pone-0005242:
Eating far fewer calories extends life in many species, yet the mechanism in mammals is still largely unknown. Estep and colleagues put male mice on short-term calorie restriction and reported striking gene changes in PLOS ONE in 2009.

Gene expression in the restricted males shifted toward patterns typical of females. Key regulators in conserved aging pathways also changed, including routes tied to TOR and sirtuins. The result suggests the diet rewires deep aging circuits quickly, and that sex shapes how the rewiring plays out. The fact that the shift starts in days, not months, is key, since it shows diet can move deep aging paths much faster than once thought.
plos-pone-0005342:
HER2-positive breast cancers can be treated with the antibody drug trastuzumab, but resistance is common. Flowers and Thompson tested a fatty acid called t10c12 conjugated linoleic acid on HER2-driven cancer cells, reported in PLOS ONE in 2009.

In SKBr3 breast cancer cells, the fatty acid suppressed the HER2 protein itself. It also enhanced apoptosis, the cells' self-destruct program, possibly through the COX2 pathway. Lowering the very target that drives these cancers is a promising angle against resistant disease. Fat in food is a long shot as a drug. Yet a safe food part that trims a key cancer protein may aid care for women whose tumors no longer heed the main drug in use.
plos-pone-0005442:
Giuliana Gatti and co-authors studied a cancer gene and a common drug in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. The gene Myc can push cells to grow, and its role in cell death is not simple. At times it seems to shield cells from death, and at times it makes death more likely.

The team tested what Myc does when cells meet paclitaxel, a drug used against cancer. They found that Myc stopped the death the drug would cause and boosted a process where cells copy their DNA without dividing. That helps explain why some tumours with high Myc resist drug treatment.
plos-pone-0005542:
Alexandre Prieur and co-authors studied a protein that helps turn genes on in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. The protein DRIL1 can make normal mouse cells live indefinitely and can team with cancer genes to drive growth. It also helps switch on the genes for antibody heavy chains.

The team found that a small tag added to DRIL1 steers its activity toward genes specific to white blood cells. That steering may explain how the protein helps blood cells develop their identity. It also hints at how the same protein can turn harmful in cancer.
plos-pone-0005642:
Katie Herbst, Michael Allen, and Jin Zhang reported a pitfall in kinase studies in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. Many lab tests of cell signalling rely on light made by an enzyme from a sea animal. A common drug used to block the kinase PKA turned out to dim that light directly.

Their finding means some past results may reflect the test, not the biology. Workers who use the light-based tests must control for the drug's effect on the light itself. Careful tool checks like this keep whole fields from chasing false leads.
plos-pone-0005742:
Emil Karaulanov and co-authors mapped a partnership of cell-surface proteins in frog embryos in 2009. The proteins FLRT3, Unc5B, and Rnd1 meet at the cell surface and shape how cells stick to each other. FLRT proteins were already tied to growth signals and nerve wiring.

A screen for FLRT3 partners netted the netrin receptors Unc5B and Unc5D as strong matches. Adding Rnd1, the trio tunes cell adhesion as tissues form. Such tuning decides whether cells hold fast or move during development. The results help explain how embryos sort their cells into clean layers and organs.
plos-pone-0005842:
Christopher Reigstad and co-authors showed in 2009 that gut bacteria help set the level of an inflammatory protein in mouse colon and fat. The gut microbiota is now seen as a factor in metabolic and inflammatory disease. Bacterial products like LPS can trigger weight gain and insulin resistance in mice.

The team found the protein SAA3 in colon lining and fat tissue responds to the microbiota's presence. That response links gut microbes to a known inflammation marker. It offers a measurable readout for studies of how changing gut bacteria alters body-wide inflammation. Such readouts are prized in the fast-growing microbiome field.
plos-pone-0005942:
Fat-like molecules can act as signals that switch cell behavior on or off. Giulio Muccioli, Angela Sia, Paul Muchowski and colleagues built a yeast toolkit in 2009 to study one such signal, called palmitoylethanolamide. Their PLOS ONE paper describes yeast strains changed by design to make or to break down this lipid.

A simple yeast that can be tuned this way lets labs find the enzymes that build and clear the signal. Those enzymes are the first step to grasping what the lipid does in the body. The strains are tools other teams can use, and the work opens a path into a signaling system that was barely mapped before.
plos-pone-0006042:
Adults will work to look at a baby's face, but not all faces pull alike. Rinah Yamamoto, Dan Ariely, Won Chi and colleagues measured that pull in 2009. Their PLOS ONE study gives healthy men and women two lab tasks, pressing keys to lengthen or shorten the time they view babies, some typical in looks and some with abnormal features.

The title gives the result: sex differences in how adults process babies hinge on the baby's facial attractiveness. Looks thus shape the urge to care, and shape it differently in men and women. The work speaks to how caregiving motivation is built, with honest weight for babies whose faces may draw less of it.
plos-pone-0006142:
Conscious sight may arrive in beats, not in a smooth stream. Sam Doesburg, Jessica Green, John McDonald and colleagues tested that rhythm with binocular rivalry in 2009, the effect where two eyes' images take turns in awareness. Their PLOS ONE paper reads the large-scale oscillatory network dynamics behind visual perception.

Their proposal casts each moment of perception as a brief joining of gamma-synchronous cell groups, forming and dissolving at a theta rhythm. Rivalry, where perception flips on its own, is the perfect test bed for such beats. The work gives the science of consciousness a timed mechanism to test, rather than a vague claim that rhythms matter.
plos-pone-0006242:
People with rheumatoid arthritis die of heart disease more often than others. Jonathan Graf and colleagues measured C-reactive protein, an inflammation marker, in arthritis patients in a 2009 PLOS ONE study. In the general population, levels above set cut-offs mark high and very high heart risk.

Such risky levels proved prevalent among the arthritis patients studied. Inflammation from the joints appears to travel with danger for the heart. The finding supports checking heart risk in arthritis care as a routine step. It also strengthens the case that controlling inflammation protects more than joints.
plos-pone-0006342:
Smallpox is eradicated, but its relatives, including monkeypox and cowpox, still infect people. Mark Eshoo and colleagues built a rapid, high-throughput test for the whole orthopoxvirus genus in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Several members can cause human infection, and fast identification matters in any outbreak.

The method pairs PCR copying with mass spectrometry to detect and identify the virus present. Speed plus specificity is what biodefence and clinics both need. The platform can process many samples at once. It strengthens readiness for natural outbreaks and deliberate releases alike. Fast, sure naming of the virus at hand is the core gain for clinics and labs.
plos-pone-0006442:
Hervé Vaucheret wrote a 2009 PLOS ONE paper on how a plant protein keeps its own levels in balance. The protein, AGO1, binds microRNAs, tiny RNA pieces that guide it. AGO1 then cuts target messages or blocks their use, quieting genes. Its own control depends on one of those microRNAs, miR168.

The study shows that two genes, MIR168a and MIR168b, make miR168 in two sizes. One form runs twenty-one units long, the other twenty-two. AGO1 also helps stabilize the microRNA that restrains it. This loop keeps gene silencing steady. The details matter for understanding how plants tune their own genes.
plos-pone-0006542:
Laura Wardrope, Ewa Okely, and David Leach studied DNA repair after chromosome cutting in PLOS ONE in 2009. DNA double-strand breaks can be repaired by homologous recombination. That process involves formation and resolution of Holliday junctions, cross-shaped DNA links. In E. coli, the RuvABC complex and RecG help resolve these joint molecules.

The team studied resolution following cleavage of the E. coli chromosome by the EcoKI restriction enzyme. Controlled cutting lets them watch repair in action. Knowing how bacteria resolve joint molecules matters for understanding genome stability. It also informs work on recombination in all organisms, including humans.
plos-pone-0006642:
Saif Ahmad, Tim Ramsay, Lothar Huebsch, and colleagues tested continuous monitoring for early sepsis detection in PLOS ONE in 2009. Early diagnosis of sepsis enables timely resuscitation and antibiotics and prevents subsequent morbidity and mortality. Clinical approaches relying on point-in-time analysis often detect sepsis late. The team used continuous multi-parameter heart rate variability analysis.

Their title reports the analysis heralds onset of sepsis in adults. Heart rhythm patterns change before obvious symptoms. Continuous monitoring turns an ICU data stream into an early warning system. Earlier antibiotics are the strongest lever for sepsis survival.
plos-pone-0006742:
Anne-Elise Tobin and co-authors measured ion channel genes in rhythm-generating neurons in PLOS ONE in 2009. Identified neurons can be recognized across individual animals. The authors asked how much their ion channel expression varies. They also asked whether some channels rise and fall together. Such relationships might be conserved across animals.

They studied neurons that fire in a steady rhythm. Channel levels were measured cell by cell. Correlations between channel messages appeared despite individual variation. Conserved correlations suggest rules that keep rhythms stable. Those rules matter because the same neuron type must work in every animal. The findings inform how nervous systems balance variety with reliability.
plos-pone-0006842:
Leonard Bosgraaf and Peter J. M. Van Haastert explained how crawling cells steer toward chemical signals in PLOS ONE in 2009. Chemotaxis guides cells in immunity, development, and wound healing. Shallow gradients do not trigger new pseudopods, recent work showed. That finding broke many steering models. Cells extend foot-like pseudopods to move. If gradients do not create them, something else must steer.

The authors propose parallel signaling to two controls. One control sets pseudopod persistence, how long a foot keeps going. The other sets orientation, which way feet point. Steering by bias, not by creation, fits the evidence. The model reshapes how chemotaxis is taught and simulated.
plos-pone-0006942:
Stephanie Hesselson, Pär Matsson, James Shima, and colleagues mapped variation in transporter genes in PLOS ONE in 2009. Membrane transporters move small molecules into and out of cells. Their cargoes include nutrients, environmental toxins, and many clinical drugs. The team focused on the promoter regions that control two large transporter families, ABC and SLC.

They asked whether common genetic variation in those promoters changes gene activity. They linked variants to liver and kidney specific expression patterns. Promoter differences could explain why people handle drugs so differently. The catalog they built helps predict which patients might clear a drug unusually fast or slowly.
plos-pone-0007042: Emily Almberg, L. David Mech, Douglas Smith, and colleagues surveyed infectious disease in Yellowstone National Park's canid community in PLOS ONE in 2009. Their method was serological, reading antibodies in blood samples from the park's wild canids. A survey like this records which diseases these wolves and other canids have met. That record helps managers judge disease risks to a famous and closely watched wildlife population.
plos-pone-0007142:
James Wiley, Laura Richert, Steve Swain, and colleagues boosted lung immunity in mice in PLOS ONE in 2009. Lung damage after viral infection comes from the virus and from inflammation alike. The team used a protein cage nanoparticle to change the lung's defenses. The particle induced bronchus-associated lymphoid tissue, local immune stations in the airways.

Mice with these induced stations resisted diverse respiratory viruses better. Ready-made immune outposts in the lung act fast, before systemic immunity arrives. A single treatment protecting against many viruses is attractive. It could serve as a broad shield during new outbreaks.
plos-pone-0007242:
Peter J. Mazzone, Nicola Marchi, Vince Fazio, and colleagues asked a brain imaging question about lung cancer in 2009. Lung cancer often spreads to the brain as metastases. When doctors image the brain to find those metastases, they also frequently see small vessel ischemic disease, damage from poor blood flow.

The authors ask whether that small vessel disease protects against developing brain metastases. They compare patients with and without the finding. Their PLOS ONE study tests a counterintuitive idea about the brain environment. Results could shape how doctors interpret scans and judge metastasis risk.
plos-pone-0007342:
Deng Pan and Liqing Zhang built an atlas of gene family size changes in animals in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Gene duplication is commonly accepted as a source of new genes and functions. Yet that assumption rested more on theory than on genome-wide proof when the study appeared in print.

The authors generate an atlas of copy number change rates. They measure how quickly animal gene families gain or lose copies. Their atlas turns a general evolutionary claim into measured rates. Those rates help researchers judge which gene families expand fast enough to drive adaptation.
plos-pone-0007442:
Matthew Shortridge and Robert Powers published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 comparing two proteins that look unrelated on the surface. One is PrgI, the needle protein of a bacterial injection system that delivers toxins into host cells. The others are Bcl-2 proteins, which control programmed cell death in animals. Overall sequence and structure match poorly between them.

Looking at active sites instead of whole shapes revealed a striking likeness. Functionally important regions stay conserved even when the rest of a protein drifts. On that basis, PrgI and the Bcl-2 family share working features. The study shows a way to spot hidden kinship between proteins from very different organisms. Such matches can hint at shared mechanisms across the tree of life.
plos-pone-0007542:
Cyrielle Clapé and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on a small RNA lost in prostate cancer. MicroRNAs are short, non-coding RNAs that dial genes down. One, miR-143, is found at lower levels in prostate cancer cells. The team measured its expression in human prostate tumors. They then restored it in mouse models to test whether it could slow the disease.

Restoring miR-143 interfered with ERK5 signaling, a growth pathway the tumors use. In mice, that interference abrogated prostate cancer progression. The small RNA acts as a natural brake that tumors must release to advance. Brakes of this kind interest drug developers, because replacing a lost microRNA is conceivable. The study moves miR-143 from a marker of disease to a possible lever against it.
plos-pone-0007642:
Pavel Katsel, Weilun Tan, and Vahram Haroutunian published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on the oldest-old, people past ninety. In that age group, Alzheimer's plaques and tangles do not line up strongly with dementia. Some very old brains carry the damage yet stay sharp. The team searched for other biological indices that separate the cognitively normal from the demented. They compared brain immune activity between the groups.

Those who stayed sharp showed a gain in brain immunity. Stronger immune gene activity, not less, marked the intact minds. That flips the usual story in which inflammation is purely harmful. In extreme old age, a vigorous brain immune system may be protective. The finding redirects the search for what preserves thought at ninety-plus. It also counsels care: suppressing brain immunity wholesale could backfire in the oldest patients.
plos-pone-0007742:
Zhiqiang Meng and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It asks which brain areas are needed for a classic addiction test. In conditioned place preference, animals learn to favor a place tied to a drug. Here the drug was morphine.

Sensory input is thought to feed drug-related behavior. The team tested whether the somatosensory cortices, which process touch, are required. Silencing those areas blocked the animals from learning the preference. The result gives touch-processing regions a role in addiction memory. It widens the map of brain circuits that drugs of abuse can hijack.
plos-pone-0007842:
Klara Stefflova and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It reads the genetic ancestry of people from Philadelphia and Dakar. Ancestry can be traced through two special lines of DNA. Mitochondrial DNA follows the mother, and the Y chromosome follows the father.

Comparing them can reveal sex-biased mixing in a population's past. The authors evaluated group ancestry in both cities. They set the results in the wider context of admixture in the Americas. Such work shows how migration and unequal mixing shaped modern populations. It also matters for medical genetics, where ancestry affects disease studies.
plos-pone-0007942:
Catherine Teyssier and colleagues asked what happens to bones when a certain receptor is missing, in PLOS ONE in 2009. The receptor, ERR alpha, is found in places where bone is forming. Female mice bred without it were watched as they aged or lost estrogen, the hormone drop behind much bone loss.

The mice without the receptor kept their bone far better than normal mice did. Age and hormone loss, which thin the bones of normal females, left these mice largely spared. The result suggests that blocking this receptor might one day shield human bones, a hope for the many women at risk after menopause.
plos-pone-0008042:
Stephen Emrich and colleagues studied visual search and memory in PLOS ONE in 2009. They asked whether hunting a scene with the eyes uses the same brain store as holding pictures in mind. Visual working memory holds a few items at once, and brain waves show a known mark when it loads. The mark is called contralateral delay activity.

Searching a cluttered scene raised that very mark. The act of looking for a target thus draws on the memory store, not just the eyes. The link helps explain why busy scenes tire the mind and why memory training might sharpen search.
plos-pone-0008142:
Fang Chen and colleagues bred DNA strands that grip a hepatitis C protein in PLOS ONE in 2009. The target is E2, a protein on the virus's coat. The breeding method, cell-surface SELEX, sifts a vast pool of random strands on living cells and keeps only the tight grippers.

The winning strands, called aptamers, clung to E2 with high strength. A tight gripper can anchor a test that finds the virus, or a drug that gums its entry into liver cells. The work is a first step, but aptamer tools have a good record of reaching clinics.
plos-pone-0008242:
Agua Sobrino and colleagues studied the hormone estradiol in cultured cells in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. Estradiol affects blood vessels, but clinical and lab studies disagree on how. The team used DNA microarrays to map gene activity in human endothelial cells. These cells line blood vessels and came from umbilical veins. They were exposed to a low dose of estradiol.

Estradiol stimulated pathways that widen vessels and pathways tied to metabolism. The gene patterns show both effects starting in the same cells. That helps reconcile conflicting views of the hormone's action. It may also inform hormone therapy research.
plos-pone-0008342:
Rinki Minakshi and her team wrote in PLOS ONE in 2009 about a protein of the SARS germ. The SARS virus kills the cells it gets into, and some of its proteins push cells to die. One such part is the 3a protein. It sits in a part of the cell where new proteins are made and packed for use. That place made the team think the protein puts stress on the cell's own shops.

They found that 3a does put such stress on that part of the cell. It also cuts down the cell's ear for type 1 interferon, a key alarm drug the body makes. With that ear dulled, the germ can hide from the body's guards with more ease. The work shows a two-part trick of the virus.
plos-pone-0008442:
Yuehui Wang and co-authors study food protein uptake in mice in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. A small part of the protein we eat survives digestion whole. It can cross the gut in a form the immune system can sense. In most cases that leads to tolerance, not illness. But in celiac disease or food allergy, it can cause harm.

The team track a test protein called ovalbumin. They find that chylomicrons help move it from gut to body. Chylomicrons are fat carriers made in the gut after a meal. The work shows a route by which food proteins spread. That route may shape both tolerance and allergy.
plos-pone-0008542:
Sara Monteiro and co-authors trace a protein's fate in lupin seeds in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. During germination, a seed storage protein called beta-conglutin is cut into pieces. Limited proteolysis processes many of its subunits into a smaller polypeptide. That product, termed blad, is about twenty kilodaltons in size. Blad is the main component of a sugar-linked oligomer. It accumulates exclusively in the cotyledons of Lupinus seeds.

The authors map the unique biosynthetic route from gene to blad. They follow the beta-conglutin gene through expression to final processing. Understanding this route clarifies how seeds mobilize stored protein. Blad itself has antifungal interest beyond seed biology.
plos-pone-0008642:
Diane Lebesgue and co-authors test estrogen-like drugs after stroke in rats in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Pre-treatment with estradiol strongly protects young animals from loss of blood flow. Such loss, called ischemia, is what happens in stroke. Whether the drug still helps in aging animals was largely unknown. Giving it after the insult is also more like real care. The team give new estrogen receptor drugs soon after ischemia in middle-aged female rats.

The drugs reduce loss of nerve cells in the hippocampus. Protection holds even when treatment starts after the insult. The new drugs may avoid some side effects of classic estrogen. The work supports post-stroke use of this drug path in older brains.
plos-pone-0008742:
Gusti Zeiner, Kara Norman, J. Michael Thomson, and colleagues asked how a common parasite rewires its host. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study covers Toxoplasma gondii, a germ that infects most warm-blooded animals. It can live inside nearly any cell type with a nucleus. Such range means it exploits basic cell machinery shared across hosts. Small RNAs called microRNAs tune much of that machinery.

Infected cells raised the levels of certain key microRNAs. Other microRNAs stayed flat, so the change was selective. Shifting these tuners could help the parasite settle in. The finding names specific host pathways that infection quietly bends.
plos-pone-0008842:
Paul Roy, Sasha Tetu, André Larouche, and colleagues read the complete genome of an odd, drug-resistant germ. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Pseudomonas aeruginosa PA7 came from a patient in Argentina. It resists many antibiotics at once. Early gene checks showed it sits apart from its species, a taxonomic outlier. Outliers can reveal how the species evolves and resists drugs.

The full sequence gives PA7's complete genetic inventory. Comparisons with relatives highlight its resistance toolkit. A reference genome for an outlier sharpens species definitions. It also helps track where multidrug resistance genes travel.
plos-pone-0008942:
Perry Evans and co-authors searched HIV proteins for docking spots used by human enzymes, in PLOS ONE in 2010. As HIV infects a cell, it borrows the cell's own machinery to copy itself. Two human enzymes, ERK1 and ERK2, tag HIV proteins with phosphate groups. Before tagging, an enzyme must first grip its target at a docking site.

The team lined up the sequences of HIV proteins and looked for known docking patterns. Several possible docking motifs turned up on proteins the virus needs to multiply. If those grips are real, blocking them could slow the virus down. The study gives drug researchers a shortlist of places worth testing in the lab.
plos-pone-0009042:
Steven Platek and Devendra Singh scanned men's brains while they viewed women's body shapes, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Waist-to-hip ratio is a body cue tied to fertility. Other cues, like facial symmetry in men, also advertise reproductive quality. The researchers asked what the preferred ratio does inside the brain.

Images of women with ratios near the supposed optimum lit up reward centres. Those brain areas respond to things the brain counts as valuable. The study sits in evolutionary psychology, reading attraction as a health signal. Critics of this field debate how much such scans can really prove.
plos-pone-0009142:
Mériam Ben Hamida-Rebaï and Charles Robert rebuilt a fleeting molecular moment inside a computer, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Ras-family G proteins are switches flipped by swapping GDP for GTP. Helper proteins called GEFs speed that exchange step up enormously. The swap passes through a short-lived state that no microscope can catch.

The study recreated that intermediate state and followed its magnesium ion. Magnesium sits at the very heart of the exchange chemistry. Simulations showed where the ion moves as the protein switch flips. Such fine details guide drugs aimed at Ras switches in cancer.
plos-pone-0009242:
Marc Trimborn and co-authors published this mouse genetics study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Faults in the human gene MCPH1 cause primary microcephaly, where the brain develops too small. Cells with the fault show a striking error: chromosomes condense too early, then unfold too slowly after division. The gene makes a protein called microcephalin.

The team built a mouse model whose Mcph1 gene was misregulated the same way. The mice let them study the faulty chromosome timing in a living animal. Such a model connects a human birth defect to its cell-level cause. It also gives researchers a test bed for understanding how brain size is set.
plos-pone-0009342:
François Gonzalvez and co-authors published this cell death study in PLOS ONE in 2010. When death signals arrive, a protein called Bid is cut into its active form, tBid. tBid travels to the mitochondria, the cell's power plants, and triggers the release of cytochrome c. That release is the point of no return in this kind of cell suicide.

The team studied how tBid's hairpin-shaped section interacts with cardiolipin, a fat found in mitochondrial membranes. The details of that contact decide how tBid does its deadly work. Understanding the mechanism matters because this pathway is a target in cancer, where cells refuse to die on cue.
plos-pone-0009442:
Juliana Yordanova and co-authors studied sleep and sudden insight in PLOS ONE in 2010. People sometimes solve a hard task in a flash after sleep. The team used a task that hides a simple rule behind many moves. Volunteers tried it, slept for part of the night, and then tried again.

Sleep early in the night and sleep late in the night did not act the same. Brain states tied to each part of the night changed the chance of a sudden insight in distinct ways. The work shows that when we sleep can shape what kind of thinking sleep helps. It refines the old advice to sleep on a problem.
plos-pone-0009542:
Gildas Merceron and colleagues tested what tooth surfaces can reveal about diet in PLOS ONE in 2010. The teeth of extinct mammals carry tiny wear marks from food. Older methods relied on a person picking out marks in flat images. Newer methods scan the surface in three dimensions and measure its texture. The team asked whether those textures can tell apart what single animals ate.

If texture records the meals of one animal, fossils could reveal personal diets, not just species habits. Their tests weigh how much detail the method truly captures. That matters for rebuilding the lives of extinct species. It also sharpens how we read the daily lives of living animals from their teeth.
plos-pone-0009642:
Heike Goehler and co-authors tested how disease linked protein stretches affect yeast in PLOS ONE in 2010. Long runs of the amino acid glutamine occur in proteins tied to Huntington's disease. Yeast have their own prion proteins, Sup35 and Rnq1, which can fold into amyloid fibers. Those fibers normally form rarely on their own. The team asked whether glutamine rich tracts can trigger that folding.

The tracts proved to be potent triggers of amyloid formation in both yeast prions. One misfolded protein can thus seed others into the same state. This cross seeding may explain how damage spreads between proteins in brain disease. Yeast gives a fast, simple system for studying that spread.
plos-pone-0009842:
The tiny spines on brain cells grow and shrink as memories form. Albert Hung and colleagues studied a protein system that trims those spines in rat brain neurons. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010.

Dendritic spines are the small bumps where most excitatory synapses land. The system centers on GKAP, a scaffold protein in the postsynaptic side of a synapse. TRIM3, a ubiquitin ligase, drives GKAP degradation, tagging it for disposal. The work was done in rat hippocampal neurons, cells from the brain's memory center. Controlling spine shape helps explain how synapses stay flexible.
plos-pone-0009942:
A single helper protein can push protein building forward and tidy up when cells are stressed. Chi Ho Li and colleagues mapped three jobs for that helper in one study. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010.

The helper is eIF5A, a factor in translating RNA into protein. It promotes translation elongation, the step where the protein chain grows. It also promotes polysome disassembly and stress granule assembly, two ways cells manage stalled work. One factor linking growth and stress helps explain cell economy. Stress granules are clumps where stalled protein work waits.
plos-pone-0010042:
The authors were Joern Boeke, Catherine Regnard, Weili Cai, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study covered how chromosomes pack their DNA. A protein called SU(VAR)3-9 helps build heterochromatin, the tightly packed form of DNA. Packing is closely controlled as animals develop, so the protein's activity must be controlled too.

The team showed that another protein, the kinase JIL-1, adds a phosphate tag to SU(VAR)3-9. That tagging is a common way cells switch proteins on or off. The result adds a control step to the story of how genes get locked away in packed DNA.
plos-pone-0010142:
The authors were Adam Handel, Lahiru Handunnetthi, Antonio Berlanga, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study followed up gene hunts for multiple sclerosis. Genome-wide studies had found single letter DNA changes linked to MS risk. MS itself is a complex nerve disorder shaped by both genes and environment. A risk variant alone says little without knowing what it does.

The team asked whether those variants change how nearby genes are expressed. Linking a DNA change to a change in gene activity is a step toward mechanism. Such links can turn a statistical hit into a target biologists can test.
plos-pone-0010342:
Bettina Pause, Katrin Lübke, Joachim Laudien and colleagues asked how the brain handles the smell of anxiety, in PLOS ONE in 2010. People can signal fear or stress through body odor, even without words. Past work using behavior tests and brain scans had already shown this channel exists. The team wanted to see how fast the brain responds to such smells. They also compared people with and without social anxiety.

Odor samples came from donors waiting for a major school exam. Listeners' brains were watched with fine timing as the smells arrived. Brains seemed to invest extra effort in processing these chemical anxiety signals. That effort differed by how socially anxious a person was. The study treats smell as a real social signal, not a curiosity.
plos-pone-0010442:
Yanlong Sun and Hongbin Wang studied how people remember physical spaces in PLOS ONE in 2010. Mental maps of rooms and places are not perfect copies. They come out distorted and chopped into segments. The authors ran two experiments on why that happens. Their idea: the mind stores space in layered frames, like nested maps at different scales.

Multiple frames explain both the bends and the breaks in recalled layouts. A person may know each sub-space well yet misjudge how they join. Such errors affect navigation, witness accounts, and building design. Knowing the frames helps predict where people will get lost. The study treats memory of place as an organized system, not a faded photograph.
plos-pone-0010542:
Po-Yen Huang and colleagues tested whether symptom patterns alone can flag flu in a quiet season in PLOS ONE in 2010. During flu outbreaks, everyone wants to know which symptoms mean real infection. The team ran a prospective study at a community clinic in a metropolitan area. Patients there lived in a low-prevalence setting, where most flu-like illness is not flu. Throat swabs provided the truth against which symptoms were judged.

In low-prevalence times, even classic symptom sets mislead often. That is a base-rate lesson every clinician relearns each season. Syndromic guessing can still guide testing, but not replace it. The study quantifies how far symptoms carry in a community clinic. It supports lab confirmation when decisions matter.
plos-pone-0010642:
Bart van den Berg and colleagues argued that gene catalogs must be refreshed before computer modeling, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Systems biology builds models from large gene activity datasets. Those datasets rely on annotations that say what each gene is and does.

Annotations age quickly as knowledge grows. Old labels can assign genes to the wrong jobs or miss jobs entirely. The authors show how stale labels distort model results, using functional genomics data. They then lay out why re-annotation should be a routine first step. Careful bookkeeping sounds dull, but wrong labels can sink an entire study.
plos-pone-0010742:
Ge-Fei Hao and Guang-Fu Yang simulated how the plant hormone auxin is sensed, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Auxin steers plant growth, from root branching to fruit set. Its receptor, TIR1, works by gripping target proteins once auxin is present, marking them for removal. Two phenylalanine building blocks sit near the grip site.

Computer simulations of the moving protein showed both blocks guiding the target into place. Without them, the grip formed poorly in the model. Such atomic detail is hard to catch in still crystal pictures. It can guide design of new growth regulators that fit the receptor more precisely.
plos-pone-0010842:
Rajarshi Bhadra, Hongbing Guan and Imtiaz Khan published this infection study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Toxoplasma gondii is a common parasite, and killer CD8 T cells are central to keeping it under control during both early and lasting infection. Two related immune signals, IL-7 and IL-15, help these cells develop, but their joint role was unclear.

Mice missing only one of the two signals kept a fairly normal CD8 response during acute infection. Mice missing both, however, built a much weaker response, with fewer mature cells, less of a key defense chemical, slower growth, and poorer killing power. Bhadra and colleagues show the two signals back each other up. That backup system helps explain how the body keeps its parasite defenses from failing when one pathway is lost.
plos-pone-0010942:
Emma Robinson, Nickolai Titov, Gavin Andrews and co-authors ran this trial of internet therapy for anxiety, published in PLOS ONE in 2010. Generalized anxiety disorder means constant, hard-to-control worry, and online cognitive behavioral therapy had already helped when a clinician guided it. The authors asked whether a technician's support could match a clinician's, at lower cost.

One hundred fifty community volunteers with the disorder were assigned at random to clinician-guided treatment, technician-guided treatment, or a waiting group. Both guided groups completed six online lessons with homework and weekly contact across ten weeks, and the clinician group also had a moderated discussion forum. Robinson and colleagues framed the study as a non-inferiority test. If technicians do as well, anxiety treatment could scale to many more people online.
plos-pone-0011042:
Kerry Wilson, Mainak Das, Kathryn Wahl and co-authors published this bioengineering study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Living muscle grown on micro-devices could serve as a sensor for toxins and a test bed for muscle performance, if its contractions can be measured precisely. The authors grew embryonic rat muscle fibers on tiny silicon cantilevers, diving-board structures that bend under force.

Using an atomic force microscope detection system, they watched muscle behavior in real time and selectively triggered contractions, reading the bending as a measure of contractile stress. Wilson and colleagues demonstrate a working bio-MEMS muscle assay, where living tissue itself is the sensing element. Paralyzing toxins would register as lost force within minutes, giving such devices a role in toxin screening that animal tests currently fill.
plos-pone-0011142:
Shi, Santander, Brenneman and colleagues built test vaccines in PLOS ONE in 2010. They used live, weakened typhoid bacteria as a carrier to deliver a piece of another germ. The goal was to see whether one gene in the carrier, called rpoS, changes how strong the immune response is.

Their constructs let them isolate the role of that single gene in vaccine response. The carrier approach aims at two diseases with one vaccine, here including a lung germ that harms children. Knowing which carrier genes help or hurt response guides better design. That could lead to cheaper combined vaccines for places that need them most.
plos-pone-0011242:
Proverbio, Riva, Martin and colleagues tested face reading in women for PLOS ONE in 2010. Textbooks long said face processing lives mainly in the right side of the brain. The team recorded brain responses while women viewed several hundred faces and analyzed which brain areas coded them.

Face coding in the female brain proved to use both sides, not one alone. That result revises a simple picture taught for years. Sex differences in brain organization matter for fair neuroscience: rules drawn from mostly male samples may not hold. The study encourages testing both sexes before general claims are made.
plos-pone-0011342:
Anna Christensen and co-workers examined plant versions of calreticulin in 2010, using the small weed Arabidopsis. Calreticulin is a protein found in the cell's inner workshop, where it helps fold new proteins and manage calcium stores. Animals have forms of it with clear jobs, but what the several plant forms each do was much less clear.

Arabidopsis carries three related forms, and the team tested how each one behaves and where it acts. The forms turned out not to be simple backups. Each had taken on distinct, specialized duties as plants evolved. That split helps explain how plants handle stress and growth with a partly shared toolkit. It also guides crop research, since calcium handling and protein folding both affect how plants cope with drought and disease.
plos-pone-0011442:
Michiel van Boven and co-authors tracked flu spread inside homes during the 2009 H1N1 pandemic in a 2010 study. Households were ground zero for transmission, and close contacts of patients were often given antiviral drugs in advance to prevent infection. Whether that drug shield held up inside a real home, with shared air and close contact, was an open question.

Following households where members took preventive antivirals, the team measured how often the virus still passed to contacts. Their transmission data let officials judge how much protection the drugs truly add at home. That judgment shapes pandemic plans: preventive drugs are costly and in short supply, so they must go where they work. The study gives planners household-level numbers instead of hopeful guesses for the next pandemic.
plos-pone-0011542:
Jia Hu, Karen Doucette, and Lisa Hartling gathered the world's evidence in 2010 on treating hepatitis C in children. The virus infects children as well as adults, mainly through medical exposure or from mother to child, yet nearly all treatment trials had been run in adults. A systematic review collects every eligible study, weighs its quality, and states plainly what is known and what is not.

Their synthesis tells pediatricians which treatments work in children, how safe they are at young ages, and where the evidence runs thin. Children are not small adults in drug handling or in the decades of life over which side effects and cures play out. A dedicated review prevents two errors at once: denying children treatments that would help, and giving them regimens whose risks were only ever measured in grown bodies.
plos-pone-0011642:
Carlos Goller and Patrick Seed screened for chemicals that strip a protective coat from E. coli bacteria, in PLOS ONE in 2010. This germ is the leading cause of urinary tract infections, and drug resistance is rising. Instead of killing the germ, so-called anti-virulence drugs aim to disarm it so the body can clear it.

The pair ran a high-throughput screen for blockers of the group 2 capsule, the sugary shield many harmful strains wear. The screen found candidate chemicals that stop capsule building. Such hits could lead to treatments that weaken infection while putting less pressure on bacteria to evolve resistance.
plos-pone-0011742:
Paolo Uva and co-authors set surface proteins of real tumours next to those of lab-grown cancer lines, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Cell lines are the workhorses of cancer research, yet how well their surface traits match the tumours they came from was poorly known. That gap matters, because surface proteins are prime drug targets.

From gene activity data, the team compared the full set of membrane proteins between tumours and derived lines. Their side-by-side test gauges what the lab lines keep and what they lose. The verdict helps researchers judge when results from a cell line can be trusted for therapy work.
plos-pone-0011942:
William Kelly and colleagues mapped in 2010 the sugar-processing toolkit of a bacterium that helps cattle digest grass. Butyrivibrio proteoclasticus lives in the rumen, the fermentation chamber of the cow stomach, and is skilled at breaking down plant polysaccharides, the tough sugars of fiber. It also makes butyrate, a useful energy product for the animal.

The team's survey of its glycobiome, the full set of genes for handling sugars, shows a microbe adapted in detail to a polysaccharide-rich home. Each enzyme cataloged is a candidate for improving feed digestion or industrial fiber breakdown. Better rumen science feeds directly into how much milk and meat a given pasture can support.
plos-pone-0012042:
Erik Meijaard and colleagues set in 2010 the ape counts of the age of Wallace next to counts from our own time, to gauge how far orangutans have fallen. Orangutans in Borneo now live thin on the ground, and to see one in the wild is a rare treat. Set by that, the old logs startle: collectors in the time of Alfred Russel Wallace could shoot apes day in, day out.

Working through those logs, the team found that the rate at which a searcher meets an ape has fallen steeply. The apes, they argue, were once spread far more thickly over their home woods. A long base line moves the goal for those who guard the apes: to raise today's thin counts back to health would still leave the apes far short of their old plenty.
plos-pone-0012142:
Dharanesh Gangaiah, Zhe Liu, Jesús Arcos, and co-authors studied a food-poisoning bacterium in PLOS ONE in 2010. Campylobacter jejuni is a leading cause of diarrheal illness, and it survives stress and infects people with the help of a stored chemical called polyphosphate. One enzyme builds that store, while a second one, PPK2, spends it to make an energy-rich signal.

The authors show PPK2 is a fresh factor in how this bacterium handles stress and causes disease. Blocking an enzyme the germ needs under stress is a classic drug strategy. Naming PPK2's role gives researchers a new target in a very common pathogen, one that grows harder to treat as drug resistance spreads.
plos-pone-0012242:
Serign Ceesay, Climent Casals-Pascual, Davis Nwakanma, and co-authors reported malaria's continued fall in The Gambia in PLOS ONE in 2010. Malaria cases had already dropped sharply in the country's west over several years up to 2007, raising a once-unthinkable idea: elimination. Since then, bed nets, spraying, and better treatment had been scaled up further with outside support.

Their report checks whether the decline held or bounced back as efforts expanded. A sustained fall strengthens the case that this once heavily burdened region could aim at zero local cases. It also supplies other African countries a worked example of which combined measures coincided with lasting gains.
plos-pone-0012342:
Jin Qian and Huajian Gao published a modeling study in PLOS ONE in 2010 on how cells hold on to the surfaces around them. Single bonds between cell receptors and target molecules break fast, yet whole tissues stay firm for long spans. The authors asked how the softness of the surface under those bonds changes the way groups of bonds share the load.

Their model shows that soft surfaces weaken the teamwork among bonds, so clusters fail sooner than they would on stiff ground. The work helps explain why cells behave so differently on soft gels and firm tissue. It also gives engineers a rule of thumb for building soft materials that cells must grip, from wound dressings to lab-grown tissue scaffolds.
plos-pone-0012442:
Marcel Stoop, Vaibhav Singh, Lennard Dekker and colleagues compared proteins in spinal fluid from two forms of multiple sclerosis, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Most patients have the relapsing-remitting form, with attacks and recoveries, while others worsen steadily from the start in the primary progressive form. Whether the two are one disease or two is still argued.

Proteomics — reading hundreds of proteins at once — showed the fluids differ in measurable ways. Distinct protein profiles hint that the forms run on somewhat different biology. Such profiles could sharpen diagnosis and may explain why drugs that help relapsing patients often fail in progressive disease.
plos-pone-0012542:
Daria Gavriouchkina, Sabine Fischer, Tomi Ivacevic and colleagues studied a light-controlled repair switch in zebrafish embryos, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Light triggers many cell responses, and fish embryo cells literally sense light themselves, but how the signal reaches the genome was an enigma. One transcription factor, thyrotroph embryonic factor, responds to light.

The team showed the factor regulates light-induced transcription of DNA repair genes in embryonic cells. Coupling repair to daylight makes sense: sunlight itself damages DNA. The zebrafish system offers a clean model for how light, clocks, and genome protection are wired together in early life.
plos-pone-0012642:
Libby and Glass used maths to ask how big a judging committee should be, and who should sit on it. Hiring panels, juries, election counts and skating judges all face the same design problem. Too few judges gives noisy verdicts, while too many can add cost without adding truth.

Their 2010 paper works out how accuracy changes with the number of judges and their skill mix. The results give a rule of thumb for building panels in fields far apart. It is a neat case of one simple model serving many real decisions.
plos-pone-0012842:
Schuchmann and Siemers measured how loud the sonar calls of horseshoe bats are within one bat community. A bat's call strength sets the size of the world it can sense, since faint echoes from far prey get lost. Data on call intensity across species were only starting to gather when they wrote in 2010.

They asked whether species sharing one habitat split call strength to divide food resources, or use it to signal each other. Either answer links a physical trait to community life. Such work sharpens the ecology of night hunting.
plos-pone-0319542:
Joe D. Piper and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE on young children in rural Zimbabwe who were exposed to HIV before birth but not infected. Worldwide, millions of such children exist thanks to treatment that prevents transmission from mother to child, yet they still face higher rates of illness and stunting than unexposed children. Piper's team measured body size and composition at age two in a subgroup of a large nutrition and sanitation trial.

Compared with unexposed children, the exposed group was shorter and lighter, with smaller arms and calves. Electrical measurements and skinfold tests showed they carried both less lean tissue and less fat. Lower birthweight did not explain the gap, and neither did stunting on its own. The authors suggest this early pattern of reduced body tissue may help explain why these children remain more vulnerable to sickness and slower development.
plos-pone-0327442:
Jiaxiang Zheng, Moxi Cao, and Chongbin Zhang built a computer system that can pick out the lead instrument in recordings of Chinese traditional music, reported in PLOS ONE in 2026. In an ensemble, many instruments play at once, and telling them apart by ear or software is hard, especially when two flutes sound nearly alike.

Their method works in two stages: first it separates the mixed audio into single-instrument strands, then a classifier names the instruments present. On a new dataset they built, accuracy and related scores rose clearly over earlier approaches, with the biggest gains on sound-alike pairs such as the dizi and xiao flutes. They offer the tool for preserving and studying Chinese musical heritage.
plos-pone-0329042:
Snead and colleagues describe a 2026 study protocol set in rural Karonga, in northern Malawi. The team wants to learn what drives steady loss of kidney function in adults there. Kidney disease is rising worldwide and hits poorer countries hard. Blood tests based on creatinine, the usual marker, can miss cases in African populations.

Adults who took part in earlier health surveys will give new blood and urine samples and answer questions on risks at home. Samples from three points in time will be tested with both creatinine and cystatin C, a marker the authors note gives closer readings. The main outcome is a lasting drop of about a quarter in estimated kidney function. Findings should help Malawi aim screening and care at the people most at risk.
plos-pone-0341242:
Katja Bøhling Dybdahl and colleagues, including the DANCAVAS trialists, published this 2026 Danish cohort study of gout drugs and aortic aneurysms. A swollen belly aorta can rupture fatally, and urate-lowering gout medicines had been suggested to slow its growth. The team followed nearly a thousand screened men for five years through national registries.

Only a small share used the medicines, and their aneurysms grew no slower than other men's. Surgery, rupture, and death rates also showed no benefit. Dybdahl concludes these drugs should not be expected to protect men with aneurysms, whatever their value for gout.
plos-pone-0341642:
Denis Omara and colleagues provide step-by-step guidelines for making vaccine and gene-therapy vectors from a dog adenovirus. The usual human adenovirus used for such delivery is blunted by widespread prior immunity in people. The canine virus type 2 rarely infects humans and slips into airway and nerve cells well. It also keeps delivered genes switched on for a long time without inserting into the genome.

Their protocol covers growing the non-replicating vector, purifying it, and measuring its strength, the practical details a laboratory needs to reproduce the work. Because the vector provokes immunity on its own, it needs no added booster chemicals in vaccine designs. Sharing a vetted recipe lowers the barrier for groups wanting to build vaccines on this platform.
plos-pone-0341942:
Crystal Suei Cheng Wong and colleagues test whether a single dose of patterned magnetic brain stimulation sharpens vision when the eyes are deliberately blurred. A dozen adults with normal sight wore lenses that fogged their view, then received one of two stimulation patterns or a sham at the back of the head across separate visits. Sight and contrast tests ran right before and right after each session, under a registered plan with neither side knowing which session was real.

Neither active pattern changed contrast judgment or sharpness beyond the sham session. Sharpness did improve slightly over time in every session, a practice effect the authors flag. Wong and colleagues read the null result as evidence that one session cannot retune a healthy visual system under blur, whatever later sessions might do.
plos-pone-0343442:
Yuting Luo and colleagues build in 2026 a warning system for hidden stock manipulation in China's main share market. Past cases punished by the national regulator were labelled by month, then matched with company reports, online investor mood, and trading patterns. A learning model joined the text and number signals to score risk for each firm each month.

The joined model beat models using only one kind of signal, and it was far better at catching the riskiest cases early in a ranked list. The authors read this as proof that odd moves across disclosure, mood, and trading together reveal manipulation, giving regulators a practical screening tool.
plos-pone-0344142:
Xiaoqing Ye and seven colleagues published this 2026 cancer study testing a small peptide against stomach tumors. Drugs that block the growth factor VEGF can slow new blood vessels feeding a tumor, but the antibody versions are large and reach tissue poorly. A doubled peptide called D6, designed to grip VEGF, was their smaller alternative.

In cell tests and in mice carrying human stomach tumors, D6 slowed growth about as well as the standard antibody used for comparison. The catch was dose: the peptide needed repeated injections at higher amounts. Ye's group is now refining the molecule toward a more practical treatment.
plos-pone-0344742:
Claudia Nery Teixeira Palombo and colleagues interviewed just over five hundred mothers of young children in Salvador, Brazil, about their trust in vaccines. Most children there are registered with family health units, giving the team a clear window on everyday attitudes. Mothers answered questions on family circumstances, their children's vaccination records, and how safe and necessary they believe vaccines to be.

Confidence ran high overall, with more than four in five mothers trusting vaccines, yet about a quarter showed some hesitancy. Mothers with more schooling trusted more, while a poor or neutral relationship with clinic staff dragged trust down and pushed perceived risk up. Mothers who had refused a new vaccine were notably less confident overall. The authors urge services to invest in warmer, steadier relationships with parents.
plos-pone-0344942:
Parkpoom Chaisiriprasert and Apicha Deearom built a learning system to tell sea turtle species apart in underwater photos. Telling species apart supports counts and protection, yet murky water, poor light, and blocked views fool both people and models. Their system feeds both colour photos and edge maps that trace shell and flipper outlines into a shared network with smart blending steps.

The best blending version led on precision, recall, and overall detection scores, beating simpler fusions. Adding outline cues helped most where species look alike in colour alone. Automated, accurate sorting could let survey teams process far more dive and drone photos, building better maps of where each turtle species lives.
plos-pone-0345742:
Kathryn M. Yount and co-workers develop a short survey module that national statistics offices can use to measure women's empowerment. Countries lack routine data for tracking global gender goals. Their 2026 study builds the module for face-to-face surveys. It tests the module in Bangladesh, Malawi, and Nepal. The checks ask whether question groups hold together, and whether they mean the same thing across genders and countries.

Most question groups formed sound, distinct measures tied to empowerment ideas. A smaller set behaved the same across men and women, and fewer still across countries. Links with outside measures were mostly weak, though a few matched expectations well. The team concludes the module needs more refinement before scores can be compared fairly everywhere.
plos-pone-0346542:
Yan Zhang, Wei Chen, and Gang Yang published a study on virtual camera movement in PLOS ONE in 2026. Digital twins and AI-built 3D scenes need camera paths for tours and reviews. A poorly planned path swings and jerks, leaving viewers confused or even queasy.

Zhang's team guided path planning with how human vision works, aiming for views people can follow with ease. Their framework keeps tours smooth and readable at large scale. Designers of virtual site visits, training scenes, and city models face this need daily. Better camera paths mean reviewers spend their attention on the scene itself, not on fighting the viewpoint, which improves the value of every digital twin walk-through.
plos-pone-0347642:
HaoBo Yang and colleagues investigated how sodium nitrite, a preservative found in processed meats and a widespread contaminant, might help clog arteries. Hardening of the arteries kills millions each year, but the molecular route from nitrite exposure to disease was sketchy. Their 2026 study is a computer and data-mining exercise, stitching together gene databases, machine learning, and molecular simulations rather than new lab experiments.

The analysis singled out four suspect proteins, with an inflammation signal called IL-1 beta at the centre. Virtual docking showed nitrite binding stably to it, and diseased artery tissue showed heavier infiltration by immune cells. The authors frame the work as a hypothesis map for future laboratory testing, not proof of harm.
plos-pone-0348142:
Charuai Suwanbamrung and a multinational team studied in 2026 how households in southern Thailand understand dengue control and the surveillance system that tracks mosquito larvae. Dengue is spread by mosquitoes that breed in water containers around homes, so household practice decides much of the risk. Health workers use larval indices, counts of breeding sites found in surveys, to judge where outbreaks may ignite.

Their mixed methods study combined surveys with interviews of household representatives, the people who actually receive and act on dengue advice. Knowing what residents understand, and where the official message misses their reality, lets health programs teach more effectively. The study speaks for the household end of a surveillance chain that usually gets described only from the office end.
plos-pone-0348842:
Dong Yan and co-workers devise a smarter way to choose stitch lines when joining radar satellite images into one big map. Mismatched brightness and slight shifts between scenes can leave ugly seams. Their 2026 method first groups pixels into tidy super-regions. These regions stay consistent across overlapping images. Neighbors then merge by texture and edge evidence. Finally, the method picks the cheapest clean path through a network of candidate seams.

Tests on real radar scenes checked each step of the pipeline. Compared with two classic methods, the new route preserved whole objects and hugged their boundaries better. Cleaner mosaics matter for flood mapping, land monitoring, and any wide-area work built on radar imagery.
plos-pone-0348942:
Rehab Osman Taha and co-workers look for gene patterns in Thai patients with a bile duct cancer linked to a liver fluke parasite. The cancer is aggressive and common where the fluke infects people through raw fish. Their 2026 study compares just over a hundred cancer patients with fluke-infected people and healthy controls, reading a panel of cancer and stress-pathway genes.

Changes in one gene turned up in half the cancer patients, far more than in either comparison group, and carrying two copies raised risk most. Changes in a second gene appeared only in cancer patients. A famous cancer gene varied widely in everyone and told little. The pattern may be specific to this fluke-linked cancer and could sharpen screening in Thailand.
plos-pone-0349042:
Alahdal and colleagues screened a modified plant compound against lung cancer targets in a 2026 computer study. Lung cancer kills more people than any other cancer, and tumors often stop responding to single-target drugs. Seven proteins tied to lung tumor growth were chosen as docking targets from a drug database search.

The compound, a phosphate form of a common plant pigment, was tested for fit against all seven targets, a multi-target strategy the authors call heptapharmacology. Strong fits would nominate it for lab testing. Computer docking cannot prove a drug works, but hitting several cancer pathways at once is a rational way to hunt for resistance-proof candidates.
plos-pone-0349142:
Emmanuel K. Sam and co-workers read the full genetic code of Salmonella bacteria taken from typhoid patients in Ghana. Typhoid fever still sickens and kills many people there, yet local data on which strains circulate remain thin. Their 2026 study works with isolates grown from blood and stool samples at Ghanaian care sites.

Sequencing showed wide variety among the strains. One typhoid type grouped closely with strains from nearby West African countries, which points to spread across borders. A type linked to severe invasive illness also turned up in stool. Many strains carried genes tied to harming the body, so the results give health teams a firmer base for tracking outbreaks and drug resistance.
plos-pone-0349242:
Yuhang Li and colleagues analysed fourteen years of Chinese news coverage of HIV and AIDS to watch the story change. From a large body of articles published between twenty ten and twenty twenty-four, computer methods extracted the main topic clusters. They pulled out the words used for people living with the virus and the metaphors wrapped around the disease. Then they mapped how these choices connect.

Coverage organised itself into five big themes, from prevention to medicine and society, and drifted steadily toward official, large-scale narratives and away from individual human stories. Neutral, de-identified labels for people with HIV became the norm, yet stigmatising terms survived in many forms. War, journey, and thing metaphors formed the core imagery. The authors describe media institutions adapting to a state-led system while old stigma quietly persists underneath.
plos-pone-0349442:
Yanping Feng, Yilin Wang, and Binyou Wang explored whether handgrip strength, a cheap bedside measure, mirrors brain activity in people living long-term in hospital with stable schizophrenia. Ninety-six patients squeezed a grip meter while a cap using near-infrared light tracked blood flow in the front of the brain during a word-naming task. The team compared grip patterns, including differences between the two hands, with the brain signals.

An uneven grip between hands lined up with stronger frontal brain responses in simple comparisons. Once age, sex, and other differences between patients were accounted for, that link faded and no grip group stood apart. The authors treat the work as exploratory: grip strength alone does not yet earn a place as a stand-in for brain function in this group, and larger studies would be needed.
plos-pone-0349942:
