Anna J Dreyer and colleagues in Cape Town, South Africa, asked in 2026 what shapes thinking test scores before any HIV infection. Scores are often blamed on the virus, yet childhood poverty and schooling also leave marks that studies rarely measure.

Adults with and without HIV took a broad set of thinking tests, plus a knowledge test used as a stand-in for earlier ability. Life circumstances from childhood and adulthood were grouped into clusters. The analysis traced how those clusters feed into later scores, partly through earlier ability. The lesson is that fair reading of HIV and the brain must start with a person's whole history.
plos-pone-0350042:
Jing Liu and colleagues hunted for ageing signals in lungs harmed by radiation treatment for chest cancers. Radiation lung injury can scar lungs and spoil treatment gains. Gene data from injured lungs were crossed with known cell ageing gene lists, which flagged a growth factor called GDF15. Rat lungs exposed to radiation then showed damage, scarring, and ageing marks.

Blocking or boosting the factor in lung lining cells shifted ageing markers along a known signalling path. Injured tissue carried far more of the factor alongside DNA damage signals. If human work agrees, the factor could serve as both a warning marker and a drug target for easing radiation lung harm.
plos-pone-0350142:
Richard May and seven colleagues grade the evidence reviews published in behaviour analysis journals. Their 2026 umbrella review gathered every systematic review and meta-analysis in seven field journals up to 2023. Sixty-four reviews counted, sixteen with meta-analyses. Two standard tools scored how sound their methods were. The plan was logged in advance. The headline result is sober reading for the field.

Every single review rated critically low on the main quality scale. Plans were rarely logged beforehand. Risk of bias in the underlying studies was assessed badly. Publication bias often went unchecked entirely. A second, more forgiving scorecard showed adherence under half, though improving slightly each year. Reviews guide real clinical and educational decisions in behaviour analysis. This audit argues the field's synthesis machinery needs repair: registered protocols, honest bias checks, and fuller reporting before its summaries deserve full trust.
plos-pone-0350342:
Zhonglan Yin and four colleagues compare metabolic health between men whose jobs chain them to a seat and men whose jobs keep them moving. Their 2026 study enrolled over two thousand Chinese workers. Bus drivers formed the sedentary group. Sanitation workers formed the comparison. Questionnaires and clinical examinations ran between mid-2023 and late 2024. Metabolic syndrome was diagnosed under current Chinese diabetes guidelines.

Raw rates favoured the movers. The drivers showed more metabolic syndrome, far more high triglycerides, and more central obesity. Then adjustment complicated the story. Once other factors entered the model, sedentary work itself showed no significant link to the full syndrome. Specific components, though, still tracked with the sitting job. The nuance matters for workplace health programmes. Blaming the chair alone oversimplifies; the drivers' whole pattern of eating, schedule, and stress may carry much of the risk.
plos-pone-0350442:
Expression of Concern: the journal flags serious unresolved doubts about this article on a sugar coated molecule said to protect mice against the parasite behind visceral leishmaniasis. Readers should treat its claims as unverified.

Editors found control lanes in one figure that appear to match a figure in another article representing different conditions, and the methods omit how animals were euthanised. Raw data promised with the article were not provided. The first author disputes the image concern and says the originals are gone. With no source files, the journal states the reliability of the counted results cannot be checked.
plos-pone-0350642:
Ruijia Yang and three colleagues study what brief isolation does to soldier crabs in this 2026 behaviour paper. These crabs gather in huge, dense swarms on tidal flats. Their groups have no leaders or fixed roles. That makes them a clean system for testing how one separated individual rejoins the crowd. Isolation in the experiments lasted from five minutes to three hours.

Crabs kept apart for five to thirty minutes came back more active than controls. They also crowded closer to their neighbours. Three hours apart produced a stranger pattern. Those crabs first moved less, then became restless while staying poorly coordinated with the swarm. Short separations seem to energise returning crabs. Long ones disturb the timing that collective movement depends on, a finding relevant to any group-living animal.
plos-pone-0350742:
Catching melanoma early saves lives, and Yada Wuttithantawee and colleagues hunted for a blood signal of the disease. Their 2026 PLOS One study grew immune blood cells alongside melanoma cells and watched which genes the blood cells switched on in response to factors the tumor released.

Of seven candidate genes, one called RPLP1 rose clearly and early. The team then measured it in blood samples from eighty-five people, including melanoma patients, patients with other cancers, and healthy volunteers. Statistical curves checked how well the signal separated melanoma from the rest. The authors present RPLP1 as a candidate marker needing larger trials before any screening use.
plos-pone-0350842:
Efundem Agboraw and colleagues used primary care records for over twelve million adults in England from 2019 to 2024 to study referrals to social prescribing. Link workers connect patients to community help for loneliness, money strain, and housing woes. Offers and completed referrals were modelled by patient traits and area traits.

About four percent of patients were offered a referral, and over three quarters of offers became referrals. Women, older people, people in richer areas, and people with many long term conditions were more likely to be offered help. Among those offered, women, minority ethnic patients, and sicker patients accepted more. Growth since national rollout is real, but poorer areas lag in offers.
plos-pone-0350942:
Ligabaw Worku and a large team in Ethiopia studied the mosquitoes that spread malaria in 2026. They worked in two towns in the northwest, collecting young mosquitoes from breeding sites in the rainy season and after it, then raising them for tests.

Adults were checked for which species they belonged to, exposed to a common insecticide, and screened for gene changes linked to resistance. Some mosquitoes survived the spray, and the resistance gene appeared in the groups tested. Knowing which species are present, and how many shrug off the main spray, helps malaria programs choose tools that still work in each place and season.
plos-pone-0351142:
Yared Asmare Aynalem and colleagues looked at care before pregnancy in Ethiopia in 2026. The country issued its first national guide for such care in 2024, yet few clinics offer it, and most past work asked only about women's knowledge.

The researchers interviewed eighteen adults, women and men, at two public hospitals in Addis Ababa. People described patchy knowledge, often gained only after a problem in pregnancy. Husbands, faith, and clinic rules all shaped whether care was sought at all. The findings argue that services must work with local beliefs and family roles, not just hand out facts, if healthy starts to pregnancy are to become normal.
plos-pone-0351242:
Wasuwit Wanchaitanawong and five colleagues report this 2026 PLOS One study of gallstones that slip out of the bile duct on their own before a planned endoscopic procedure. When a stone has already passed, the procedure becomes unnecessary, yet it can also be riskier than expected. The team reviewed more than four hundred patients at a referral center, recording who passed stones and who suffered complications afterward.

About twenty-eight percent of patients had passed their stone before the procedure. Younger patients, those with a single stone, and those with smaller stones were most likely to have done so. Unexpectedly, patients whose stone had passed developed inflammation of the pancreas after the procedure at about double the rate of others. The authors suggest confirming the duct is clear noninvasively before proceeding.
plos-pone-0351542:
Astronauts lose bone in weightlessness, which hints that bone-eating cells sense gravity itself. Natsuhiro Takahashi and colleagues spun mouse bone-eating cells in centrifuges to create stronger-than-normal gravity, in this 2026 PLOS One lab study.

Even half an hour of extra gravity disturbed the actin rings these cells use to seal onto bone and chew it. The rings dimmed and thinned, cell nuclei shifted, and the pits the cells normally dig grew shallower. Protein change scans after brief spinning pointed to the pathways involved. The authors say the cells' skeleton is a gravity sensor, which may explain part of bone loss in space.
plos-pone-0351642:
Muhammad Haider and seven colleagues trace the family tree of black kites in Pakistan's Punjab wetlands. Their 2026 genetic study samples birds at three wetlands, including two river barrages and a lake. Punjab sits at a migratory crossroads for this widespread raptor. The Milvus genus is taxonomically tangled, and Pakistan's birds were barely studied. Partial gene sequences from the kites were compared with reference sequences from around the world.

Local birds turned out genetically close, with tiny maternal distances between them. They form one freely mixing population across the wetlands. Across continents, structure was strong instead. Distances between far-apart lineages, such as West African and European birds, ran much higher. Statistical signatures suggested population expansion or steady purifying selection. For conservation, Punjab's kites can be managed as a single connected population, even while the wider species splits into distinct continental lines.
plos-pone-0351742:
Fabrizio De Massis and seven colleagues describe Italy's response to its first dog brucellosis outbreak. The 2026 report looks back to April 2020. A breeding kennel in central Italy housed over six hundred eighty toy-breed dogs. Brucella canis causes reproductive failure and spreads between dogs. Authorities restricted animal movement at once. Unusually, they chose a no-kill strategy for managing the outbreak.

A structured protocol combined neutering with repeated blood testing. Only dogs confirmed negative were cleared for adoption. More than three hundred dogs were successfully rehomed. Follow-up laboratory checks found no late infections among the adopted animals. The experience matters because culling is the default response in many countries. Italy's outcome shows that careful testing and staged rehoming can control an outbreak while keeping dogs alive and placed in homes.
plos-pone-0351942:
Isaac Osei and three colleagues untangle how heat and rainfall relate in Ghana. Their 2026 study uses weather station records from 1981 to 2020. Daily maximum and minimum temperatures move closely together. That overlap makes their separate links to rainfall hard to estimate. The authors apply a modelling method designed for such tangled predictors. Coastal and inland stations are compared as well.

Hotter days came with less rain, a clear negative link. Warmer nights came with slightly more rain. The idea that maximum temperature works through minimum temperature found no support. The model explained roughly a fifth of rainfall variation. Geography mattered. The negative link between hot days and rain was much stronger inland than on the coast. Such detail helps forecasters read temperature signals differently across Ghana's climate zones.
plos-pone-0352142:
Wen and Lim mined online posts about emergency care during South Korea's 2024 health crisis in a 2026 study. A mass walkout by trainee doctors left emergency rooms strained for months. More than a million posts and comments from major Korean platforms across that year were sorted by machine tools for feeling and themes.

Negative feeling clearly outweighed positive feeling in the posts. Beyond anger at outcomes, phrases about a medical void, being bounced between emergency rooms, and over-treatment stood out as core stressors. The analysis shows what frightened patients most during system failure. Such listening tools could warn officials early about which failures hurt public trust fastest.
plos-pone-0352242:
Christopher Campbell and Graeme Ackland rebuilt a classic model of party competition as a physics-style simulation to ask why modern politics polarizes. The classic model, with two parties chasing voters on one left-right line, predicts a rush to the center, the opposite of what many countries see. Their version spreads voters and parties across two policy dimensions and allows many parties at once.

Two-party contests still damped polarization, even when voters themselves were split into two camps. Multiparty fields did the reverse, pulling parties apart even when most voters were moderate. Adding abstention, activists, and turnout effects polarized even the two-party case. One comfort emerged: the winning party still ended up more moderate than its own supporters. The model blames the structure of competition, not just voter anger, for divided politics.
plos-pone-0352342:
Kim and colleagues built learning models to predict emergency visits in type two diabetes in a 2026 study. Records from five Korean institutions covered more than two hundred twenty thousand patients, including readings, labs, and prescriptions over time. Sudden diabetes complications often land patients in emergency rooms before worse outcomes follow.

Models trained on most of the records were tested on the rest to judge how well they flag a first emergency visit. Spotting high-risk patterns early lets primary care teams act before a crisis. Real-world records, with all their messiness, make the test more honest than tidy trial data, though care patterns differ between health systems.
plos-pone-0352442:
Goossens and colleagues set out a review plan in 2026 on injuries in padel, a fast-growing racket sport. Injury rates are high and the costs can be large, yet no full map of the evidence exists. Under the plan, the review will gather studies on injuries, risk factors, and prevention at every level of play.

A staged framework that moves from describing injuries to testing prevention will organize the work. Studies from any country, setting, or player group will count. The finished map should show where evidence is strong and where padel research is still blank, guiding coaches and health staff toward the prevention steps most worth testing next.
plos-pone-0353142:
Hakki and colleagues tracked blood counts through mild COVID-19 in a community study in a 2026 paper. Ninety-three recently exposed adults with no prior immunity or other illnesses gave blood over four weeks from first positive test. Hospital studies dominate blood knowledge, yet most infections are mild and managed at home.

More than three in ten cases showed a brief drop in a key white cell type early in infection, recovering by convalescence. Such dips could confuse doctors reading single blood tests. A timed picture of normal mild illness helps clinicians tell harmless swings from warning signs.
plos-pone-0353242:
Kim and colleagues held group talks with young Korean women about cervical cancer prevention in a 2026 study. Fourteen women in their twenties, split into those who screen and those who do not, discussed screening and vaccination. Shame around gynecology visits and sexually spread infections emerged in both groups.

Shared themes included negative views of clinic visits and stigma tied to infection. Other themes differed between screeners and non-screeners, showing where decisions diverge. Prevention fails when stigma keeps women away, even where services exist. The authors argue that shifting social views is as necessary as offering tests, and their themes point to messages that might help.
plos-pone-0353742:
Kim and colleagues reviewed research on drinking among Korean immigrant women in a 2026 paper. Drinking has risen among women in recent decades, yet this group's experience had barely been studied. The review covered work from five English-speaking destination countries and sorted the findings by theme.

All of the studies found came from the United States, leaving countries such as Canada unstudied. Three forces shaped drinking most often: adjusting to a new culture, faith life, and friendship circles. Stress from migration and Korean drinking customs appeared as well, though less steadily. The authors call for health programs that respect both culture and gender rather than treating all immigrants alike.
plos-pone-0354242: China’s provincial sports industry funds spread policy innovations unevenly. This mixed-methods analysis examined the determinants of that diffusion — strategic adaptation and institutional constraints. The findings explain why some provinces pioneer while others lag.
plos-pone-0354342:
Taiga Noguchi led a team of eight authors who measured presenteeism with smartphones, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Presenteeism means working while sick, and it costs economies heavily while staying hard to measure. Surveys ask people to judge themselves, which is unreliable. This team instead used repeated phone-based behavioral responses.

Noguchi's signals, gathered many times from each person's phone, offer a passive and ongoing gauge of who is pushing through illness. Employers and health researchers could spot patterns without constant questionnaires. The work also raises fair questions about privacy that any user of phone sensing must answer. Handled openly, such measures could help target support before sickness becomes long absence.
plos-pone-0354742:
Jill Vögelin led a team of seven authors on this 2026 scoping review of feedback in medical and health professions training. Modern assessment programs lean on feedback about past work and feedforward, guidance aimed at the next attempt. The reviewers mapped studies from 2015 onward to see how both are actually used in assessment settings.

A small set of familiar methods dominated, and future-looking guidance usually stayed implicit or fixated on performance scores. Vögelin argues that naming feedforward plainly and making it actionable could strengthen how health students build competence over time.
plos-pone-0355042:
Yang Li and co-authors measure in 2026 how common severe short sight is among adults aged fifty and older in Fujian, southeast China. A population study enrolled more than eight thousand residents, who answered questions on schooling, income, and habits and received full eye and body checks. Severe short sight raises risk of serious eye disease later in life.

About one in twenty six adults had the severe form. Living inland lowered the odds, while higher pressure inside the eye and more schooling raised them. The authors call for better access to eye care for older inland residents and for closer watching of those with higher eye pressure or education.
plos-pone-0355242:
RETRACTED: The PLOS One Editors issued this 2026 retraction notice, withdrawing an animal study that had claimed a changed implant surface shape speeds bone growing onto implants. Readers should not rely on that study's findings. Concerns covered many figures, overlap with the group's earlier papers, and stability values that did not line up.

Editors noted near identical animal and implant counts, treatments, measures, and conclusions across papers that were never cited, plus images that matched after flipping or resembled each other inside the same paper. Timelines in the text and a figure also disagreed. The overlap left the work's originality and data in serious doubt.
plos-pone-0355742:
Zhe Liu and Dan Tian improved a well-known image segmentation model so it can pick out the most noticeable object in a scene. Adapting the general Segment Anything Model to saliency detection often leaves broken masks, fuzzy edges, and lost detail, especially when objects vary in size. Their 2026 design attacks three named weaknesses of earlier adapters.

A weighted multi-scale adapter learns how to calibrate features from different viewing scales instead of using fixed rules. A cross-fusion module ties levels together by meaning, not mere stacking. Wavelet processing rescues the fine, high-frequency detail that ordinary operations discard. Liu and Tian argue the three fixes together sharpen saliency maps for complex, textured scenes.
plos-pone-0355842:
Ella Barnum and seven colleagues use rats on a shift-work schedule to trace how circadian disruption reaches the gut, and whether the harm differs by sex, in this 2026 study. Earlier work from the team showed that shifted light cycles worsen stroke outcomes more in males. Two cohorts of rats lived for fifty days under either a fixed light-dark rhythm or one advanced by half a day every five days. The researchers then examined gut microbes, gut structure, and inflammatory signals.

Shifted males, but not females, lost microbial diversity, and the abundance of beneficial gut bacteria tracked with stroke survival. Their gut lining showed shortened, blunted villi, loosened barrier proteins, lower levels of a protective fatty acid, and higher circulating endotoxin and an inflammatory signal. Females were largely spared. The authors suggest this gut pathway helps explain why circadian disruption hits male stroke outcomes harder.
plos-pone-0356142:
Soyoung Kim and seven colleagues test whether gallstones quietly signal dangerous heart artery disease in people who feel perfectly well, in this 2026 study from South Korea. More than nine thousand adults with no heart disease history received both an abdominal ultrasound and a CT scan of their coronary arteries during health checkups. The team compared plaque types and narrowing severity between those with and without gallstones, adjusting for standard risk factors and matching patients on background traits.

About one participant in eighteen had gallstones. Those individuals were significantly more likely to carry noncalcified plaque, the soft, higher-risk kind, and to have a coronary narrowing severe enough to count as clinically significant. The authors conclude that finding gallstones should prompt attention to cardiovascular risk factors, since the same patients may harbor hidden, riskier plaque.
plos-pone-0356242:
Wenjie Zhao and three colleagues build an artificial intelligence system that spots Aspergillus mold in sample images, in this 2026 computer vision study. The fungus matters in medicine and food safety, but its tangled shapes, subtle features, rare strains, and partly hidden colonies defeat simple detectors. The team upgraded a current real-time detection framework with three new modules. One fuses complex structural features. One scores matches by shape to cope with blurred or blocked edges. A third adapts to colonies of different sizes.

The resulting model identified Aspergillus with precision above ninety percent and strong recall, while staying compact enough for practical deployment. The authors report that the shape-aware matching and multi-scale attention were key to handling occlusion and strain variety. They present the system as a faster, more reliable alternative to manual microscopic inspection for laboratories and screening programs.
plos-pone-0356542:
Pengfei Xu and five colleagues fine-tune a warm-up trick used by strength athletes in this 2026 experiment: doing heavy squats shortly before jumping to boost jump height. Twelve trained men each performed four squat protocols at a demanding load, varying depth, deep versus half squats, and whether the set stopped just short of failure or went all the way. Jump height was then measured at several points over the following twelve minutes.

All four protocols raised jump performance. Sets that stopped short of failure paid off sooner, lifting jumps by about four minutes, while sets taken to failure peaked later, around eight minutes. Half squats produced the stronger boost overall. The authors suggest a small set of heavy half squats, stopped before failure, as a time-efficient way to prime explosive performance before competition or training.
plos-pone-0356642:
Guillermo Puebla and five colleagues tested why people believe false health claims, using more than six hundred Chilean university students who judged true and false COVID-19 headlines. In their 2026 experiment, half the students held numbers in memory while judging, to load their working memory, and everyone completed measures of reflective thinking, pseudoscience belief, and tolerance for impressive-sounding nonsense.

The memory load slowed students down but did not make them more gullible. What predicted mistaking false headlines for true ones was a person's habits of belief: credulity toward pseudoscience and empty jargon, and weak reflective thinking. The results suggest that fighting health misinformation works better by strengthening how people evaluate claims than by simply slowing them down or reducing distractions.
plos-pone-0356742:
Huahan Zhan and seven colleagues test a gruesome-sounding claim in this 2026 study: can a common bathroom drain fly actually live inside the human gut? Larvae of this moth fly turn up in stool samples from time to time, raising fears of true intestinal infestation. The team raised the flies in the lab and confirmed their identity by shape and DNA.

Simulated stomach fluid proved lethal, wiping out eggs and nearly all larvae, and gut fluid finished off most survivors. Even when mice were fed live eggs and young larvae directly, nothing passed through, no tissue damage appeared, and no infestation took hold. The authors conclude that most supposed cases are probably contamination of samples or a brief false alarm, not a real infestation, which should reassure both patients and doctors.
plos-pone-0357042:
Teresa Kisi Beyen led a team of five authors mapping esophageal cancer in Ethiopia, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. This cancer occurs in clusters in central Oromia, but the exact pattern was unclear. The team used spatial statistics, including autocorrelation and scan methods, to map where cases concentrate.

Beyen's hotspots give health officials concrete targets for screening programs. Clustering also guides research into local causes, such as diet or environmental exposures shared in one area. Esophageal cancer is often caught late, when treatment helps least, so targeted early screening in hotspots could save lives. Geographic evidence turns a vague regional worry into a list of places to act first.
plos-pone-0357142:
Jin Sothornwit and colleagues used Thailand's national hospital database from 2017 to 2024. They counted thyroid storm, the rare, life-threatening flare of an overactive thyroid. They also looked for what kills the patients it strikes. Their 2026 study compared more than a thousand storm admissions against several thousand admissions for thyroid overactivity without storm.

Storm cases grew steadily across the period. They roughly doubled per head of population. Death in hospital struck nearly one in five storm patients. Without storm, it struck one in a hundred. Storm itself multiplied the odds of death many times over. Septic shock, heart failure shock, and kidney injury were the strongest companions of death. The authors urge hospitals to treat those complications as the true battleground.
plos-pone-0357442:
Gregg E. Moore and coauthors published a 2026 ecology study in PLOS ONE revisiting a Massachusetts marsh six years after a winter storm buried it in sediment. Storm Grayson in 2018 dumped an uneven layer across the Great Marsh; one season later, buried plots showed thinner cover and shifted soil chemistry. Six seasons on, the team returned to test whether the sediment helped or harmed the marsh, measuring vegetation, soil chemistry, and living roots by depth.

Plant cover and height no longer differed by sediment amount, and species richness held. Salinity had fallen since 2018, while oxygen-related chemistry and sulfides shifted mostly in thinly covered plots. Roots told the most positive story: living density was strong in moderately covered plots, as if the marsh grew into its new elevation. Natural sediment deliveries of a few centimeters, they conclude, can feed marshes facing sea-level rise without lasting damage.
plos-pone-0358042:
Gary B Wilkerson, Mohammad Joghataee, and Ashish Gupta hunt for a measurable fingerprint of repeated concussion inside virtual reality, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Standard clinical tests miss subtle thinking damage after head injuries, especially as hits pile up. The team pooled data from two hundred two adolescents and young adults. They measured how fast and steadily participants turned, reached, and lunged at moving visual targets inside a headset.

Machine learning and theory driven statistics agreed on a leading signal. A neck movement score combining speed and correctness of response best separated people with several past concussions from those with one or none. Its variability partner moved the other way, as a decision model would predict. Together the pair may mark a cumulative, lingering deficit that ordinary symptom checklists pronounce healed. The authors propose such metrics for return to play calls that now rest on self report.
plos-pone-0358242:
Felistar Mwakasungura and colleagues published a 2026 analysis in PLOS ONE of people carrying both HIV and hepatitis B in Tanzania, drawing on a large national household survey from 2022–2023. Carrying both viruses speeds up illness even with treatment, yet country-level numbers were missing. The survey tested more than thirty thousand people aged fifteen and older across all regions of the country.

Each virus alone was fairly common, but dual infection was rare in the general population, at well under one percent. Among people living with HIV, however, about one in sixteen also had hepatitis B. Risk of the double infection rose with age and was higher for people not in a union, while having had only one lifetime sexual partner was strongly protective. The authors say Tanzania's overall burden is low, but screening people in HIV care for hepatitis B remains essential because that subgroup's risk is real.
plos-pone-0358342:
Ji Won Kim and four colleagues test whether an artificial intelligence reconstruction changes heart calcium scores, in PLOS ONE in 2026. The score, built from CT images, sorts patients into risk categories that drive statin decisions. A deep learning method promises cleaner images from the same scan. The team scored a cardiac phantom and one hundred thirteen patients three ways: the classic reconstruction, an iterative method, and the deep learning one at high strength.

In the phantom, all three agreed. In patients, the deep learning scores ran significantly lower than the classic method's, while matching the iterative method. Category agreement stayed high overall. Individual patients, though, could shift substantially between methods, with differences large enough to matter near the cutoffs where risk labels change. The authors' caution is practical: a score is only comparable when the reconstruction behind it is held constant.
plos-pone-0358742:
Wenwei Liu leads a team of eight shrinking a vision model until it can grade roses on a cheap device at the farm, in PLOS ONE in 2026. A rose's price depends on grade. Human grading is slow and inconsistent. The small computers in packing sheds cannot run heavyweight software. Their framework, Flora-YOLO, rebuilds a compact detector with four changes. The changes sharpen faint petal textures and protect detail under leaf clutter. They amplify weak signals from young buds and respect the irregular shapes of flowers.

Across cross validation on their rose dataset, the model reached accuracy near eighty-seven percent on the standard overlap measure. It beat its baseline while cutting computing load by more than a quarter. It needs under two million parameters, small enough for edge hardware. The work points toward grading lines where a camera, not a tired human eye, makes the call on every stem.
plos-pone-0358942:
Juan Hurtado, Carson Allan, Sergio Castrezana, Jeremy Bono, and Luciano Matzkin published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It is a catalog, a systematic list, of messenger RNAs that males pass to females when mating, in two fruit fly species, Drosophila arizonae and Drosophila mojavensis.

Messenger RNA carries instructions for making proteins, so molecules transferred in mating could affect the female after fertilization. Listing exactly which RNAs move across gives other biologists a reference set for studying reproduction and how species diverge. Work of this kind also feeds into understanding how new fly species form in the deserts these insects inhabit.
plos-pone-0359542:
Nickson Erick Otieno published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It uses GIS mapping, remote sensing from satellites, and linear models to fight erosion and sediment transport in the Lake Victoria watershed in Kenya. The aim is prioritizing spatially explicit action: choosing exactly where anti-erosion work should happen first.

Sediment washing into Lake Victoria clouds water, harms fish, and chokes the lake's bays. Maps built from satellite data and terrain models show which slopes and streams deliver the most sediment. Watershed managers with limited budgets need that ranking to place soil conservation where each shilling buys the most protection.
plos-pone-0360242:
Chen Li, Sijia Gao, and Meng Li reported in 2026 on blending laboratory paper analysis into the traditional craft of restoring ancient Chinese books. Their case study is a Chinese medical text named Yi Men Pu Du. Restorers have long judged old paper by eye and touch, choosing treatments by inherited experience.

The authors bring experimental analysis of the paper itself into that process, testing its makeup and condition before deciding how to repair it. Matching modern measurement with craft judgment aims to make restoration choices more precise and less likely to harm fragile pages. The study speaks to libraries and archives across China, where large holdings of ancient medical and scholarly books await careful repair.
pmc-13238242:
Kakeshita and colleagues report a rare cancer arising in a repaired aorta in a kidney transplant patient. The patient had earlier received a stent graft for an abdominal aortic aneurysm, then a successful living-donor kidney transplant. Graft function stayed stable on immune-suppressing drugs, the normal bargain that keeps a donated kidney alive.

Within the old aneurysm, doctors later found a spindle cell sarcoma, an uncommon cancer of spindle-shaped cells. Whether the stent, the immune suppression, or chance played a part is an open question. Single cases cannot answer it, but they put transplant and vascular teams on notice to watch repaired aortas for late, strange growths.
pmc-13241442:
Santana and colleagues in São Paulo pooled trials of curcumin for prostate swelling in a meta-analysis. Six studies covered six hundred ninety-seven men already taking standard prostate drugs. Symptom scores led the list, with prostate size and urine flow alongside. Random-effects models pooled the comparisons against placebo.

Curcumin users beat placebo groups by about four points on symptom scores. Prostate volume, residual urine, and a blood marker all shrank modestly while flow grew stronger. Benefit ran larger alongside alpha-blockers alone than with combination therapy. Santana urges bigger trials, citing wide variation between studies.
pmc-13242342:
Liu and colleagues at Qingdao Agricultural University correct a figure in their 2023 study of pig skin progenitor cells. The paper mapped gene activity in multipotent dermal fibroblast progenitors with germline potential. One fluorescence image in Figure 6 was the wrong one. The panel showed PRDM1 staining in lab-grown germ cell-like cells.

Its humor sets it apart from the solemn Fama and Confessio. The evidence notes no public-domain text has yet been located for this entry.

Edwin Arnold's Song Celestial, published in 1885, sings the Bhagavad Gita as English poetry. Arnold's verse introduced Victorian England to Hindu scripture on a large scale. On Kurukshetra's field, Arjuna despairs at the prospect of killing kin and teachers drawn up against him.

Krishna answers with the revelation of his universal form and a call to selfless action performed without attachment to results. Arnold softens Sanskrit philosophy into Victorian lyric, a choice readers can judge against prose translations in this library. V1 evidence recommends reading it for the music as much as the message; for many first readers, the music is what made the message stick.
tob-4042:
Arthur Schopenhauer published his masterwork The World as Will and Representation in 1818, under this edition's title The World as Will and Idea. Volume one lays out the system. The world we perceive is representation, ordered by our minds; behind those appearances, Schopenhauer argues, churns a blind, striving Will that wants without purpose and never rests.

From that bleak ground he develops his accounts of nature, the body, and art, with escape glimpsed in aesthetic contemplation and compassion. Pessimism never had a more brilliant advocate. Later readers from Nietzsche to Buddhist-influenced thinkers wrestled with the book, and volume one remains the necessary doorway into Schopenhauer's system.
tob-4142:
Basil Valentine praises antimony, the grey mineral he calls the prince of medicines, in the Triumphal Chariot of Antimony. Waite translated the work in 1893. Part chemistry, part mystic praise, the treatise belongs wholly to the seventeenth century in spirit.

Valentine describes purifying antimony and preparing its medicines step by step, with warnings earned from hard practice. The drug healed some patients and poisoned others, and its fame swung between wonder cure and royal killer. Waite's notes guide the modern reader through the dangers and the lore. Verified from the 1919 edition, the Chariot remains antimony's great monument.
tob-9242:
Augustine of Hippo looked back on his youth and wrote the Confessions, a prayer and a life story in one. E. B. Pusey's translation long served as the classic English version. Augustine tells how he stole pears as a boy, chased pleasure and fame, and felt restless for years.

His search ends in a garden in Milan, where he hears a child's voice and reads words that change his life. He tells God, you made us for yourself, and our hearts are restless until they rest in you. Later books turn to memory, time, and creation. Western writers learned from Augustine how to describe an inner life.
un-ga-res-42: Arms cuts were on the table within the UN's first year. Resolution 42, passed on 14 December 1946, backs a same-day Assembly call for rules on the regulation and reduction of armaments. It asks the Security Council to decide, as soon as it can, what facts member states should supply about their forces, so the arms plan can take effect.
un-ga-res-a-69-42:
Thousands of nuclear weapons still sit ready to fire within minutes, and Resolution A/69/42, from the General Assembly's sixty-ninth session, takes aim at that fact. High alert was a habit of Cold War days. The text notes with care that trust has grown since that era ended, yet the hair-trigger stance lives on in the arsenals of the nuclear states.

Keeping arms at such readiness, the Assembly argues, raises the risk of a launch by error or by chance, with ruinous results for all. Talks in world disarmament forums back fresh cuts to that readiness. Each step down in alert, the text holds, guards peace and helps the longer march toward disarmament.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl: The General Assembly adopted Resolution 42 on 14 December 1946, at the sixty-third plenary meeting. It is a one-step follow-up on arms cuts. The Assembly wanted the same day's resolution on the principles for regulating and reducing armaments put into effect as soon as possible. It called on the Security Council to decide promptly what information member states should be asked to supply to give it effect.

Resolution 69/42 of the General Assembly concerns the operational readiness of nuclear weapons. Several thousand nuclear weapons remain on high alert, ready for launch within minutes. This holds even decades after the Cold War. Noting that, the Assembly calls for practical steps to lower that readiness. The steps are to last until all nuclear weapons are off high alert. It looks to the 2015 Non-Proliferation Treaty review conference to take up the issue. It asks states to report their progress to the Assembly.
un-sc-res-1042:
Western Sahara's referendum mission was extended against a stalemate on 31 January 1996. The Secretary-General's report of 19 January set out both sides' views. His special envoy had visited the region from 2 to 9 January. The voter identification process, core of the settlement plan, had stalled. Without progress there, the whole plan stood frozen.

The Council restated its pledge to a free, fair, and impartial referendum on self-determination for Western Sahara, without further delay. It extended MINURSO's mandate until 31 May 1996. Deep concern was voiced at the identification stalemate and the lack of progress it caused. Morocco and the Polisario Front were called to work with the Secretary-General and the mission. They had to restart identification, clear its blocks, and apply the rest of the settlement plan. Both sides were also urged to find fresh ways to build trust between them.
un-sc-res-1342: The text numbered Resolution 1342 belongs to the Security Council's official record, catalogued at 2000. Year by year, these decisions build the written history of how the world body handled the crises of its time. The transcription keeps the preamble and numbered clauses in their official order, as the Council adopted them. As a public record, it has long been open to scholars and general readers alike.
un-sc-res-142: The Republic of the Congo sought United Nations membership at independence in 1960. On 7 July 1960 the Security Council examined its application. The text names the capital, Leopoldville, to identify the new state. The Council recommended to the General Assembly that the Congo be admitted. The vote was unanimous. The Congo took its seat days later, even as crisis engulfed the country.
un-sc-res-1442:
The peacekeeping force in Cyprus gains six more months under United Nations Security Council Resolution 1442, adopted unanimously on 25 November 2002. Cyprus had agreed the force should stay past 15 December. Patrol limits set in June 2000 remained a sore point. The fate of missing persons still lacked answers.

The Council extends the force, called UNFICYP, until 15 June 2003. It urges the Turkish Cypriot side and Turkish forces to lift the 2000 limits. The old military position at Strovilia should be restored. Both sides are pressed to treat the missing as an urgent human issue. A report is due by 1 June 2003.
un-sc-res-1542:
Haiti was still in turmoil when Resolution 1542 set up a full UN mission there in 2004. President Aristide had fled weeks earlier, armed groups held parts of the country, and daily life was unsafe. The new mission, called MINUSTAH, took over from the short-term foreign force.

The text gives the mission soldiers and police to secure towns, protect civilians, and back the interim government. It also assigns work on disarming gangs, guarding aid, and preparing fair elections. Readers see how the Council builds a peacekeeping mission piece by piece, task by task, in one founding document.
un-sc-res-1642: Resolution 1642 closes part of the Council's mid-2000s sequence in this collection, preserved from the official record via Wikisource. The fifteen members who voted it acted for the UN on a peace and security question, the Council's core charge. The entry gives their full text, findings and decisions together, in the arrangement they approved.
un-sc-res-1742:
The United Nations mission in the Congo received a short bridge extension on 15 February 2007. The Democratic Republic of the Congo had completed the elections that closed its transition. The Congolese permanent representative had written to the Council on 15 January 2007. The Council said the country still threatened peace in the region and wanted regular dialogue with its authorities.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council extended the mandate and troop strength of MONUC to 15 April 2007, on the terms set by its earlier resolutions. The Secretary-General had to report by 15 March 2007 on his consultations with the Congolese authorities. His report would recommend changes to the mission's mandate and size for the post-transition period. The two-month renewal was deliberate: it held the mission steady while the Council and Kinshasa negotiated what a smaller, reshaped presence should do next.
un-sc-res-1942: Under the number 1942, the Security Council placed a formal decision in its official record, preserved here via English Wikisource. The act follows the body's settled architecture, recitals before decisions. Preserving the architecture along with the words matters, because in Council practice the recitals are part of how a decision's meaning gets argued later.
un-sc-res-242:
Five months after the Six-Day War, the Council laid down terms for peace in the Middle East. Resolution 242 was adopted unanimously on 22 November 1967. It stresses that land may not be gained by war. Every state in the area must be able to live in security. Few Council texts have been cited as often since.

Two linked principles stand at the core of the text. Israeli armed forces must withdraw from territories occupied in the recent conflict. In return, all states must end claims of war and respect each other's sovereignty, borders, and independence. The resolution also calls for free navigation of international waterways in the area. A just settlement of the refugee problem is required as well. Guarantees, such as demilitarized zones, are named. The Secretary-General was to appoint a special representative to help the parties reach agreement.
un-sc-res-342:
The Council closed its Namibia contact effort in December 1973. The Secretary-General had reported on two years of talks with South Africa. His mission rested on resolution 309 of 1972. On 11 December 1973 the Council thanked him for the report. It then decided to stop further efforts on that basis. The talks had not moved Pretoria toward letting Namibians choose freely.

The Secretary-General had to keep the Council informed of any major new events. The question of Namibia stayed on the United Nations agenda. The decision marked the end of a quiet-diplomacy phase. Pressure then shifted toward sanctions debates and support for the liberation movement. Namibia's independence came only in 1990, by a different route.
un-sc-res-42:
Palestine's plan hung in doubt when the Security Council passed Resolution 42 on 5 March 1948. The Assembly had voted in November 1947 to split the land into two states. The UN Palestine Commission had now sent its first monthly report, and a special report on the grave lack of safety in the land. The Council asks its five permanent members to meet and talk.

The five must tell the Council, within ten days, what the state of Palestine is. They must also counsel what guides the Council should give the Palestine Commission to help it do its work. All states and peoples, in and near Palestine, are begged to take all steps to bar fresh strife. The plea went out as the land slid toward open war.
un-sc-res-442: Listed under 1978, Resolution 442 preserves formal action taken by the United Nations Security Council. Behind each numbered text lies a meeting, a draft, and a vote, even when the final wording runs to a few lines. Read in sequence with its neighbours, it helps trace how Council practice grew across the postwar decades. No summary replaces it; the record itself is the content of the entry.
un-sc-res-642: Resolution 642 stands in the official record of the United Nations Security Council, catalogued here with a 1989 date. Such texts can call for cease-fires, set up missions, impose duties, or settle points of UN procedure and membership. Its value lies in the primary wording: the decision as adopted, kept through the Wikisource transcription of the record. No summary replaces it; the record itself is the content of the entry.
un-sc-res-742:
Security Council Resolution 742, adopted on February 14, 1992, recommended Azerbaijan for membership in the United Nations. The Caucasus republic had declared its independence from the Soviet Union the previous October, restoring a statehood it had briefly held after the First World War. Its bid reached the council even as fighting grew with Armenia over Nagorno-Karabakh.

The Assembly seated Azerbaijan on March 2. The resolution itself is the standard short form, making no mention of the war. That silence is part of the record. The machinery of admission ran on stated rules about statehood and the Charter. Meanwhile, one of the post-Soviet world's hardest conflicts was already taking shape on the ground.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
Western Sahara's stalled referendum is the subject of Resolution 1042, adopted on 31 January 1996. Morocco and the Polisario Front had both accepted a Settlement Plan built around a free vote on self-determination for the people of the territory. The UN Mission for the Referendum in Western Sahara, MINURSO, ran the process, but work to identify voters had ground to a halt.

The Council extends MINURSO's mandate until 31 May 1996 and repeats its pledge to hold the vote without more delay. It voices deep worry about the stalemate and calls on both sides to restart voter identification and carry out the plan. If no real progress comes, it backs the Secretary-General bringing the matter back at once, with a plan for pulling MINURSO out in stages.

Only two more months are granted to MINURSO, the Western Sahara referendum mission, on 27 February 2001. The mission's job was to prepare a free vote on self-determination under the Settlement Plan. The parties still disagreed over the plan's main terms, so the vote stayed out of reach.

The mandate now ran only to 30 April 2001, a short bridge rather than a long renewal. The Council expected the parties to keep meeting under the Secretary-General's Personal Envoy, working through the problems that blocked the plan. The aim was a political solution both sides could accept, and a fresh report was due before the new term ended.

Two states calling themselves Congo sought UN seats in 1960. One had been French, the other Belgian. Resolution 142, adopted unanimously on 7 July 1960, dealt with an early application from the Republic of the Congo. The papers were filed as document S/4361. A sister resolution for the other Congo followed in August.

The Council recommended the republic's admission to the General Assembly. The recommendation came as Congo's independence turmoil dominated the news. Names alone caused confusion in New York. Clerks noted capitals to tell the two republics apart. This resolution belongs to the rush of July 1960, when decolonization applications arrived faster than diplomats could process them.

The divided island of Cyprus fills Resolution 1442, adopted unanimously on 25 November 2002. UNFICYP, the UN peacekeeping force there, had patrolled the buffer zone since 1964. Cyprus's government agreed the force should stay. The Secretary-General's report of 15 November 2002 supported renewal. It also pressed both sides about missing persons from past fighting.

Members extended UNFICYP's mandate until 15 June 2003. They asked for a progress report by 1 June. The text also criticizes limits placed on the peacekeepers since June 2000. Turkish Cypriot forces had restricted their movements. The Council demanded those limits be lifted. It wanted the old military balance restored at Strovilia.

Haiti gets a United Nations Stabilization Mission, MINUSTAH, in this text of 30 April 2004. An interim multinational force had been holding the country since the February crisis. The Secretary-General's April report recommended a longer United Nations presence, and the Council backed it, while deploring human rights abuses and impunity in Haiti.

MINUSTAH is set up for an initial six months, with authority passing from the interim force on 1 June 2004. Leftover interim-force units could keep working for up to 30 days into the handover if the new mission asked. A Special Representative would direct all United Nations activity in Haiti, and the mission's work centres on security, the political process, human rights, and rebuilding the rule of law.

Cyprus's peacekeeping force, UNFICYP, is extended on 14 December 2005. The Secretary-General's November report found the island stable and the Green Line calm, with fewer incidents overall, though some events still caused concern. The Committee on Missing Persons had been working again since August 2004, and a new third member was to join it in January 2006.

The force's mandate is renewed for a further period. The Turkish Cypriot side and Turkish forces are again called on to restore the military position at Strovilia to what it had been before the restrictions of July 2000. Both sides are urged to avoid steps that could raise tension, and the need to treat the missing persons question with urgency, as a humanitarian matter, is restated.

Resolution 1742, adopted on 15 February 2007, gives the UN mission in Congo a further lease on life. MONUC had backed the peace deal signed at Pretoria in 2002 and the elections that crowned the transition. Congo's government had written to the Council in January about the mission's future, and talks were under way on reshaping it for the post-transition period.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council extended MONUC's mandate and its authorized personnel strength as set out in earlier resolutions. The renewal was a holding move: members wanted consultations with Congolese authorities on adjustments finished before settling the mission's longer-term size and tasks. Congo's stability, the Council repeated, still depended on the mission's presence.

Weeks before long-delayed elections in Côte d'Ivoire, the Council adopted Resolution 1942 on 29 September 2010. The final list of voters had just been agreed by the Ivorian parties. A United Nations official had checked and certified the list, which cleared the way for the vote to go ahead.

Acting under Chapter VII of the United Nations Charter, the Council authorized a temporary increase in the United Nations Operation in Côte d'Ivoire, known as UNOCI. Its strength could rise from 8,650 to 9,150 soldiers and police. The extra five hundred people could deploy at once, but only for up to six months. The short boost was meant to keep the election period safe. It was not a permanent growth of the mission.

Five months after the Six-Day War, the Council set down its peace formula. On 22 November 1967, it adopted Resolution 242 without dissent. The war had left Israel holding land taken from Egypt, Jordan, and Syria. The Council declared that seizing land by war is not allowed. It voiced grave concern at the state of the Middle East.

Two linked rules form the core of the text. Israeli armed forces must pull out of lands seized in the war. Every state in the area may live in peace within safe, agreed borders. Those borders must be free of threats and force. The text also backs free shipping through world waterways. It calls for a just fix for the refugees. This land-for-peace bargain guided talks for decades.

Namibia diplomacy hits a dead end in Resolution 342, adopted unanimously on 11 December 1973. For two years the Secretary-General had pursued contacts under an earlier mandate, resolution 309, exploring whether South Africa might yield on the territory it occupied. His report on those efforts lay before the Council.

After noting the report with appreciation, the Council decided to discontinue further efforts on that basis. It asked the Secretary-General to keep it fully informed of any important new developments on the Namibia question. The resolution is an admission that one negotiating track had failed. Pressure on South Africa over Namibia continued through other channels until independence finally came in 1990.

Fighting spread in Palestine after the General Assembly adopted its partition plan in November 1947. A United Nations commission sent to carry out the plan reported on the worsening security situation. Resolution 42 was adopted on 5 March 1948, as the disorders grew.

The Council called on its permanent members to consult together. They had to report back on the situation in Palestine. Their report would include recommendations on the guidance the Council might give the commission. The aim was to help carry the partition plan through. The Council also appealed to all governments and peoples. Those in and around Palestine were named in particular. Everyone was asked to take every possible action to prevent or reduce the disorders then occurring in Palestine.

Dominica, an island state in the Caribbean, asked to join the United Nations late in 1978, soon after it won freedom from Britain. Resolution 442 was adopted on 6 December 1978 with all votes in favor. The Council read the bid. It told the General Assembly that Dominica should be let in as a member. That short note is the whole text.

The observer group watching the cease-fire between Iran and Iraq received another term on 29 September 1989. A report from the Secretary-General, dated 22 September, covered the group's work. The cease-fire of 1987 still had no full peace settlement behind it. Resolution 642 deals with the group, called UNIIMOG.

The Council called once again on the parties to carry out Resolution 598 of 1987 at once. That text had demanded the cease-fire and a settlement of the war. UNIIMOG's mandate was extended for a further six months, until 31 March 1990. At the end of that period, the Secretary-General had to report on developments. His report also had to cover the steps taken to put Resolution 598 into effect. Renewals like this one kept the observers in place while diplomacy moved slowly.

Azerbaijan's bid reached the Council as war clouds gathered in 1992. On 14 February, it adopted Resolution 742 without a vote. The Azerbaijani Republic had declared its freedom restored the autumn before. The Soviet Union had just broken apart. Former Soviet lands rushed to claim seats and standing. The Nagorno-Karabakh conflict was heating up at the same time.

Having weighed the bid, the Council urges the Assembly to admit Azerbaijan. The Assembly did so on 2 March 1992. Membership gave the new state a world platform at a hard moment. War with Armenia was growing fiercer by the month. The seat let Baku plead its case to all states at once.
villars-comte-de-gabalis-1742:
The Abbe de Villars wrote this small French book on the Count of Gabalis, first in 1670. The text here is the 1742 print, in French. Villars was a priest with a taste for the occult lore of his age.

The Count tells a young priest of the beings of the four elements: nymphs of water, sylphs of air, and their kin. He holds that these beings seek to wed men, to gain souls that last for ever. The book fed the lore of elementals to all Europe, and gave Fouque his Undine.
vyse-operations-pyramids-gizeh-vol-3-184:
Survey notes and odd scraps round out Richard William Howard Vyse's record in Vol. 3 of his Operations, out in 1842. The first tomes told the dig of 1837 and showed its plans. This last tome is a store of sums, lists, and short tracts by hands who worked on the site in those years.

Few fans read a store room cover to cover. Yet digs that came next mined these pages for sums no one else had kept. The tome ends the first full record of work on the heaps. Its worth is in its facts.
widger-s-quotations-from-the-project-gut: David Widger gathers the brightest lines from the memoirs of Casanova. The famous lover's wit, charm, and sharp eye for people shine here. Each quote captures a moment of his storied life. A treasury for fans of the great adventurer.
